selection: Round 1 was an online aptitude test (quant, logical, and a tiny English paragraph) that lasted 45 mins. Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked basic chemical engineering concepts – material balance, corrosion basics and a quick problem on heat exchangers. I fumbled a bit on the heat exchanger but managed to explain the theory. Round 3 was the usual HR chat – introduce urself, why Hindalco, salary expectations and a bit of relocation talk for Kolkata.
preparation: Did a week of aptitude from Indiabix and a couple of GFG sets on basic chemistry formulas. Watched a few YouTube videos on material balance and read the first 3 chapters of my 2nd year textbook. Seniors gave me a copy of their old interview questions and a quick mock HR session.
experience: Overall it was okay – the aptitude was straight forward, the technical was a bit too niche for a campus placement but manageable. HR guys were friendly, though a bit repetitive. SPOC helped when the OA link kept crashing.
advice: Brush up on core chemical concepts, not just the textbook examples. Practice aptitude in timed mode, because the online portal can be laggy. Be ready with a short story about why you want to work in aluminium sector.
tips: dont over‑prepare on fancy topics – basic equations and clear explanations win. Keep a pen and a calculator handy during OA. Talk slowly in HR, it shows confidence.

selection: The whole UIUC process had 5 steps. First was a referral email from a senior who knew a professor – that got me past the initial screen. Second was a core CS written test (data structures, algorithms and a couple of probability q's). Third came a coding OA on LeetCode style – 2 problems, one medium array and one hard graph. Fourth was a technical interview with a faculty panel where they dug into my projects, linear regression and asked me to explain a CNN architecture. Fifth was the final admission interview where they asked about my SOP, GRE scores and LORs. I got the admit after clearing all of them.
preparation: Spent 2 months on Striver DSA sheet (≈200 problems) plus daily LeetCode easy/medium. GRE prep was 3 hrs/week on Magoosh, wrote two drafts of SOP with help from a senior. Collected LORs early – asked my thesis guide and a summer internship manager. Also revisited core subjects using NPTEL videos.
experience: It felt like a marathon – the referral made the first hurdle easy but the core test was tough, especially the probability part. Coding OA timed me out on the graph problem, but I managed to get partial credit. Technical interview was intense but the faculty were encouraging. The final interview was more like a chat about my future goals.
advice: Don’t ignore the non‑coding parts – GRE, SOP and LORs matter a lot. Practice core CS concepts, not just coding. Get a referral if possible, it cuts down one round.
tips: Start GRE prep early, aim for 320+. Keep a one‑page SOP template and tweak per program. Do mock interviews with seniors – they know the faculty style. And sleep well before the OA!

selection: Only 1 round – a puzzle‑heavy OA followed by a quick HR chat. The OA had 3 logic puzzles (like river crossing and a seating arrangement) and a short coding question on arrays. I solved 2 puzzles, missed the third, but still cleared the OA. Then the HR guy asked about my B.Tech, why consulting, and my availability. Ended with an offer and they mentioned a PPO after 6 months if I perform well.
preparation: Did a bunch of puzzle books from my brother, practiced GFG puzzles and solved a few LeetCode easy array problems. Also read a couple of ZS interview experiences on Quora. My seniors gave me a cheat‑sheet of typical ZS puzzles.
experience: The puzzles were weird but fun, felt like a brain teaser session. The HR person was chill, just wanted to know my timeline. Got the offer quickly – within a week.
advice: Practice logical puzzles daily, even the weird ones. For the coding part, stick to O(N) array problems. Show enthusiasm for consulting in HR.
tips: keep a timer while solving puzzles, it trains speed. Have a short intro ready – why consulting after ECE. And smile, HR notices confidence.

selection: Round 1: HR screening call – basic intro, CGPA check and why I want to join Mercedes‑Benz R&D. Round 2: Core technical interview on structural analysis, soil mechanics and a mini‑case on bridge design. Round 3: A group discussion with 3 other candidates on a sustainability topic. Round 4: Technical interview with a senior engineer – they asked me to sketch a reinforced concrete beam and discuss load calculations. Round 5: Final HR round – salary expectations, relocation to Kolkata and a quick personality test.
preparation: Re‑read my 3rd year civil notes, solved past NITK core questions from GATE prep, and did a couple of mock GD sessions with my batchmates. For HR, I practiced common questions with seniors and recorded myself answering to improve fluency. Also brushed up on basic automobile R&D topics from a YouTube playlist.
experience: The process was long but organized. Core interview was tough, especially the beam sketch, but I managed. GD was a bit chaotic, some candidates talked too much. HR rounds were smooth, they were polite.
advice: Don’t skip the GD prep – it’s part of the evaluation. For core, focus on fundamentals, not just formulae. Have clear reasons for wanting to work in automotive R&D, not just “good salary”.
tips: Carry a pen and graph paper to the technical interview – they love sketches. Keep your answers concise in GD, let others speak. And ask about relocation support early on.

selection: Round 1: Resume shortlisting – the SPOC sent an email asking for my latest resume and a 1‑page project summary. Round 2: Core interview – they dug into chemical process design, thermodynamics and asked me to solve a simple mass balance on a reactor. Round 3: HR round – typical “tell me about urself”, strengths/weaknesses, and why Vedanta Pune.
preparation: Polished my resume with help from the career cell, added a concise project description. Did a quick GFG brush‑up on thermodynamics equations and practiced a few mass balance problems from my 4th year notes. For HR, rehearsed answers with a senior who had done Vedanta before.
experience: Resume round was painless, they just wanted a PDF. Core interview was moderate – I stumbled on a specific unit conversion but recovered. HR was friendly, they even asked about my hobbies.
advice: Make your resume one‑page and highlight any industry‑relevant project. Review core chemical formulas before the interview, especially units. Show genuine interest in mining and metals sector.
tips: keep a cheat‑sheet of common unit conversions handy for the interview. Practice a quick 2‑minute self‑intro. And smile – HR remembers it.

selection: 4 rounds. Round 1: Aptitude test online. Round 2: DSA round with 2 coding problems and a debugging section. Round 3: ML round with questions about my ML internship project, loss functions, gradient descent. Round 4: Personal interview with questions about my research and why I want to go to UIUC.
preparation: Leetcode (around 300 problems), ML from the book Hands On ML plus my internship experience. Mocks with 3 seniors before the interviews. GRE prep with ETS materials.
experience: Very intense but the interviewers were professional and friendly. The ML round was a bit scary but I had done my prep well.
advice: Have a clear 2 min summary of ur ML project. Practice implementing basic algorithms without libraries.
tips: Ask seniors for referrals early, it really helps with shortlisting. After that its all u. Sleep well before interviews, seriously.

selection: 5 rounds. Round 1: Aptitude test online. Round 2: DSA round with 2 coding problems and a debugging section. Round 3: Core concepts round with questions about power systems and control theory. Round 4: Personal interview with questions about my projects and why I want to go to TU Munich. Round 5: Bar raiser with LP questions and a design question.
preparation: Leetcode (around 300 problems), core concepts from my textbooks and revision. Mocks with 3 seniors before the interviews. GRE prep with ETS materials.

selection: 2 rounds. Round 1: Aptitude test online. Round 2: Puzzles round with 10 puzzles and a debugging section. They also asked about my project and why I want to join ZS Associates.
preparation: Not really, since cgpa is low i just wanted to get something. Did a few mock tests and basic python practice.
experience: The whole thing was kind of disorganised, long waiting in the hall without updates and the interview lasted like 10 minutes. Stipend is not great either.
advice: Communicate the schedule better and dont make everyone wait all day.
tips: If ur cgpa is low like 6, just keep applying to mass recruiters and dont get demotivated. It's tough but there is a place for everyone. Work on projects so u have something to talk about.

selection: 4 rounds. Round 1: OA with 2 coding problems and a debugging section plus work simulation. Round 2: DSA + OS round - asked a heap problem, then what is a deadlock, difference between process and thread, how does virtual memory work, paging vs segmentation. Round 3: OOPs round, they asked about my OOPs project, inheritance, polymorphism, and a coding problem implementing a basic OOPs concept. Round 4: HR round with questions about my hobbies and why I want to join TCS.
preparation: Leetcode (around 300 problems), OS from Galvin notes and revision, OOPs from my textbooks and revision. Mocks with 3 seniors before the interviews.
experience: Very intense but the interviewers were professional and friendly. The OOPs round was a bit scary but I had done my prep well.
advice: Have a clear 2 min summary of ur OOPs project. Practice implementing basic algorithms without libraries.
tips: Ask seniors for referrals early, it really helps with shortlisting. After that its all u. Sleep well before interviews, seriously.

selection: 5 rounds. Round 1: Aptitude test online. Round 2: DSA round with 2 coding problems and a debugging section. Round 3: Core concepts round with questions about data structures and algorithms. Round 4: Personal interview with questions about my projects and why I want to join Texas Instruments. Round 5: HR round with questions about my hobbies and why I want to join Texas Instruments.
preparation: Leetcode (around 300 problems), core concepts from my textbooks and revision. Mocks with 3 seniors before the interviews.

selection: 5 rounds total. Round 1 was a brutal OA with 3 sections: 2 leetcode mediums, 10 DBMS mcqs, and 2 OOPs theory qs. Round 2 was a 1:1 DSA round where they asked striver sheet problems like next permutation and kth smallest in BST. Round 3 was a system design round where they asked to design a distributed cache. Round 4 was a lowkey HR round where they asked about my projects and why Arista. Round 5 was a final interview with a director where they asked about my internship at a startup and how I handled conflicts.
preparation: did leetcode daily for 3 months, finished striver sheet twice. Revised DBMS from gate smashers videos and made notes. OOPs was from college notes. Seniors helped with system design prep.
experience: felt like a marathon. Interviewers were chill but the OA was tough. Got the result in 3 days which was a relief.
advice: dont skip the basics. Arista loves DSA and system design so be ready.
tips: practice mock interviews with seniors. Also, keep ur resume updated with projects and internships.

selection: 5 rounds. Round 1 was an aptitude test with 60 qs in 60 mins. Round 2 was a coding round with 2 qs: one on arrays and one on strings. Round 3 was a technical interview where they asked OOPs concepts and DBMS basics. Round 4 was a group discussion round where they gave a random topic. Round 5 was an HR round where they asked about my family background and why Wipro.
preparation: did aptitude on indiabix and m4maths. For coding, did GFG and leetcode easy-mediums. OOPs and DBMS were revised from college notes.
experience: felt like a grind. The GD round was the most random part. Got the result in a week which was okay.
advice: dont underestimate the aptitude round. Wipro loves their aptitude tests.
tips: practice time management for aptitude. Also, keep ur resume simple and to the point.

selection: 2 rounds. Round 1 was an OA with 3 sections: 2 leetcode mediums, 10 DBMS mcqs, and a case study on data analysis. Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked about my projects and a few OOPs concepts. They also asked me to explain a data science project I did in my internship.
preparation: did leetcode and GFG for DSA. Revised DBMS from gate smashers videos. For the case study, practiced with seniors who gave me random business problems.
experience: felt like a breeze compared to other companies. Interviewers were friendly and the case study was fun.
advice: be ready to explain ur projects in detail. They love that.
tips: practice explaining ur projects clearly. Also, keep ur resume updated with relevant projects.

selection: 1 round. It was a resume-based interview where they asked about my projects, internships, and core subjects like thermodynamics and material science. They also asked about my summer training at a steel plant. No coding or aptitude, just a chill discussion.
preparation: revised all core subjects from college notes. Prepared for common questions about my projects and internships. Seniors helped with resume review.
experience: felt like a walk in the park. Interviewers were super chill and the discussion was more about my interests than technical qs.
advice: just be confident and explain ur projects well. They care more about ur passion than ur grades.
tips: keep ur resume updated with all relevant projects and internships. Also, practice explaining ur projects clearly.

selection: 2 rounds. Round 1 was a technical round where they asked core ECE subjects like power systems, control systems, and digital electronics. Round 2 was an HR round where they asked about my family background, why L&T, and my plans for the future. They also mentioned my PPO from a summer internship at a power plant.
preparation: revised all core subjects from college notes. Prepared for common HR questions with seniors. Also, revised my PPO project details.
experience: felt like a mix of technical and personal. Interviewers were friendly and the HR round was more about getting to know me.
advice: be honest about ur plans and interests. They care about ur fit in the company.
tips: practice explaining ur projects and internships clearly. Also, keep ur resume updated with all relevant details.

selection: 5 rounds total. round1 was a quick referral chat (senior from NITK gave me a call, just a few mins). round2 was an online test on core subjects (DSA + maths + statistics) on Hackerearth, 60 mins. round3 was a technical interview where they asked me to explain my semester projects (predictive maintenance & sentiment analysis) and threw a couple of medium DSA problems. round4 was HR where they asked about why UIUC, my GRE scores and future goals. round5 was the final admission interview with a professor panel – they dug into my SOP and LORs and asked a few research‑oriented questions.
preparation: did striver A‑Z sheet daily + leetcode easy‑medium for 2 months. brushed up core subjects from our 3rd yr notes (linear algebra, probability). started GRE prep 3 weeks before – vocab apps, quant practice from Magoosh. wrote SOP after reading a few blogs, got feedback from seniors and a prof. asked two professors for LORs early. also polished my project demos and made a short video for the referral senior.
experience: felt super nervous in the online test but managed to finish. the technical interview was chill because the interviewer liked my project and gave hints. HR was generic but they seemed impressed with my GRE 322. the final panel was intense – they asked about a paper I read, but I managed to answer.
advice: don’t underestimate the GRE part even if you think the university cares only about coding. have a clear story for each project and be ready to link it to data‑science topics. also, get your SOP reviewed by someone who has been through US grad admissions.
tips: start GRE prep early, set a target score (320+). practice coding under timed conditions – use a timer like in real OA. keep a 1‑page project summary ready (problem, tech stack, impact). ask a senior for a referral, it saves a lot of hassle.

selection: 5 rounds. round1: resume screening – they called me after seeing my GitHub and a referral from a senior. round2: online aptitude + basic DSA (2 coding q’s) on HackerRank, 45 mins. round3: technical interview – deep dive into my ML project (image classification) and a couple of data‑structures problems. round4: HR chat about why CS, my GRE and future research interests. round5: final interview with a professor where they asked about my SOP and a few theory questions (algorithms & probability).
preparation: cracked striver sheet + leetcode 2 hrs daily. revisited CS fundamentals from our 4th sem (algorithms, operating systems). GRE prep with Magoosh for 1.5 months, focused on quant. wrote SOP after reading UIUC CS blog, got it edited by a senior who got his MS there. asked two profs for LORs and sent them my project repo link.
experience: the OA was easy, I solved both q’s in 12 mins. technical interview was a bit tough – they asked me to optimise my model pipeline, but I managed to explain trade‑offs. HR was standard. the professor interview felt like a mini‑thesis defense, but I was ready.
advice: if you list a project, be ready to discuss every design choice. GRE score matters more for CS than for Data‑Science, so aim for 325+. keep your SOP concise – 1 page max, no fluff.
tips: use a spreadsheet to track GRE vocab words. practice explaining your project to a non‑technical friend – helps for interview clarity. keep a cheat‑sheet of core CS formulas (big‑O, memory hierarchy).

selection: 3 rounds. round1: OA on Hackerearth – 2 coding q’s (one medium DSA, one easy system‑design style where we had to design a notification service). round2: system‑design interview – they asked me to design a real‑time feed ranking system, I sketched high‑level components and talked about scaling. round3: HR + PPO discussion – they talked about intern‑to‑PPO path, compensation and next steps.
preparation: solved Striver sheet + leetcode medium for 1.5 months. watched System Design Primer videos on YouTube and read Grokking the System Design Interview. practiced OA on Hackerearth every weekend. asked a senior who interned last year for a referral and got some insider tips. brushed up basics of databases and caching.
experience: OA was okay – the DSA q was a bit tricky but I used two‑pointer technique. system‑design round was fun, the interviewer liked my use of Kafka & Redis. HR was straightforward, they mentioned a PPO if I clear the intern project.
advice: don’t just memorize system‑design answers, understand why you pick a particular tech. be ready to talk about trade‑offs and cost. also, if you get a referral, mention it early – it speeds up the process.
tips: keep a one‑page cheat‑sheet of common design patterns (micro‑services, caching, load balancer). practice coding on a plain text editor to simulate OA environment. ask clarifying questions in design interview – they love that.

selection: 4 rounds. round1: online aptitude test (quant + logical reasoning) on TalentSprint, 40 mins. round2: case‑study interview – they gave a small data‑problem (customer churn) and asked how to approach it, what metrics to use. round3: technical interview – 2 DSA coding questions (one array, one graph) and a quick talk about my Kaggle project. round4: HR round – behavioural questions and salary discussion.
preparation: did GFG aptitude practice for 3 weeks, focused on speed. solved a few case‑study examples from consulting prep sites. leetcode easy‑medium for DSA, especially arrays & graphs. refined my Kaggle project (sales forecast) and prepared a 2‑minute pitch. asked a senior who works at an analytics firm for interview tips.
experience: aptitude test was a bit stressful, I made a couple of silly mistakes. case‑study was interesting – they liked my suggestion of using XGBoost and ROC‑AUC. technical round went smooth, I solved both coding q’s. HR was friendly, they talked about work‑life balance.
advice: for Mu Sigma, they care a lot about business sense. practice turning a data problem into a story. also, speed matters in aptitude – use shortcut formulas.
tips: keep a list of common metrics (accuracy, precision, recall, F1, ROC‑AUC) ready. practice mental math tricks for quant. rehearse your project story in front of a mirror.

selection: 3 rounds. round1: HR screening – they asked about my CGPA, why banking, and a few situational questions. round2: DSA coding interview on Codility – 2 problems (one string manipulation, one DP). round3: final round – mix of technical (talk about my IoT project) and HR (PPO prospects, location preference).
preparation: revamped my resume with help from the placement cell, highlighted projects. solved Striver sheet + leetcode medium for 1 month focusing on strings & DP. read up about Deutsche Bank’s tech stack (Java, Kafka) from their tech blog. practiced mock HR calls with seniors.
experience: HR screen was quick, they seemed impressed with my 9.24 CGPA. coding round was tough – the DP question took me 30 mins but I finally got it. final round was nice, the interviewer appreciated my IoT project and discussed possible PPO after the internship.
advice: show genuine interest in finance tech – know a bit about trading systems or risk analytics. even if you’re from CSE, connect your projects to banking use‑cases.
tips: prepare 2‑3 bullet points linking each project to finance (e.g., real‑time data processing). practice DP on paper before the interview. keep a polite but confident tone in HR chats.

selection: OA was easy, 2 questions on DSA, 1 on OOPs. Round 1 was a technical interview, mostly on digital electronics. Round 2 was HR, introduce urself, strengths/weaknesses, relocation, etc. They asked about my projects in the HR round.
preparation: DSA from leetcode, OOPs from GFG. Digital electronics from my course notes.
experience: Easy to medium. Interviewers were nice, asked me to explain my projects clearly.
advice: Revise DSA, OOPs, and core thoroughly. Be confident in english.
tips: Do not take a safe company lightly, many get rejected because of careless OA. Treat each interview as practice.

selection: OA was aptitude + 2 coding questions (easy-medium). Round 1 was a technical interview, mostly on machine learning. Round 2 was a case study, and Round 3 was HR, introduce urself, strengths/weaknesses, relocation, etc. They asked about my projects in the HR round.
preparation: Aptitude 1 hour a day for a week. Coding from leetcode. Machine learning from a youtube playlist. Asked a CSE friend to take a mock for me.
experience: Honestly good, interviewers did not treat me differently for being non-CSE. Waiting for results was the painful part.
advice: Non-CS branches should show some skill clearly on resume (ML/Python) so they dont drop u in the resume screen.
tips: Dont feel bad about branch. Core companies for mining come very few, so apply to IT services also if u are ok with it. :) Start hackerrank practice early, the OA UI is awkward.

selection: OA was 3 questions on DSA, 2 on ML. Round 1 was a technical interview, mostly on ML. Round 2 was a case study, Round 3 was a technical interview on CN, and Round 4 was HR, introduce urself, strengths/weaknesses, relocation, etc. They asked about my projects in the HR round.

experience: Easy to medium. Interviewers were nice, asked me to explain my projects clearly.
advice: Revise DSA, ML, and CN thoroughly. Be confident in english.

selection: OA was 2 questions on DSA, 1 on core. Round 1 was a technical interview, mostly on core. Round 2 was a case study, Round 3 was a technical interview on projects, Round 4 was a case study, and Round 5 was HR, introduce urself, strengths/weaknesses, relocation, etc. They asked about my projects in the HR round.

selection: Microsoft VLSI placement had 5 rounds: 1) Online coding test with DSA and bit manipulation questions, 2) Technical interview on digital electronics and microelectronics basics, 3) Another coding round with system design lite (design a simple ALU), 4) HR round on relocation and bond, 5) Final interview with hiring manager about projects and future plans. Took 3 days to get result.
preparation: Did leetcode mediums for DSA, brushed up on digital electronics from NPTEL, watched some system design videos for the ALU question. Seniors helped with the VLSI specific stuff.
experience: Interviewers were chill but strict on fundamentals. The ALU design was tough but they guided me when i got stuck. Overall good experience but the process was long.
advice: Dont ignore ur core subjects even if u r in ECE. Microsoft expects strong fundamentals in digital and microelectronics.
tips: Practice bit manipulation and digital logic questions. Also, be ready to explain ur projects in detail.

selection: Accenture Analyst placement had 2 rounds: 1) Online assessment with aptitude, english and basic programming questions, 2) HR round where they asked about projects, internships and why Accenture. Result came in a week.
preparation: Did some aptitude prep from indiabix, revised basic C and java from GFG. Seniors gave me their SPOC links for mock OAs.
experience: Pretty straightforward. The OA was easy but the HR round was a bit random with questions like 'tell me about a time u failed'.
advice: Accenture cares more about ur soft skills and projects than ur CGPA. Keep ur resume clean and updated.
tips: Practice aptitude and english. Also, be ready to explain ur projects in simple terms.

selection: Hindustan Unilever Process Engineer placement had 2 rounds: 1) Online test with aptitude, technical questions on fluid mechanics and thermodynamics, 2) Technical interview with panel asking about core subjects and a case study on process optimization. Result in 3 days.
preparation: Revised core subjects from notes, did some aptitude prep. Seniors shared their notes on process engineering topics.
experience: The technical interview was tough but the panel was supportive. The case study was interesting but i messed up the calculations a bit.
advice: They really want to see ur understanding of core subjects. Dont skip classes for core subjects.
tips: Revise ur core subjects thoroughly. Also, practice case studies on process optimization.

selection: Oracle ML Engineer placement had 2 rounds: 1) Referral shortlist then an OA with DSA and OS questions, 2) Technical interview with coding and ML basics. Result in 2 days.
preparation: Did Striver sheet for DSA, revised OS from a lecture series. Seniors helped with the ML basics part.
experience: The OA was tough but the interview was chill. They asked about my ML projects and some basic ML concepts.
advice: Be good with DSA and OS. Oracle expects strong fundamentals in both.
tips: Practice DSA questions and revise OS concepts. Also, be ready to explain ur ML projects in detail.

selection: Intuit SDE placement had 2 rounds: 1) Online coding test with DSA questions, 2) Technical interview with coding and resume discussion. Result in a week.
preparation: Did leetcode mediums and hard, revised OOPs and system design basics. Seniors shared their OA experiences and prep tips.
experience: The coding test was tough but the interview was smooth. They asked about my projects and some DSA questions.
advice: Intuit cares about ur problem-solving skills. Be good with DSA and ur projects.
tips: Practice DSA questions and revise ur projects thoroughly. Also, be ready to explain ur thought process while coding.

selection: Round 1: a 45‑min online coding test focused on OS concepts (process scheduling, deadlocks) plus a quick 10‑question aptitude section. Round 2: HR + PPO chat where they asked about my summer stint at Sprinklr research and how I handled a kernel bug. Since I already had a PPO, the tech interview was just a formality.
preparation: brushed up OS notes from my semester, solved a few GFG OS questions, and revisited the code I wrote during my intern project. Did some light aptitude practice on indiaBIX just to be safe.
experience: the coding test was a bit tricky cause they love edge‑case questions, but the HR person was chill and actually asked about my intern learnings, which felt good.
advice: if u have a PPO, highlight the exact things you delivered there, it can turn the HR round into a win. Also don't ignore the OS part – many think it's easy but they dig deep.
tips: keep a one‑pager of your intern achievements (numbers, impact) ready. practice at least 5 OS MCQs a day before the test, and solve a couple of LeetCode medium problems to stay sharp on DSA basics.

selection: Round 1: OA with 2 ML‑flavoured coding problems (matrix multiplication optimisation and a simple regression on a synthetic dataset) plus a short situational questionnaire. Round 2: technical interview where they probed my understanding of ML pipelines, feature engineering and asked me to explain a recent Kaggle project I did.
preparation: finished the Striver sheet for core DSA, then switched to ML – went through Coursera ML course notes, did GFG "Machine Learning" articles, and re‑ran my Kaggle notebooks. Also practiced a few coding OA on HackerRank.
experience: the OA was moderate – time limit a bit tight but doable. interviewers were friendly, they liked that i could talk about data preprocessing without rambling.
advice: be ready to discuss a real ML project end‑to‑end, not just theory. also, brush up on python libraries (pandas, sklearn) because they love quick code snippets.
tips: keep a cheat‑sheet of common ML algorithms with time‑complexities. solve at least one end‑to‑end ML problem a week before the interview. ask seniors who cleared Cisco for their OA experiences.

selection: Round 1: GRE verification interview – they asked about my scores, study plan and why I want US grad studies. Round 2: SOP review session with a faculty member where I defended my research interest in Materials Science. Round 3: LOR discussion – my professors gave a brief on my project work and asked me to elaborate on my role. Round 4: final admission interview – a mix of ML knowledge (for materials informatics) and project deep‑dive, plus a few generic "why UIUC" questions.
preparation: spent summer prepping for GRE (Magoosh + practice tests), wrote multiple drafts of SOP focusing on my ML‑driven materials project, collected LORs early from my supervisors, and revisited my senior year capstone to be able to explain every detail.
experience: the process felt academic and a bit stressful, especially the LOR chat, but overall the interviewers were supportive and seemed genuinely interested in my research ideas.
advice: don't treat SOP as a generic essay – tailor it to UIUC's labs. also, be ready to discuss how ML can help material discovery, they love that cross‑disciplinary angle.
tips: make a one‑page bullet list of your projects (objective, methodology, results) to quickly reference during interviews. schedule mock GRE speaking sessions with friends. keep all your transcripts and certificates organized in a folder.

selection: Single round: a 60‑min combined OA that covered aptitude (logical reasoning, quantitative), a short DSA segment (array & string problem) and a quick HR questionnaire at the end asking about my expectations and campus placement preferences.
preparation: did daily aptitude drills on IndiaBIX, solved a couple of LeetCode easy‑mediums for DSA, and skimmed through TCS past papers. Also kept a short note of my ECE projects to answer HR quickly.
experience: the test felt rushed because they jammed everything together, but the HR part was just a few checkbox questions, so not too bad.
advice: manage time well – allocate 30 mins for aptitude, 20 for coding, 10 for HR. Even if you’re strong in DSA, the aptitude can kill you if you’re slow.
tips: practice full‑length mock OAs that mix aptitude + coding. keep a timer. have a one‑sentence answer ready for the HR questionnaire (e.g., "looking for growth & learning opportunities").

selection: Round 1: single technical round, mostly core metallurgy ques (phase diagrams, heat treatment, material properties). Asked about my final year project on alloys. No coding, no HR. Offer in 2 days.

experience: felt like a walk in the park compared to other companies. interviewers were very supportive.
advice: core companies for metallurgy are rare, so dont stress too much. just be clear with ur core subjects.

selection: Round 1: aptitude + 2 coding ques (easy). Round 2: technical, OOPs and basic DSA (arrays, strings). Round 3: PPO conversion round, more DSA and system design basics. Round 4: HR, general questions. Offer in 3 days.
preparation: did leetcode easy-medium for 2 months, striver sheet for DSA. OOPs from geeksforgeeks. seniors helped with resume review.

selection: Round1 was a 45‑min online assessment – DSA questions from leetcode easy/medium and a couple of networking MCQs (OSI layers, TCP handshake). Round2 was a live coding on a whiteboard (binary tree traversal + a simple socket program). Round3: a 30‑min technical interview focused on core ECE – RF basics and signal integrity, they even asked about antenna gain. Round4: a short HR chat where they talked about PPO chances (they said if you clear all rounds they will convert the offer). Round5: final HR/HR‑L1 where they discussed stipend, location and asked a couple of behavioural questions.
preparation: Started late summer, did the Striver DSA sheet daily, solved networking problems from GFG and watched NPTEL CN videos. Practised OOP basics for the coding round, and brushed up RF notes from 3rd year. Also read some senior's interview experiences on campus forum.
experience: first round was nerve‑wrecking, the network MCQs caught me off guard but I survived. coding round felt okay cause I had practiced trees. technical interview was intense – professor‑like questions, but I managed to explain my project on SDR. HR rounds were chill, they were friendly and kept mentioning PPO which gave me hope. overall mixed – tiring but rewarding.
advice: Don’t ignore the core ECE stuff even if it’s a software role. they love to test your fundamentals. keep a one‑pager of your projects ready for the HR guys. if they mention PPO, ask about the timeline – it shows interest.
tips: Start prepping DSA 2‑3 months before. mix leetcode with GFG networking quizzes. talk to seniors who cleared Boeing – they have the exact question bank. stay hydrated on the day of the OA, and remember to breathe.

selection: Round1: a short 20‑min HR screen where they asked about my CGPA, why chemical and what I did in labs. Round2: a single technical interview – they dug into my final year project (process simulation) and threw a couple of case‑study questions on plant safety and cost optimisation.
preparation: Focused on project details – re‑read my thesis, prepared a 2‑minute pitch. Practised common HR questions on indiabix and brushed up basic chemical engineering concepts from GATE prep notes. No heavy coding, just some logical aptitude.
experience: HR was friendly, they just wanted to see if I was a team player. Technical felt like a chat with a senior consultant – they asked me to explain a distillation column diagram, which I could do because I had the slides handy. overall smooth, no surprise rounds.
advice: Make your project the star – have clear numbers, challenges, and what you contributed. For HR, be ready with a short story about a lab mishap you fixed – it shows problem‑solving.
tips: Don’t ignore the little HR round – they can be a make‑or‑break. Keep a one‑page summary of your project and rehearse it. If you’re low on CGPA, highlight internships or certifications.

selection: Round1: OA – 60‑min online test with 3 DSA sections (arrays, graphs, DP) and 2 OOP questions (inheritance, polymorphism). Round2: technical interview – a deep dive into my internship at a startup, plus a live coding problem on hash maps and a design question about building a simple CRM system. Round3: final HR round – salary negotiation, cultural fit and a quick resume walkthrough.
preparation: Did the Striver sheet religiously, solved at least 2 graph problems daily. For OOP, revisited Java design patterns from GFG. Built a mini‑CRM on my laptop to have a real example for the design question. Also polished my resume with bullet points and got it reviewed by seniors who got into Salesforce before.
experience: OA was brutal – the DP question ate half my time, but I survived. technical interview was intense; the interviewer liked my startup story and asked me to optimise a query, which I could do because I had rehearsed. HR was relaxed, they even joked about the Bangalore traffic. got the offer same day – super happy!
advice: Treat the OA as a mini‑contest – time‑box each question. For the design round, have a small project you can talk about, it saves you from winging it. Salary talk: know the market rates for Hyderabad SDEs.
tips: Start OA prep 2 months early, mix leetcode medium + hard. Keep a cheat‑sheet of OOP concepts. Practice mock HR calls with friends – it builds confidence.

selection: Round1: Online assessment – 40 DSA problems (mix of arrays, trees, strings) and a short OS quiz (process states, deadlock). Round2: technical interview – they asked me to write a producer‑consumer solution in C++ and discuss memory management. Round3: another technical – deep dive into operating systems, especially scheduling algorithms, plus a networking question (TCP flow control). Round4: HR interview – behavioural questions and discussion about campus life. Round5: final HR‑HR round where they went through compensation, relocation and asked a couple of brain‑teaser puzzles.
preparation: Did the Striver DSA sheet for 2 hrs daily, solved OS questions from GATE notes, watched NPTEL videos on process synchronization. Practised C++ STL and wrote a few producer‑consumer programs. Also read senior’s experiences on Oracle placements for HR style questions.
experience: OA was long – I ran out of time on the last few problems but cleared the cutoff. technical rounds were tough; the first one felt like a coding marathon, the second was pure OS theory – I was glad I revised deadlock detection. HR guys were chill, they asked about my hobbies and why NITK. final HR was just paperwork, but they threw a puzzle about crossing a river which I solved after a minute.
advice: Balance DSA and core CS prep – Oracle loves OS and networking fundamentals. For coding, focus on writing clean code fast. During HR, be genuine; they can sense rehearsed answers.
tips: Create a weekly schedule: 3 days DSA, 2 days OS/CS, 1 day mock interview. Use GFG for OS MCQs. Keep a list of your projects ready for quick reference.

selection: Round1: OA – 50‑min test with 2 coding problems (arrays + greedy) and a short OOP quiz (encapsulation, abstract classes). Round2: technical interview – they gave me a real‑world scenario to design a tax‑calculation module, asked me to write code on the whiteboard and discuss scalability. Round3: HR round – salary expectations, cultural fit and a quick recap of my resume.
preparation: Followed the Striver DSA sheet for 1.5 hrs daily, solved greedy problems from leetcode. brushed up OOP concepts from GFG and wrote a few design snippets in Java. Updated my resume with impact metrics and asked a senior who got into Intuit for feedback. Did a mock HR with a friend.
experience: OA was okay, the greedy question was tricky but I remembered the interval scheduling pattern. technical interview was the highlight – the interviewer liked my approach to break the problem into modules and asked follow‑up on test coverage. HR was relaxed, they joked about Bangalore’s monsoon and asked about my long‑term goals. got the offer next week – felt relieved.
advice: For the OA, practice time‑management – don’t spend >15 min on a single problem. In the design round, speak aloud your thought process; they love hearing the trade‑offs. Salary talk – know the Bangalore market, don’t undervalue yourself.
tips: Mix leetcode with GFG design questions. Keep a one‑page cheat sheet of OOP principles. Practice explaining a project in <2 minutes – it’s gold for HR.

selection: OA with 2 coding questions and 1 MCQ section. First coding question was easy, but the second was a bit tough and required a good approach. MCQs were easy, but a few of them were tricky. Overall, the OA was decent.
preparation: Did the striver sheet for DSA. Practiced a few mock tests for aptitude. Worked on my projects and updated my resume.
experience: The OA was decent, but I felt a bit underprepared for the second coding question. Overall, I think I did well.
advice: Focus on your DSA skills. Work on your projects and keep your resume updated. Don't stress too much about the MCQs, they are usually easy.
tips: For DSA, focus on the striver sheet. For aptitude, practice mock tests. For projects, make sure they are relevant to the role you are applying for.

selection: round 1 was an online aptitude test (quant, logical & a bit of data‑interpretation) lasting 45 mins. round 2 was a technical interview where they dug deep into my chemical projects – especially the process‑optimisation one I did in 2nd year and the little data‑analytics demo I built with python. round 3 was a short HR chat, they asked about why analytics, my campus‑life and salary expectations.

tips: keep your project slides ready, explain the impact in 2‑3 mins. practice speed‑math for aptitude and do a mock OA a day before. dont forget to ask about training programs during HR.

selection: first round was a core technical interview – they asked about thermodynamics, material‑strength and a couple of design‑calculations (shaft design, stress analysis). second round was HR + PPO discussion – they talked about campus culture, relocation to Kolkata and the possibility of a PPO after 6 months if you clear the probation.
preparation: re‑read my core mech notes, solved past year papers from the college SPOC and did a quick GFG revision of strength formulas. also chatted with seniors who cleared Coal India last year, they gave me a list of typical core questions. for HR I read up on the company's recent mining projects on their website.

advice: more practice problems on machine‑design would help, and a clearer roadmap for PPO eligibility would be great.
tips: make a cheat‑sheet of key equations, practice solving them on a whiteboard. be ready to talk about any lab work you did – it shows hands‑on vibe. ask about the PPO timeline in HR.

selection: round 1 – a 60 min OA on hacker‑rank with 2 DSA problems (one array, one graph) and a tiny ML‑theory MCQ. round 2 – a pure DSA interview, medium‑hard LeetCode style (binary‑tree dp and sliding window). round 3 – an ML round where they asked about basic regression, overfitting and a mini‑case on sensor‑data cleaning. round 4 – a system‑design style chat (design a data‑pipeline for VLSI test logs). round 5 – HR round, salary, relocation to Bangalore and some behavioural q’s.
preparation: finished the Striver's DSA sheet, did daily LeetCode medium practice, and watched Andrew Ng’s ML course for fundamentals. also solved a few OA mock tests on CodeSignal and read GFG ML cheat‑sheets. seniors gave me a list of typical system‑design topics for hardware data pipelines.
experience: the OA was a bit time‑pressured but manageable. DSA interview was tough, I fumbled on the dp but recovered. ML round felt okay because I had brushed up basics. overall a roller‑coaster, but the HR guys were super nice.
advice: the OA could be a bit more balanced between coding and ML – sometimes the MCQs feel random. also a quick intro about the VLSI team would help candidates align expectations.
tips: do at least 3 full‑length OA mocks a week before. keep a one‑page summary of ML concepts (bias‑variance, regularisation). practice explaining a system design in 5 mins – draw on paper.

selection: round 1 – online OA (hackerearth) with 2 coding problems (one array manipulation, one recursion) and a short OOPs MCQ set. round 2 – technical interview focused on OOPs concepts, design patterns and a live coding on inheritance & polymorphism. round 3 – HR & ML chat, they asked about my interest in machine learning, a simple project I did on image classification and salary expectations.
preparation: revamped my OOPs notes from the CSE syllabus, solved Striver's sheet for recursion, and did a few ML project tutorials on Kaggle. practiced OA on Codeforces contests and asked a senior who interned at Amazon for mock interviews.

advice: maybe separate the OOPs MCQ from the coding part in OA, it feels a little disjointed. a quick overview of the team you’ll join would be nice.
tips: write down the 4 SOLID principles and be ready to give examples. do at least one OA daily for 2 weeks before the interview. have your ML project demo ready on GitHub for quick reference.

selection: round 1 – aptitude test (numeric, logical & a quick data‑interpretation set). round 2 – project discussion where I presented my metallurgical research on corrosion‑resistant alloys and answered questions on methodology. round 3 – a technical interview on core material‑science topics (phase diagrams, heat treatment). round 4 – another HR round focusing on communication, teamwork and why Deloitte. round 5 – final HR/fit interview with a senior manager, they talked about consulting life and asked about my long‑term goals.
preparation: solved aptitude packs from previous campus drives, revisited my final year project slides, read GFG articles on material‑science basics and did mock HR with seniors from the placement cell. also brushed up on consulting case basics just in case.
experience: the aptitude was easy, project round was the highlight – I could talk passionately. core interview was a bit dense but I survived. HR rounds were pleasant, the manager was really encouraging.
advice: more case‑study practice would help, even for a technical role. also give a brief about the kind of consulting projects Deloitte handles in the materials domain.
tips: prepare a 2‑minute pitch for your project, include numbers (e.g., % improvement). keep a fresh list of common aptitude formulas. ask about training programs in the final HR – it shows interest.

selection: PPO conversion, 1 round: technical interview with a plant head. They asked about my internship at a smelter plant, safety protocols, and process control. HR was clubbed in the end, mostly about relocation and bond.

advice: Be thorough with your internship project and safety protocols. They will ask a lot about what you built and how you handled safety incidents.
tips: If you have a PPO, work on one thing properly instead of 5 half things. Also, dont ignore the HR round, they can make or break your offer.

selection: Round 1: an online aptitude & case‑study OA (30 MCQs on quantitative, logical & data‑interpretation plus a short business case where u had to suggest a data‑driven solution). Round 2: HR interview where they asked about my ECE projects, teamwork experiences and why I wanted a PPO at ZS.

selection: round 1: resume shortlisting – they screened for embedded projects and a minimum cgpa (6.5). round 2: online dsa test – 3 questions (heap, linked list, bit‑manip). round 3: technical interview – deep dive into my raspberry‑pi sensor node, asked about interrupts, timers and low‑power modes, plus a tiny coding task on C pointers.
preparation: spent a week on striver sheet for dsa, revisited c pointer tricks from gfg, built a mini‑drone project to show on resume, and read nvidia’s recent papers on edge AI. also asked a senior who interned there for interview tips.
experience: the dsa test was tough for a low‑cgpa kid but I survived. the interview felt like a chat with a senior engineer – they loved my sensor node demo.
advice: show hands‑on hardware work, even if cgpa is not stellar. concrete results (e.g., 30% power saving) impress them.
tips: don’t panic if you miss a dsa q; focus on explaining your thought process. bring a photo of your project on phone for quick reference.

selection: round 1: oa – 30 min mix of coding (two leetcode easy‑medium), a short ml case (interpret a confusion matrix) and an os question (process vs thread). round 2: dsa interview – they asked about segment trees and binary search tricks. round 3: system design – design a real‑time recommendation engine for uber rides. round 4: ml deep‑dive – talk about your kaggle project, feature engineering and model eval. round 5: hr – salary expectations, relocation to gurgaon and cultural fit.
preparation: crammed striver sheet for dsa, solved ml problems on kaggle (housing price), refreshed os concepts from nptel, and practiced oa on hackerearth. also did mock HR with a friend from cse batch.
experience: the whole process stretched over two weeks, felt exhausting but each round was different so it kept me engaged. the ml round was the toughest, but I managed to explain my feature pipeline.
advice: balance your prep – don’t just do dsa, allocate time for ml & os too. also keep your resume bullet points quantifiable.
tips: take short breaks between rounds, drink chai, and have a cheat‑sheet of common ml metrics ready.

selection: single round: a combined oa + hr chat on zoom – 20 min logical puzzle set, then a quick HR Q&A about why mu sigma, salary expectations and campus life.
preparation: solved gfg aptitude sets, practiced case studies from previous mu sigma candidates, and polished my resume to highlight the 9.28 cgpa and data‑analysis project.
experience: the round was short and sweet, the recruiter was friendly and moved fast to the HR part after the puzzle.
advice: be ready to explain any number you put on resume – they love to probe your data‑analysis experience.
tips: stay calm during puzzles, and have a one‑liner ready for why u want mu sigma (e.g., love problem‑solving & analytics).

selection: R1: online assessment with aptitude, verbal, and 2 coding problems (easy and medium).

experience: The online assessment was straightforward. I felt prepared and confident.
advice: Referral is a big plus, so ask around. Be thorough on ML and CN.

selection: 5 rounds total, started with an aptitude test (indiabix level), then a group discussion on a random topic like 'should plastic be banned'. preparation: did leetcode mediums and striver sheet for DSA, revised strength of materials and machine design from NPTEL. Also brushed up on GD topics from previous seniors' notes. My PPO at a metal company helped a lot.

tips: apply early for core companies, even if cgpa is not 9+. hindalco came in first week itself. keep resume clean with projects and internships highlighted.

selection: just 1 round after resume shortlist: a 30-min case study + puzzle round with 2 managers. they gave a business scenario about optimizing a pharma supply chain and asked me to explain my approach. then a few puzzles like 'how many golf balls fit in a bus' and 'why are manhole covers round'. HR questions were basic like why ZS, location preference, notice period. result same day.
preparation: did GFG puzzles and some case study videos on youtube. also revised basic probability and stats since the case was data-heavy. seniors said HR is straightforward so no need to overprepare.
experience: managers were very professional, gave real-world problems. felt like a mini-consulting interview. got offer immediately, pay was great too.
advice: dont panic if u blank on puzzles, they just want to see ur thought process. case study is more about communication than perfect answer.
tips: ZS comes early in nittk, so apply as soon as portal opens. resume shortlist is key, so highlight any analytics projects or certifications.

selection: 3 rounds: first was an online test with MCQs on stats, probability, and SQL basics. then a group discussion on 'data-driven decision making in healthcare'. final round was a technical + HR interview where they asked about my PPO project on customer segmentation using ML. also asked to write a python function to clean a messy dataset. result after 3 days.
preparation: revised stats from coursera course, did leetcode SQL problems, and practiced explaining my PPO project to friends. also brushed up on basic ML concepts like bias-variance tradeoff.
experience: GD was boring, but interviewers were nice. they seemed impressed by my PPO work. got ppo converted, which was a big relief since i wasnt sure about placements.
advice: for mu sigma, focus on stats and SQL more than DSA. they dont ask hard coding questions.
tips: apply for mu sigma even if u dont have ML experience, they train u. also, dont skip the OA, it's a major filter.

selection: 5 rounds: aptitude test (TCS pattern), then a technical round with questions on DBMS (normalization, joins), OS (process vs thread), and a coding question to reverse a linked list. next was a managerial round with HR questions like 'tell me about yourself' and 'where do u see yourself in 5 years'. then a final HR round with salary negotiation and location preference. result after 2 weeks.
preparation: did tcs-specific aptitude sets, revised DBMS and OS from gate smashers videos, and practiced coding on GFG. also did a few mock interviews with seniors.
experience: technical round was stressful, but the coding question was easy. managerial round felt like a formality. got the offer, but pay was low compared to other companies.
advice: dont underestimate the aptitude test, it's the main filter. also, practice coding on paper, not just laptop.
tips: TCS is a safe option, but dont expect high pay. apply early, they have a lot of rounds and results take time.

selection: 4 rounds: first was a resume-based shortlist, then a coding round with 2 DSA questions (one medium, one hard) on leetcode patterns. next was a technical interview with questions on embedded systems (RTOS, interrupts, PCB design) and a system design question on designing a traffic light controller. final round was an HR interview with questions about why Nvidia, location preference, and notice period. result after 1 week.
preparation: did striver sheet and leetcode hard problems, revised embedded systems from NPTEL and made notes on RTOS concepts. also brushed up on system design basics from grokking the system design interview.
experience: coding round was tough, but i managed to solve both questions. technical interview was intense, but interviewers were helpful. HR round was straightforward. got the offer with a great pay, which was a huge relief.
advice: for Nvidia, focus on DSA and embedded systems. system design is also important, so dont skip it.
tips: apply for Nvidia even if ur cgpa is not 9+, they value skills more. also, prepare for the coding round thoroughly, it's the main filter.

selection: round 1: an online aptitude test (quick MCQs on quantitative, logical and a tiny bit of verbal) – 30 mins, timed tight so speed mattered. round 2: a technical interview with a senior TCS lead – they asked me to explain OOP concepts, inheritance vs composition, a couple of design‑pattern questions and a simple coding problem on arrays (basically leetcode easy). round 3: HR round – they went through my resume, asked why I want digital specialist role in Mumbai, and threw a few situational questions about teamwork and handling deadlines.
preparation: i did leetcode easy‑medium for 2 hrs daily, followed the striver dsa sheet for quick revision. gfg notes for OOPs and design patterns, plus watched a couple of NPTEL core videos on digital signal basics (just in case). senior batchmates shared their TCS interview experiences and we did mock HR chats on Discord. also brushed up my resume with quantifiable projects (got help from the CDC SPOC).
experience: overall the process was smooth, but the aptitude test felt a bit rushed. technical interview was chill, the guy was friendly and actually liked my project on IoT sensor. HR was polite but a bit generic – asked about family and relocation. got the offer same week, happy but also a tad nervous about the huge onboarding training.
advice: TCS values clear fundamentals in OOP and decent speed in aptitude. show genuine interest in digital domain and be ready with a couple of project anecdotes. keep your resume crisp – no fluff.
tips: don't ignore the tiny coding question – solve it on paper first. practice timed MCQs on gfg's aptitude set. wear smart casual for HR, and keep a backup copy of your resume on your phone.

selection: round 1: an offline OA at the campus – 40 questions covering statics, thermodynamics and a short CAD sketch; time limit was strict. round 2: technical interview with a senior design engineer – they probed my understanding of stress‑strain curves, asked me to explain a gearbox design I did in 4th sem, and gave a mini‑case on optimizing a suspension component. round 3: a group discussion on "future of autonomous vehicles" with 5 other candidates, 15 mins each. round 4: HR round – typical behavioural questions, salary expectations and why Kolkata.
preparation: re‑read my 3rd‑4th sem core notes (mechanics of materials, fluid dynamics) and solved past OA papers from the college portal. used striver sheet for quick DSA just in case, but mostly focused on core subjects. watched a few SPOC videos on CAD basics and asked seniors from the mechanical club for interview tips. practiced GD with friends over chai evenings.
experience: the OA was intense – some questions felt like final exam. technical interview was deep; the interviewer actually liked my project on lightweight chassis and asked follow‑up on material selection. GD was a mixed bag – a couple of candidates were too loud, but I managed to contribute. HR was friendly and gave a clear picture of the role. got the offer with a decent package, but the onboarding paperwork was a bit messy.
advice: Mercedes looks for solid core fundamentals and the ability to communicate design ideas clearly. be ready to sketch quickly and explain trade‑offs. in GD, keep it concise and back opinions with technical facts.
tips: revise core formulas on a cheat‑sheet before the OA. bring a pen and ruler for CAD sketch. dress smart (blazer works). and don’t forget to mention any internship at an auto firm – it adds brownie points.

selection: round 1: referral screening – a quick HR chat (10 mins) where the employee asked about my EEE projects, why I want Walmart tech and checked my CGPA. round 2: coding round on the onsite platform – 2 DSA problems (one array manipulation, one medium‑hard graph) with a 45‑minute limit. they also asked a couple of basic VLSI questions (gate delay, flip‑flop timing).
preparation: since i had a referral, i focused on leetcode medium‑hard set (especially graphs) for 1.5 hrs daily. used the striver sheet to polish up array tricks. gfg’s VLSI basics notes for the quick quiz part. also did a mock HR with a senior who works at a fintech firm – he gave me the typical referral questions. watched a few YouTube videos on Walmart’s tech stack.
experience: the referral chat was super casual, the employee was nice and told me about the team culture. the coding round was tough – the graph problem was similar to a recent leetcode contest, but I managed to solve it after a few attempts. the VLSI bits were easy because I’d refreshed before. got a PPO after 2 weeks, felt relieved.
advice: for Walmart, a solid DSA base is a must, but they also like domain knowledge (VLSI, hardware). keep the HR conversation light and show enthusiasm for the retail tech side.
tips: solve at least one graph problem a day before the interview. keep a one‑page cheat sheet of VLSI terms. be ready to talk about any internship with numbers (e.g., reduced power consumption by 12%).

selection: round 1: aptitude & puzzles – 30 MCQs (quant, logical, a couple of riddles) timed 20 mins. round 2: technical interview – they threw a case about optimizing a telecom network rollout, asked me to draw a high‑level block diagram and discuss cost‑benefit, plus a quick OOP question on inheritance. round 3: HR round – typical behavioural questions, strengths‑weaknesses, why EY and my future plans.
preparation: practised aptitude from gfg’s ‘placement prep’ set and did a few puzzle books (the ones seniors recommended). for the case, read up on telecom basics and watched a couple of NPTEL videos on network design. brushed up OOP concepts using Striver’s sheet and solved a few leetcode easy problems. also did a mock HR with a friend from the consulting club.
experience: the aptitude was a bit tricky – some puzzles were weird but manageable. technical interview felt like a mini‑consulting case; I stumbled a bit on cost numbers but the interviewer was patient. HR was straightforward and actually asked about my long‑term goals, which I appreciated. overall, decent vibe and got the offer with a decent salary.
advice: EY looks for problem‑solving speed and clear communication. be ready for case‑style questions even for pure tech roles. keep your resume focused on quantifiable achievements.
tips: do at least 5 puzzles a day before the interview. practice explaining a technical solution in under 2 mins – it helps in both tech and HR rounds. dress business casual and bring a notebook for the case.

selection: round 1: online coding challenge (Google Form) – 3 leetcode‑style problems (easy, medium, hard) with 90‑minute timer. round 2: another coding round (on-site) – 2 medium‑hard array/DP questions, strict 45 mins each. round 3: system design interview – design a distributed cache service, discuss scalability, CAP theorem, and some trade‑offs. round 4: deep dive OS interview – questions on processes, threads, memory management, page replacement algorithms. round 5: HR/leadership round – behavioral questions, "Googleyness", and a brief discussion on my side projects.
preparation: intense leetcode grind for 2 hrs daily – focused on medium‑hard arrays and DP (striver sheet helped). watched system design videos (Gaurav Sen) and read the "Designing Data‑Intensive Applications" book notes. revisited OS concepts from NPTEL and solved past Google OA papers. did mock HR with seniors from the coding club; they gave me feedback on the "Googleyness" part. also kept my GitHub projects (a small distributed key‑value store) polished.
experience: the coding rounds were brutal – the hard problem in round 1 was a classic "minimum window substring" that ate up a lot of time. round 2 felt better after I warmed up. system design was interesting; I was nervous but managed to sketch a high‑level architecture and discuss sharding. OS interview was deep – they asked about page‑replacement LRU vs LFU and I had to explain it with a diagram. HR was friendly, asked about my open‑source contributions and why I want to stay in Bangalore. got the offer after a week, feeling ecstatic but also a bit overwhelmed by the workload expectations.
advice: Google expects top‑tier DSA skills, solid system design fundamentals, and clear communication. practice writing code on a plain editor (no IDE) to mimic the online test. be ready to talk about any project in depth – numbers matter.
tips: solve at least one hard leetcode problem every other day. rehearse system design on a whiteboard with a friend. keep a one‑page cheat sheet of OS concepts. dress smart‑casual for HR, and bring a printed copy of your top 3 projects.

selection: Hindustan Unilever GET placement. 4 rounds. Round 1: OA on a platform with 3 questions, 2 coding and 1 about circuits / ECE concepts, 90 min. Round 3: HR round, asked me about my family, hobbies and why I want to join Hindustan Unilever. preparation: Did DSA in C++, revised circuits from GFG and watched some videos on circuits. Striver sheet, and a bit of leetcode.
experience: It was good, I think the interviewer wanted me to explain more deeply. Got the result after 2 weeks and was surprised.
advice: Circuits matter. If u know python only, they might ask u to learn it. Know OOPs basics.
tips: CGPA 8.71 was fine for the shortlist, I was worried. Dont filter urself out, apply to all. Also dont panic when u forget answers, say whatever u know.

selection: Deloitte came for M&M dept placements. R1 was just resume shortlisting and an aptitude test (30 mins, 30 questions, mostly logical reasoning and basic quant). They took 2 days to announce results, super chill process. Got selected with 4.9 LPA, no interviews nothing.
