selection: Salesforce was a grind. R1: OA with 2 DSA problems (1 easy, 1 medium) in 75 mins. R2: project deep dive, they asked about my cloud project, how i handled scalability, and some basic system design. R3: OS round, questions on deadlocks, paging, and a small coding problem on semaphores. R4: OOPs round, inheritance, polymorphism, design a class for a parking lot. R5: HR round, standard stuff like why salesforce, team conflicts, and my 5-year plan. Took 3 weeks to get result, super anxious.
preparation: did striver sheet (180 problems) in 3 months, then leetcode mediums for 2 months. for OS and OOPs, went through gate smashers notes and made notes. seniors helped with mock interviews for project round.
experience: interviewers were chill but salesforce expects u to know everything in detail. i blanked on a semaphore question and they gave a hint, saved me. projects round was the toughest for me.
advice: dont just memorize striver sheet, understand the patterns. for OS and OOPs, write down everything u learn and revise before interviews.
tips: apply early even if ur CG is mid, salesforce is generous with pay. also, prepare a 2-min project pitch, they love that. dont skip the HR round prep, they ask unexpected stuff.

selection: Oracle was a mixed bag. R1: OA with 3 problems (2 DSA, 1 SQL query). R2: system design round, designed a url shortener and a chat app, they asked about scalability and trade-offs. R3: OOPs round, inheritance, design patterns, and a coding problem on factory pattern. Results came in 10 days, got 17.4 LPA.
preparation: did leetcode mediums (200 problems) and a few hard ones. for system design, watched gaurav sen videos and took notes. OOPs was from gate smashers and some youtube tutorials.
experience: system design round was fun but i struggled with trade-offs. OOPs round was straightforward, but i messed up the factory pattern question initially. interviewers were patient though.
advice: system design is about communication, not just the design. explain ur thought process clearly. for OOPs, draw diagrams to explain concepts.
tips: dont overcomplicate ur OA prep, oracle asks standard questions. also, keep ur system design answers concise, they have limited time.

selection: IISc MS was a referral process. R1: resume shortlisting (they took 3 days). R2: written test on maths, fluid mechanics, and heat transfer (3 hours). R3: interview round, asked about my project on heat exchanger design, some thermodynamics questions, and why IISc. Results came in 2 weeks.
preparation: revised core subjects from class notes and made formula sheets. for the interview, went through my project in detail and prepared for standard MS questions. seniors helped with mock interviews.
experience: written test was tough, i blanked on a few maths problems. interview round was conversational, they asked about my goals and how i see myself contributing to research.
advice: if u have a referral, apply early. core subjects are key for written test. also, prepare a strong SOP, it matters a lot.
tips: dont just mug up formulas, understand the concepts. for the interview, be honest about what u know and dont know. they appreciate that.

selection: Tata Steel was a rollercoaster. R1: aptitude test (30 mins, 30 questions, mostly logical reasoning and basic quant). R2: technical interview, asked about my core subjects (network theory, power systems) and a small coding problem on linked list. R3: HR round, standard stuff like why tata steel, teamwork examples. R4: medical + document verification, super quick. Results announced next day, got 17.3 LPA.
preparation: revised core subjects from class notes and did a few aptitude mocks. for the coding problem, did GFG easy problems. seniors said HR round is just a formality, so i didnt prep much for it.
experience: technical interview was stressful, i forgot a formula for power systems and had to derive it on the spot. HR round was chill, they asked about my hobbies and why i want to join tata steel.
advice: core subjects are important, dont neglect them. for aptitude, practice speed and accuracy.
tips: keep ur resume simple and highlight any core projects. also, be prepared for medical round, they ask about medical history in detail.

selection: round 1 was an online assessment (OA) with 2 coding problems (one array, one graph) and a quick OOPs MCQ section. I finished both coding Qs in ~25 mins each, the MCQ was easy. round 2 was a video interview where they asked me to solve a medium DSA problem on strings and then dive into OOP concepts like polymorphism, abstract classes and a small Java snippet to reverse a linked list. they also checked my resume briefly. got the offer same day.
preparation: did leetcode hard & medium daily, followed the Striver DSA sheet, solved a bunch of OA on hackerearth/gfg. brushed up OOPs from my semester notes and watched a few YouTube tutorials on Java design patterns. also practiced time‑boxing for OA.
experience: overall chill, interviewers were friendly but a bit strict on coding style. the OA felt like a mini‑contest, so stress level was moderate.
advice: make sure you can write clean code fast, and don't skip the OOP MCQ – they love to test basics before deep DSA.
tips: practice coding with a timer, keep a cheat‑sheet of common OOP concepts, and double‑check your language syntax before the interview.

selection: this one was a marathon – 5 rounds total. round1: OA (3 coding Qs, 2 DSA, 1 basic maths). round2: DSA interview – they gave a tough tree DP problem and asked me to optimise it. round3: computer networks (CN) – questions on TCP/IP, routing, and a scenario on congestion control. round4: OOPs interview – deep dive into Java inheritance, design patterns, and a small coding task to implement a singleton. round5: HR round – typical intro, strengths/weaknesses, and why Adobe. got the final offer after a week.
preparation: heavy leetcode + Striver sheet for DSA, revisited my CN textbook and watched NPTEL videos, and did a bunch of OOP mock interviews with seniors. also solved past Adobe OA on geeksforgeeks. kept a resume checklist ready.
experience: exhausting but good – each round felt different so it kept me on my toes. interviewers were professional, some were super talkative which helped relax a bit.
advice: don't underestimate CN – many ignore it and get stuck. also be ready to explain OOP concepts with real‑world examples.
tips: spend at least 2 weeks on CN basics, practice whiteboard coding for system design style questions, and rehearse your intro for HR.

selection: got a referral from a senior, so the process was short: round1 was a quick HR call (fit interview) – they asked about my campus projects and why Flipkart. round2 was a technical DSA interview – a medium level problem on sliding windows and a follow‑up on hash‑maps. they also peeked at my resume for the referral note. got the PPO within 3 days.
preparation: since I had a referral I focused on polishing my resume and solving a few sliding‑window problems on leetcode. also brushed up basics of hash‑maps and ran mock HR calls with friends.
experience: pretty smooth, the HR was nice and the tech interview was straight to the point. felt lucky with the referral.
advice: if you have a referral, treat it like any other interview – don't get over‑confident. still be ready for DSA.
tips: keep your resume one‑pager, know the projects inside out, and practice explaining them in <2 mins.

selection: 5 rounds in total. round1: OA on HackerRank – 2 coding questions (one DP, one strings) and a short logical puzzle. round2: DSA interview – they gave a tricky graph traversal problem and asked for both BFS & DFS solutions. round3: system design – design a scalable video streaming service, talk about CDN, load balancer, caching. round4: resume review – they dug into my AI project, asked about datasets, model choices, and why I used PyTorch. round5: HR – typical campus HR questions and salary discussion. got the offer after a week.
preparation: intense leetcode (hard) for DSA, watched system design videos (Gaurav Sen) focusing on distributed systems, and revisited my AI project code. also did mock resume interviews with seniors and practiced explaining my project metrics.
experience: tough but fair. the system design round was the hardest part, but the interviewers were encouraging and gave hints when I stalled.
advice: be clear on trade‑offs in system design and know your own projects inside out. for DSA, write clean code, not just solve.
tips: use a whiteboard (or virtual) to sketch architectures, rehearse your project story, and do timed OA practice every other day.

selection: 3 rounds focused on core mechanical stuff. round1: written test on thermodynamics and material strength (multiple choice + short problems). round2: technical interview – they asked me to explain the mining cycle, a case study on rock breakage, and a small design question on a ventilation system for underground mines. round3: HR round – intro, why Mercedes‑Benz R&D, and future goals. got the placement offer after 10 days.
preparation: revived my 3rd year core notes, solved previous year papers for thermodynamics, watched YouTube videos on mining engineering basics, and did a mock interview with a senior from the mechanical department. also polished my resume to highlight the mining project.
experience: pretty intense on the core knowledge side, but the interviewers were supportive and gave me time to think. HR was casual.
advice: focus on core subjects – you can't wing thermodynamics. also be ready with a real‑world example from your projects.
tips: solve at least 5 past core exam papers, prepare a 2‑minute pitch about your mining project, and keep a small cheat‑sheet of key formulas handy.

selection: Vedanta had just one round: a technical interview with a civil engineer. He asked about civil engineering basics like types of soil, concrete mix design, and a few numerical problems. No HR round.
preparation: Did some civil engineering from GFG and some numerical problems from mine own notes. Also updated my resume with a project on soil stabilization.
experience: The engineer was very nice and explained everything in detail. The interview was a bit long but it was good.
advice: Be very solid with civil engineering basics and have a good project to show.
tips: Civil guys, update your resume with a good project and be ready for some numerical problems.

selection: Texas Instruments had only one round: an online assessment with DSA questions and a few DBMS questions. They also asked me to write a SQL query.
preparation: Did the leetcode easy-medium questions and some DBMS from gate smashers. Also practiced writing SQL queries.
experience: The OA was a bit tough but I managed to solve most of the questions. The experience was good.
advice: Be very solid with DSA and DBMS. Also, practice writing SQL queries.
tips: CSE guys targeting SDE roles, do the leetcode easy-medium questions and some DBMS from gate smashers.

selection: Flipkart had 5 rounds. First was an online assessment with DSA questions. Then a technical interview with a few DSA questions and a system design question. Then a coding round where I had to code a solution to a problem. Then a manager round where I had to explain my solution and answer some questions about my project. Finally, an HR round.
preparation: Did the leetcode easy-medium questions and some system design from the system design interview book. Also worked on a project with ML.
experience: The rounds were a bit tough but I managed to clear all of them. The experience was good.
advice: Be very solid with DSA and system design. Also, have a good project to show.
tips: CSE guys targeting ML Engineer roles, do the leetcode easy-medium questions and some system design from the system design interview book.

selection: Mercedes-Benz R&D had only one round: a technical interview with a mechanical engineer. He asked about mechanical engineering basics like types of engines, thermodynamics, and a few numerical problems. No HR round.
preparation: Did some mechanical engineering from GFG and some numerical problems from mine own notes. Also updated my resume with a project on engine design.
experience: The engineer was very nice and explained everything in detail. The interview was a bit long but it was good.
advice: Be very solid with mechanical engineering basics and have a good project to show.
tips: Mechanical guys, update your resume with a good project and be ready for some numerical problems.

selection: Cisco had only one round: a technical interview with an EEE engineer. He asked about DSA questions, a few ML questions, and a few questions about hardware design. No HR round.
preparation: Did the leetcode easy-medium questions and some ML from the striver sheet. Also updated my resume with a project on hardware design.
experience: The engineer was very nice and explained everything in detail. The interview was a bit tough but it was good.
advice: Be very solid with DSA and ML. Also, have a good project to show.
tips: EEE guys targeting Hardware Engineer roles, do the leetcode easy-medium questions and some ML from the striver sheet.

selection: single OA round, 3 coding questions in 60 mins, 2 mediums on arrays and 1 hard on dp. cleared it and was called for the next day interview.
preparation: striver sheet 3 times, leetcode mediums daily, did a few kaggle competitions for the projects. seniors helped with resume.
experience: interview was chill, they asked about my projects and some basic ML concepts. got the offer in 2 days.
advice: projects matter a lot for data science roles. dont just do leetcode, show ur work.
tips: keep ur resume updated with all projects, even small ones. OA was easy but interview was tricky.

selection: 4 rounds total. OA was 20 mcqs on thermodynamics and fluid mechanics, then 3 technical interviews. first was design of a pressure vessel, second was FEM analysis, third was GD&T and manufacturing processes.
preparation: revised all core subjects from rk bansal and khurmi. did a few online courses on ansys and solidworks. seniors shared their interview experiences.
experience: interviews were tough but interviewers were supportive. they explained concepts if u were stuck.
advice: core subjects are everything for mechanical core roles. dont skip any topic.
tips: practice drawing diagrams and explaining ur thought process. they love that.

selection: 5 rounds! OA was 2 sections: 15 aptitude mcqs and 2 coding questions (medium graph and hard tree). cleared OA, then 4 interviews: 2 DSA, 1 system design, 1 low level design. system design was about designing a distributed cache.
preparation: leetcode 700+ problems, striver sheet twice, system design from grokking the system design interview. mock interviews with friends who got into qualcomm earlier.
experience: interviews were intense but interviewers were helpful. they gave hints when u were stuck.
advice: system design is not just for seniors, start early. think aloud and communicate ur approach.
tips: OA was the hardest part for me, practice time management. dont panic if u get stuck in interviews.

selection: 2 rounds. OA was 3 coding questions in 90 mins (2 mediums on trees and 1 hard on dp). cleared OA, then 1 technical interview focused on CN and OS. asked about tcp/ip, socket programming, and some os concepts.
preparation: revised CN from forouzan and os from silberschatz. did leetcode mediums and some GFG CN problems. referral from a senior helped a lot.
experience: interview was smooth, they asked about my projects and some basic CN concepts. got the offer in a week.
advice: CN and OS are important for SDE roles. dont ignore them.
tips: referrals can be a game changer. ask seniors for help.

selection: 5 rounds! OA was 2 coding questions in 75 mins (medium on arrays and hard on dp). cleared OA, then 4 interviews: 2 DSA, 1 system design, 1 behavioral. system design was about designing a url shortener. behavioral was about teamwork and conflict resolution.
preparation: leetcode 600+ problems, striver sheet 3 times, system design from grokking. mock interviews with friends who got into atlassian earlier.
experience: interviews were fun but challenging. interviewers were very friendly and gave hints when needed.
advice: be prepared for both DSA and system design. they love to test ur problem-solving skills.
tips: PPO is not guaranteed, so dont relax after clearing the interviews. keep practicing.

selection: 5 rounds total. round 1 was a quick aptitude test (quant + logical) on google form, 30 mins. round 2 a 1‑hour technical interview where they dug into my final year EEE projects – motor drive and SCADA – and asked a few circuit theory questions. round 3 was a pure HR chat, they asked about campus life and why I want to join steel sector. round 4 was the PPO discussion (they had already offered me a summer intern slot, so this was a conversion talk about salary and location). finally round 5 was the offer‑letter call with HR confirming the CTC and posting details. all rounds were on Teams, so good internet mattered.
preparation: started with striver DSA sheet (150 easy‑medium problems) and kept a GFG notebook for aptitude shortcuts. did a couple of SPOC courses on power electronics + control systems to sound the core‑project talk. practiced OA on HackerRank (SQL + basic coding) and asked seniors who interned at JSW for interview debriefs. also rehearsed my project demo with a friend.
experience: the aptitude was a breeze, but the project interview made me nervous – I stumbled on a minor detail about PWM frequency. HR was chill, they even joked about my love for cricket. the PPO talk felt like a friendly catch‑up because my intern manager was on the panel. overall mixed vibes: stressful at times but rewarding when they finally said "congrats".
advice: for the company: give candidates a clear syllabus for the project round, it helps us focus. also try to keep the internet bandwidth stable for the OA, we lost a few points due to lag.
tips: keep a one‑page cheat sheet of your major projects, rehearse the pitch in front of a mirror. do mock OA on hackerrank, and solve at least 30 aptitude puzzles from previous years. dont forget to stay hydrated during long video calls.

selection: 3 rounds. round 1 was an online assessment on Codility – 2 coding problems (arrays & strings) and a 10‑question OS quiz about processes, deadlocks and memory management. round 2 was a technical interview focused heavily on OS concepts, they gave me a scenario about a producer‑consumer problem and asked me to write a semaphore solution on a whiteboard. round 3 was the HR round where they talked about Bangalore office culture and asked about my future goals.
preparation: spent 2 months on leetcode (mainly medium tag "system design" and "operating‑system" problems) and brushed up OS notes from the NPTEL SPOC. did the Striver sheet for fast DSA, and solved past OA from Arista on geeksforgeeks. my seniors who cleared Arista last year shared their interview scripts, which helped a lot.
experience: the OA felt like a timed quiz, I barely finished the second coding problem but the OS MCQs were smooth. the technical interview was intense – the interviewer kept asking follow‑up on my semaphore code, but I managed to explain the logic. HR was friendly, offered some insight about work‑life balance. overall, a decent ride.
advice: Arista could share sample OS questions before the OA, that would cut down the guesswork. also, a short intro video about the team would be nice.
tips: revise process scheduling and synchronization primitives thoroughly. solve at least 5 OS‑themed problems on GFG. practice coding on a plain text editor (no IDE) because the OA uses a simple editor.

selection: 5 rounds. round 1: written aptitude (numeric, verbal) on a proctor‑invigilated portal, 45 mins. round 2: core technical interview covering power systems and analog circuits – they asked me to design a simple 3‑phase transformer model. round 3: another technical round but more focused on digital electronics and VLSI basics. round 4: HR round where they probed my interest in mining sector and asked about leadership experiences. round 5: final manager interview + salary discussion, after which they gave the offer.
preparation: cracked the core subjects by revisiting NPTEL SPOCs on Power Electronics and Digital Signal Processing. did a lot of GFG aptitude practice (especially quantitative). solved past Coal India core questions from forums. leetcode for DSA (150 problems) just in case they threw a coding question. also asked a senior from the 2019 batch for interview pointers – his notes were gold.
experience: the aptitude was straightforward, but the core interview was a bit nerve‑racking – I forgot the exact formula for per‑unit conversion at one point. the digital round was smoother thanks to my VLSI elective. HR was polite but a tad formal. the manager round felt like a casual chat about my long‑term goals. got the offer after a week, felt relieved.
advice: Coal India should give a brief on what kind of technical questions to expect (core vs. general). a small practice test before the real aptitude would calm nerves.
tips: make a formula sheet for power system calculations, and rehearse explaining them in simple terms. do at least 20 aptitude mock tests. talk to seniors who've cleared the process, their experience shortcuts a lot of prep time.

selection: 3 rounds. round 1 was an online assessment on HackerRank with 2 puzzle‑type questions (logic & lateral thinking) and a short coding problem (array manipulation). round 2: HR interview – they asked about strengths, weaknesses and why Deloitte. round 3: final manager round that mixed puzzles with a case‑study discussion on digital transformation, plus a quick DBMS question about normalization.
preparation: solved daily puzzles on brainbashers and practiced logical riddles from GFG. did the Striver sheet for coding speed, and completed a short DBMS SPOC on MySQL. practiced mock OA on HackerRank (especially the puzzle section). also got interview feedback from seniors who interned at Deloitte last summer.
experience: the OA puzzles were tricky – one asked to find the missing number in a weird sequence, I spent 12 mins on it. coding part was easy. HR was super friendly, asked about campus clubs. manager round was intense, they threw a case about migrating legacy systems and I had to outline a high‑level plan – I think I did okay. got the offer a few days later.
advice: Deloitte could share the type of puzzles (e.g., number series, chessboard) in advance, it would help candidates prepare better.
tips: spend 15 mins daily on brain teasers, and keep a cheat sheet of common DBMS concepts. do at least one mock OA with puzzles before the real test.

selection: just 1 round – a single online assessment on Codility that combined OOPs, DBMS and coding. 2 coding tasks (linked‑list manipulation and a simple SQL query) and a 10‑question MCQ section covering inheritance, polymorphism, and normalization rules.
preparation: focused on OOPs fundamentals from my C++ course, wrote small programs for each concept. did a quick DBMS refresher via a GFG playlist and solved 30 SQL queries on HackerRank. practiced OA on Codility using previous Microsoft sample tests. seniors who cleared MS shared their note‑taking template – saved me time.
experience: the assessment was tight – I finished the coding part in 18 mins, then rushed through the MCQs. I missed one subtle question about virtual destructors, but overall I felt confident. got the offer within 24 hours, which was a huge relief.
advice: Microsoft could give a short outline of topics covered in the OA, maybe a sample question. also, a 5‑minute tutorial on the test environment would avoid technical hiccups.
tips: write down OOPs concepts on a sticky note and glance at it before the test. practice writing SQL queries without IDE help. do a timed mock OA at least twice a week in the weeks before the interview.

selection: Fractal had 2 rounds. First was online assessment with 30 aptitude questions and 1 coding question on arrays. Second was a technical interview where they discussed my project on sentiment analysis using NLP. They asked about the ML models used and how I preprocessed the data.
preparation: Did aptitude from indiabix and solved around 50 easy leetcode problems. My project was on sentiment analysis using NLP, so I revised ML basics.
experience: Overall good. The OA was a bit tricky but I managed to solve the coding question. The technical interview was smooth as I had a clear understanding of my project.
advice: Prepare aptitude well, it's a numbers game. Make sure your projects are well explained and relevant to the role.
tips: Consistency is key. I did aptitude practice for about a month before the OA. Also, be confident while explaining your projects.

selection: Georgia Tech was a referral process. They asked for my resume and a recommendation letter from a professor. They also wanted a short essay on why I wanted to pursue MS in CS and how my background prepared me for it.
preparation: I had a good CGPA and a strong academic record. I also had some ML projects, so I highlighted those in my resume and essay.
experience: The process was smooth. I got a referral from a professor and they were impressed with my essay.
advice: Make sure your resume is well tailored to the university. Highlight your academic achievements and any relevant projects.
tips: Networking is key. I got a referral from a professor who was impressed with my academic record. Also, make sure your essay is well written and tailored to the university.

selection: Goldman Sachs had 5 rounds. First was an online assessment with 2 coding questions and 30 aptitude questions. Second was a case study interview. Third was a technical interview where they discussed my projects. Fourth was a behavioral interview. Fifth was a final interview with the hiring manager.
preparation: I solved around 200 leetcode problems and did a lot of case study practice. I also revised my projects thoroughly.
experience: The process was intense but I managed to clear all rounds. The OA was a bit tricky but I managed to solve both coding questions. The case study interview was smooth as I had done a lot of practice. The technical interview was a bit nerve-wracking but I managed to explain my projects well.
advice: Prepare a lot of case studies and coding problems. Make sure your projects are well explained and relevant to the role.
tips: Consistency is key. I did leetcode practice for about 2 months before the OA. Also, be confident while explaining your projects and case studies.

selection: Mu Sigma had 3 rounds. First was an online assessment with 30 aptitude questions and 1 coding question on arrays. Second was a technical interview where they discussed my ML projects. Third was a final interview with the hiring manager.
preparation: Did aptitude from indiabix and solved around 50 easy leetcode problems. I also revised my ML projects thoroughly.
experience: The process was smooth. The OA was a bit tricky but I managed to solve the coding question. The technical interview was smooth as I had a clear understanding of my ML projects.
advice: Prepare aptitude well, it's a numbers game. Make sure your ML projects are well explained and relevant to the role.
tips: Consistency is key. I did aptitude practice for about a month before the OA. Also, be confident while explaining your ML projects.

selection: Amazon had 1 round, which was an online assessment with 2 coding questions and 30 aptitude questions.
preparation: I solved around 200 leetcode problems and did a lot of aptitude practice. I also revised my projects thoroughly.
experience: The OA was a bit tricky but I managed to solve both coding questions. The process was smooth overall.
advice: Prepare a lot of coding problems and aptitude questions. Make sure your projects are well explained and relevant to the role.
tips: Consistency is key. I did leetcode practice for about 2 months before the OA. Also, be confident while explaining your projects.

selection: Just one round, 45 min. Started with resume walkthrough, then ML/DL project deep dive. Asked to explain a paper i worked on, then a DSA question on graphs (shortest path algo). Ended with HR chat about relocation and bond.
preparation: revised ML basics from andrew ng notes, did leetcode hard graphs, brushed up on my final year project. seniors helped with resume pointers.
experience: panel was chill, asked follow ups till i got it right. got ppo from my summer intern at nvidia so they were just confirming fit.
advice: dont just list projects on resume, know the math behind them. leetcode graphs are must for nvidia.
tips: if u have ppo, still go for the round, u never know when u might need to switch.

selection: 5 rounds total. 1) online test (aptitude + 2 coding qs). 2) case study round (market sizing, data interpretation). 3) technical interview (sql, excel, basic python). 4) HR round (culture fit, relocation). 5) final HR (bond, package).
preparation: did striver sheet for aptitude, practiced case questions on youtube, revised sql from GFG. seniors shared their ppt on case frameworks.
experience: case round was fun but stressful. technical round was easy since i did a data science intern. HR rounds were just formality.
advice: case rounds are about structuring thoughts, not getting the exact number. speak out ur assumptions.
tips: dont skip aptitude prep even if u r good at coding. ZS loves their number crunching.

selection: Single OA round, 2 hours. 4 sections: 1) DSA (2 medium leetcode qs). 2) ML basics (supervised vs unsupervised, bias-variance). 3) CN (tcp/ip, osi model). 4) System design (design a url shortener). Then direct interview round (1 hour) on same topics + resume.
preparation: did leetcode mediums, revised ML from fast.ai, watched gaurav sen system design videos. seniors helped with CN notes.
experience: OA was tough but fair. interview was conversational, they asked about my projects and how i would improve them.
advice: system design is not about perfect answer, show ur thought process. revise CN basics, they love asking.
tips: if u get OA, prepare for interview round too. microsoft doesn’t joke around with their process.

selection: One round, 30 min. Resume walkthrough, then a puzzle (12 balls, one heavier, find in 3 weighings). Then a quick aptitude question (time and work). Ended with HR about bond and location.
preparation: did puzzles from GFG, practiced aptitude from indiabix. seniors said ece gets easier rounds so didn’t stress much.
experience: puzzle was fun, i got it after a hint. hr was just confirming details.
advice: puzzles are about logic, not coding. speak out ur steps.
tips: for non-core roles, focus on communication. ece students, don’t ignore aptitude.

selection: 3 rounds. 1) aptitude test (10 qs, 30 min). 2) technical interview (resume projects, basic python/sql). 3) HR round (bond, location, package).
preparation: did aptitude from rs aggarwal, revised python basics. seniors shared their ppt on projects.
experience: aptitude was easy but time was less. technical round was chill since i did a python project. hr was just formality.
advice: aptitude is key for accenture. don’t ignore it even if u r good at coding.
tips: mining students, focus on aptitude and basic coding. package is low but job is stable.

selection: Round 1 was an online aptitude test (30 MCQs on logical reasoning, quantitative and basic English). I cleared it in 18 mins. Round 2 was a short 20‑minute HR chat where they asked about my interest in digital tech and why Wipro. Round 3 was a live coding OA on Hackerearth: two DSA problems (one array sliding window, one string hashing) and a small case‑study on IoT device monitoring. Finally Round 4 was a technical interview that turned into a PPO discussion – they asked me to design a simple dashboard for sensor data, and after I explained my approach they offered a pre‑placement offer on the spot.
preparation: I cracked the aptitude part by revisiting GFG "aptitude" notes and doing a few mock tests on PrepInsta. For the OA I ran through the Striver DSA sheet, did 150+ LeetCode medium problems and practiced timed contests on Codeforces. The PPO interview was helped by senior seniors from the ECE SPOC group who role‑played the dashboard question. Also brushed up basics of IoT from our 3rd year labs.
experience: Honestly felt a rollercoaster – the aptitude was a breeze, but the OA made my heart race. The PPO talk was super chill cause the interviewers were friendly and actually liked my project. Ended up with a decent package and a smooth onboarding.
advice: Don’t ignore the aptitude – many think it’s easy and skip prep, but speed matters. For the OA, focus on writing clean code fast, and be ready to explain your logic. If you get a PPO talk, show genuine interest in the role, not just the salary.
tips: Keep a cheat‑sheet of common array/string patterns, practice on a timer, and talk to seniors who got PPOs before. Also, have a one‑pager of your IoT project ready – it saves a lot of explanation time.

selection: Round 1: a 60‑minute OA on Codility with 3 DSA questions (two graphs, one DP). I solved two fully, one partially. Round 2: a technical phone interview – they dug deep into my Striver sheet solutions, asked about time‑complexity and edge cases. Round 3: a second OA but this time on HackerRank focusing on bit‑manipulation and number theory (5 quick puzzles). Round 4: an onsite coding interview (pair‑programming) where I wrote a real‑time order‑book simulator in C++. Round 5: HR + PPO round – they discussed compensation, internship experience and offered a full‑time SDE role on the spot.
preparation: Spent 2 months on LeetCode (hard/medium) especially graph and DP, completed the Striver sheet twice. Did daily OA practice on platforms like InterviewBit and HackerRank. For the bit‑puzzles I used GFG “bit manipulation” notes and solved all problems in the “Competitive Programming Handbook”. Also joined the Optiver SPOC Discord where seniors shared their interview experiences.
experience: The whole process was intense – OA’s were time‑pressured and the onsite felt like a coding marathon. The HR folks were surprisingly chill, and the PPO talk felt like a reward after the grind. Got a 37 LPA offer, which was beyond my expectation.
advice: Focus on writing bug‑free code under pressure – practice with a strict timer. Understand the underlying concepts rather than memorising patterns. And when you hit the HR round, be ready with a short story about a challenging project – it can tip the scale.
tips: Do at least 3 full‑length OAs before the actual interview, review your mistakes, and keep a list of common bit tricks. Reach out to seniors who cleared Optiver – they often have hidden gems like “always draw the graph before coding”.

selection: Single round: an onsite OA on a whiteboard where they gave me a OOP design problem – design a scalable power‑grid monitoring system. I sketched classes, interfaces and explained inheritance and polymorphism. Then they asked a quick coding snippet on arrays (easy). The whole thing lasted about 45 minutes and I got the offer the same day.
preparation: Since it was OOP heavy, I revisited the “Java OOPs” chapter in GFG and rewrote all design patterns from my 5th sem notes. Practiced a few whiteboard designs on the campus SPOC group, and solved OOP questions on LeetCode’s “design” tag. Also brushed up basic array problems for the coding part.
experience: Was super nervous at first – whiteboard can be scary – but the interviewers were friendly and gave me hints. Felt good when they liked my class diagram and gave me the offer instantly.
advice: Don’t just list classes, talk about why you chose inheritance vs composition. Keep your design simple and explain trade‑offs. Also be ready for a quick coding warm‑up.
tips: Draw neat UML on paper, practice with a timer, and have a one‑line summary for each class. A quick revision of OOP principles the night before can save you.

selection: Round 1: a 45‑minute OA on HackerRank with 2 DSA problems (one segment tree query, one combinatorial math). I cleared both in time. Round 2: a quantitative test – 20 puzzles on probability and logical reasoning. Round 3: a technical interview focusing on data structures – they asked me to implement a fast order‑matching engine (linked list + heap) and discuss time complexity. Round 4: HR + PPO discussion where they talked about my internship at a fintech startup and offered a quant developer role.
preparation: Did the Striver sheet for DSA, especially segment trees and heaps. Solved probability puzzles from GFG “quant interview” set. Practised OAs on LeetCode “contest” mode to improve speed. Also attended a few quant‑dev talks organized by seniors in the IT SPOC club, which gave me domain insights.
experience: The OA felt like a sprint, the puzzle round was mentally draining but fun. The technical interview was the toughest – I stumbled a bit on edge cases but recovered. The PPO talk was pleasant; they appreciated my fintech internship.
advice: Balance DSA practice with quantitative puzzles – both are tested. In the technical interview, clearly state assumptions before coding. And showcase any finance‑related project – it helps for the PPO.
tips: Keep a cheat‑sheet of common segment‑tree templates, practice mental math for probability, and rehearse a 2‑minute pitch about your fintech project.

selection: Round 1: resume screening – they called me for a 10‑minute call just to confirm my projects and GPA. Round 2: a puzzle‑heavy online test (15 logic puzzles, 5 pattern‑recognition). Round 3: a technical interview where they drilled into my senior project (a web‑app for data analytics) and asked me to solve a coding problem on arrays. Round 4: a second technical round focused on system design – I had to outline a scalable analytics pipeline. Round 5: HR + final fit round – they discussed my career goals, offered an analyst role and hinted at a future PPO if I perform well.
preparation: Polished my resume with help from the CSE SPOC senior, added clear bullet points for each project. Practised puzzle sites like BrainBashers and the “puzzles” section on GeeksforGeeks. For the coding part I did 120 LeetCode easy/medium array problems and revisited my own project code. For system design I read the “Designing Data‑Intensive Applications” summary notes and discussed with seniors who cleared Accenture before.
experience: The resume call was quick but nervous – I almost forgot to mention my internship. The puzzle test was tricky; I spent too much time on a single question. Technical rounds were decent; the design interview let me shine because I had built a similar pipeline in college. HR was friendly and the offer felt fair.
advice: Make sure your resume tells a story – recruiters love a clear project impact. Practice puzzles under a timer, and be ready to explain your projects end‑to‑end. In design, focus on scalability and bottlenecks.
tips: Use a one‑page resume template, keep a list of 3‑4 projects you can discuss fluently, and solve at least 10 puzzles a day a week before the test. Also, ask seniors for their Accenture interview PDFs – they are gold.

selection: Got in through a referral from a senior already at Sprinklr, so my resume skipped the random shortlisting lol. Round 1: technical interview, around 1 hour. Started with my projects (I had a motor controller thing on stm32), then 2 DSA questions, a sliding window one and a linked list one, coded on a shared doc. Result came the next afternoon.
preparation: ECE so DSA was not my strong point at first. Did Striver sheet in the 2nd year summer and 1-2 leetcode mediums daily after that. For OOPs I read a C++ book and GFG articles. Embedded stuff was mostly from microprocessors course and my project. Took 3 mock interviews from club seniors.
experience: Pretty good honestly, interviewers were calm. The bar raiser was almost 70 min and tiring but fair.
advice: Have 5-6 stories ready for leadership principles in STAR format. Know ur C++ basics properly, they go into vtable stuff. Referral only opens the door, rest is on u.
tips: Dont think ECE puts u behind for software roles, but u need to put extra time into DSA. Ask seniors for referrals early, they actually help. CGPA was high for me so cant say how much it matters. Keep a notes doc with every detail of ur projects (numbers, tradeoffs), they will ask.

selection: Got in through a referral from a senior already at Georgia Tech, so my resume skipped the random shortlisting lol. Round 1: technical interview, around 1 hour. Started with my projects (I had a motor controller thing on stm32), then 2 DSA questions, a sliding window one and a linked list one, coded on a shared doc. Round 2: another technical but more embedded flavoured. OOPs in C++ (virtual functions, vtable, why destructors should be virtual), interrupts, volatile keyword, memory layout of a C program. Round 3: bar raiser + HR mix, all leadership principle stories, like a time u disagreed with a teammate. Result came the next afternoon.
preparation: ECE so DSA was not my strong point at first. Did Striver sheet in the 2nd year summer and 1-2 leetcode mediums daily after that. For OOPs I read a C++ book and GFG articles. Embedded stuff was mostly from microprocessors course and my project. Took 3 mock interviews from club seniors.

selection: OA first, 90 mins, 3 sections: quant (puzzles n shit), DSA (2 medium leetcode style), and 1 sql query. Cleared OA, then 2 technical interviews. selection: OA with 4 sections: aptitude (rs agarwal level), ml basics (supervised vs unsupervised), 1 sql query, and a case study (like how would u improve customer retention). Cleared OA, then 1 round: case study discussion + HR. Case study was about a retail dataset, had to explain approach and metrics. HR was basic, asked about teamwork and why fractal.

advice: case study is imp, practice explaining ur thought process. ml basics are tested but not too deep.
tips: if ur branch is not core, this is a good backup. but dont expect high tech work, its more business oriented.

selection: OA first, 2 sections: quant (puzzles n probability) and 1 coding question (math heavy, like calculating binomial coefficients). selection: 5 rounds total. 1) Written aptitude test (30 Qs, mix of reasoning and maths) done in the campus hall. 2) Core Mechanical test – GD/TD on material strength, stress analysis and basic mining equipment, 45 mins. 3) Group discussion on "Sustainable mining" with 6 other candidates. 4) Technical interview – they asked about heat treatment, basic CAD drawings and a small case study on ore crushing. 5) HR round – typical "why Coal India?", strengths/weaknesses and salary expectations.
preparation: Started with Striver's DSA sheet for the aptitude part, solved ~80 LeetCode easy-medium for the technical bits. For core Mechanical, revisited GATE notes, watched a few NPTEL vids on mining fundamentals and asked seniors for past question banks. Practised GD topics from Quora and did mock HR with my batchmates.
experience: Overall it was kinda long but organised. Aptitude was straightforward, core test a bit tough but doable. GD felt a bit forced, HR was chill. SPOCs were helpful when the test portal lagged. Got the offer after 2 weeks.
advice: Brush up core subjects early – don't just rely on CP. Be ready with real examples from labs/projects for the technical interview. Show genuine interest in mining, not just the pay.
tips: Start prepping core topics at least 3 months before placements. Use GFG for quick DSA refresh, LeetCode for coding, and ask seniors for old Coal India papers. Keep a one‑page resume ready for GD/HR.

selection: 3 rounds. 1) Online Assessment – 2 coding problems (array & string) on HackerRank plus 20 aptitude Qs. 2) Technical interview – EEE core questions on power electronics, motor drives and a mini circuit design problem. 3) HR interview – fit‑culture, why Unilever and salary talk.
preparation: Did the Striver sheet for DSA (about 120 problems) and focused on easy‑medium LeetCode for the OA. For EEE core, used GFG articles on power electronics and re‑watched my 5th sem lectures on motor control. Also solved a few past Unilever OA from geeksforgeeks. Got OA tips from seniors who cleared last year.
experience: The OA was a bit glitchy, but I managed to submit. Technical interview was intense – they dug deep into my semester project on inverter design. HR was friendly, asked about my hobbies. Got the offer after a week.
advice: Don’t ignore the OA – practice coding under time pressure. For core, be ready to explain concepts with equations, not just definitions. Show that you know Unilever's sustainability drive.
tips: Do at least 2 mock OAs a week, use LeetCode's timed mode. Keep a cheat‑sheet of key EEE formulas. Talk to seniors about interview vibes, it helps reduce nerves.

selection: 2 rounds only. 1) DBMS coding round – they gave a schema and asked to write a SQL query to find top‑3 products by sales and also a small Python script to clean missing values. 2) HR interview – questions about teamwork, why data science, and a quick brain‑teaser about A/B testing.
preparation: Spent 2 months on Striver sheet for DSA basics, then focused on SQL – solved 200+ LeetCode DBMS problems and used GFG SQL cheat‑sheet. Watched Kaggle micro‑courses for basic ML concepts. My senior who interned at Walmart last summer gave me the OA link and some sample queries.
experience: The DBMS round was smooth, the portal was stable. The HR person was super nice, asked about my Kaggle projects and why I want to work at Walmart. Got the offer in 10 days, stipend was awesome.
advice: Know your SQL functions well – GROUP BY, window functions, and be ready to write quick Python pandas snippets. Show genuine interest in retail data and how you can add value.
tips: Practice SQL on HackerRank's DBMS section daily. Keep a one‑pager of your data‑science projects handy for HR. Talk to seniors who cleared Walmart – they have the exact question pattern.

selection: 4 rounds. 1) Online aptitude test – 30 MCQs (verbal, quantitative, logical). 2) Core Mechanical interview – they asked about thermodynamics cycles, material selection for heavy equipment and a mini case on pump design. 3) Resume screening – a 5‑minute talk with a senior manager focusing on my internship at a plant and leadership roles. 4) Final HR round – cultural fit, why Vedanta and salary expectations.
preparation: Did the Striver sheet for quick DSA warm‑up but mainly focused on aptitude from IndiaBix and GFG. For core, revisited my 8th sem notes, watched NPTEL videos on thermodynamics and read a few Vedanta annual reports. Seniors helped me polish my resume and gave mock resume talks.
experience: Aptitude was average difficulty. Core interview was deep – they wanted numbers, not just theory. Resume talk felt more like a casual chat, which I liked. HR was polite. Got the internship after 2 weeks.
advice: Don’t underestimate the core interview – be ready with calculations and real‑world examples. Keep your resume concise, highlight any plant‑level exposure. Show enthusiasm for the energy sector.
tips: Start core revision early, use GATE notes for quick recall. Do daily aptitude drills (15‑20 Qs). Practice a 2‑minute elevator pitch about your projects – it saves time in resume round.

selection: Just 1 round – a combined DSA + aptitude + ML test on the campus portal. 45 mins total: 2 coding problems (one array manipulation, one DP), 10 aptitude Qs and a short ML question where they gave a dataset and asked for a quick prediction approach.
preparation: Focused heavily on LeetCode (150 problems, mainly arrays & DP) and did daily 30‑min mock tests on HackerRank. For ML, completed the Coursera “Intro to ML” course and practiced a few Kaggle notebooks. Also solved aptitude from Indiabix. Senior who interned at GS gave me the exact pattern.
experience: The test was intense – time flew. Coding part was okay, I solved one fully and partially the DP. The ML question was conceptual, I wrote a few lines about linear regression. Got a call back for a PPO after 3 days.
advice: Time‑management is key – don’t get stuck on DP. For ML, they just want to see you know basic models, not heavy coding. Be honest if you don’t know something, they appreciate reasoning.
tips: Do timed LeetCode runs, keep a one‑page cheat‑sheet of common ML algorithms. Practice quick mental math for aptitude. Talk to seniors about the exact GS test vibe – it saves a lot of panic.

preparation: Did leetcode easy-medium, striver sheet for DSA, and ML concepts from Andrew Ng's course. Also practiced some ML projects from Kaggle.
experience: Good, interviewers were friendly and the process was smooth. SPOCs were helpful and kept us updated.
advice: Be thorough with leetcode and ML concepts. Projects are important too, so make sure they are well documented.
tips: Start preparing early, it's never too late. Be consistent and don't worry about rejections.

selection: round 1 was a quick HR chat on MS Teams, they asked about why I wanted to work in oil & gas and probed my CGPA, then threw a couple of situational questions like "describe a time you handled a tight deadline". round 2 was a deep dive into my semester projects – they loved the fluid dynamics sim I did for my 7th sem lab and kept asking me how I modeled the heat transfer equations, what tools I used and any roadblocks i faced. the interview lasted about 45 mins and they also hinted about a possible PPO if I performed well.
preparation: went through striver's dsa sheet just to keep basics fresh, but most of my prep was revisiting my project notebooks and reading up on basic process engineering concepts from GATE notes. also watched a few HR interview videos on YouTube to get the "tell me about yourself" flow right.
experience: the HR guy was super chill, kept the vibe light. the project round felt intense but since i had the code & results on hand, it went smoother than i expected. got the offer same week, felt pretty pumped.
advice: make sure you can explain every step of your project, not just the final outcome. HR will also test your motivation for the industry – have a couple of genuine reasons ready.
tips: keep a one‑pager of your projects handy (pdf) and practice explaining it in 2‑3 mins. also brush up on basic chemical engineering terms – they love tossing in a term like "mass balance" just to see if you nod.

selection: only one round – an online OA on HackerRank. first 20 min were puzzles (logic grid & a quick math brainteaser) that felt like a game of sudoku. then 2 coding problems: a medium level sliding‑window array question and a hard graph traversal that required Dijkstra. total time ~70 mins, and they gave instant feedback after each submission.
preparation: did the puzzles section from the "Crack the Coding Interview" book and solved daily leetcode easy‑medium for 2 months. also ran through the Striver A‑Z sheet for DSA patterns, especially graphs and two‑pointer tricks.
experience: the puzzles were a nice warm‑up, but the graph question caught me off guard – i spent too long on it and barely finished the array one. still got the intern offer, which was a surprise but happy!
advice: don't skip the non‑coding part – puzzles are there to gauge your problem‑solving speed. for DSA, focus on mastering the classic patterns rather than memorising every problem.
tips: set a timer while practicing puzzles, and after solving a coding problem, always review the editorial to see a cleaner solution. also keep a small cheat‑sheet of common graph algorithms.

selection: round 1: OA on Codility – 3 questions total. first was a simple string reverse, second a medium level DP on subsequence, third an OS‑themed question about deadlock detection using resource allocation graph. round 2: technical interview on Zoom, 1 hour. started with my AI summer project, then they asked a bunch of OS concepts – process scheduling, context switching, page replacement policies, plus a live coding on implementing LRU cache. ended with a quick HR wrap‑up about relocation to Pune.
preparation: crammed the Striver sheet for DSA, especially DP & graph sections. for OS, watched GATE Smashers videos and read Galvin chapters on memory management. also rehearsed my AI project pitch with seniors and did mock coding on LRU cache on a whiteboard.
experience: the OA felt balanced – the OS question was a curveball but i managed a decent answer. the tech interview was intense; the interviewer was very detail‑oriented but appreciated my clear explanation of the AI model. got the internship and a decent stipend, felt relieved.
advice: be ready for a mixed bag – they love to blend pure coding with system concepts. know the trade‑offs of different scheduling algorithms and be able to write clean code on the spot.
tips: practice writing OS‑related code (like LRU, producer‑consumer) on a plain editor, not IDE, to simulate the interview environment. also keep a one‑liner summary of each project ready.

selection: round 1: OA on HackerEarth – 2 coding problems (one array manipulation, one tree traversal) and 5 MCQs covering OS and DBMS basics. round 2: live technical interview (Google Meet) – started with DSA (they gave a medium level back‑tracking problem), then asked OS questions on process states and synchronization primitives, finally drilled into DBMS by asking me to design a simple schema for an e‑commerce order system and discuss normalization.
preparation: did leetcode easy‑medium daily plus a weekly deep‑dive on Striver's hard list. for OS, rewatched the GATE video series and solved past year questions. DBMS prep involved revisiting my college notes, doing a few design problems on geeksforgeeks, and sketching ER diagrams on paper.
experience: the OA was straightforward, I cleared both coding tasks within time. the interview was a marathon – the interviewer bounced between topics quickly, but I managed to keep my answers concise. got the internship and felt the process was fair.
advice: don't treat OS and DBMS as separate silos – many interviewers interlink them (e.g., locking in DBMS vs OS). be ready to write pseudo‑code for design questions, not just talk.
tips: keep a cheat‑sheet of common DBMS concepts (ACID, normalization forms) and OS terms (semaphores, mutex). practice drawing quick ER diagrams on a blank sheet – it saves time.

selection: round 1: telephonic HR screen – 10 min chat about CGPA, why Boeing, and availability. round 2: online OA on CodeSignal – 2 coding problems (one OOP‑centric class design, one DBMS query optimization). round 3: technical interview #1 – 30 min OOPs deep dive, they asked about inheritance hierarchies, virtual functions, and a live coding to implement a simple factory pattern. round 4: technical interview #2 – 35 min focused on DBMS, they gave a scenario to normalize a student‑course schema and asked about indexing strategies. round 5: final HR round – salary discussion, relocation to Bangalore, and a quick behavioural question about teamwork.
preparation: spent a month on Striver's sheet for DSA, but most of my time was on OOPs – read "Effective Java" chapters and practiced design patterns on hackerrank. for DBMS, solved GATE past papers and made flashcards for normal forms. also did a mock OA with a senior who gave me feedback on time management.
experience: the process was long but each round felt distinct. the OOP interview was the toughest – the interviewer kept pushing for edge cases. DBMS round was smoother thanks to my prep. overall, the stress was real but the offer at the end made it worth it.
advice: be comfortable writing small class hierarchies on a whiteboard and explain your design choices. for DBMS, know when to denormalize vs normalize and be ready to discuss indexes.
tips: practice the factory and singleton patterns by coding them from scratch a few times. also, sketch ER diagrams quickly on paper for DBMS questions. keep a calm mindset – five rounds can feel endless, but each is a chance to showcase something new.

selection: Salesforce SDE intern in IT branch, 4 rounds. Round 1: OA with 2 coding problems and a system design question. Round 2: DSA interview with 2 problems, one on arrays and another on DP. advice: Practice system design and DP problems. The OA was a bit tricky but I managed.

tips: Pay is lower than IT but good learning in core. Do check about service agreement and location before accepting.

selection: 2 rounds total. Round‑1 was a short online OA (45 min) with 2 core‑subjects questions – one on signals & systems and another on digital logic, both MCQ style. selection: 4 rounds. Round‑1: HR screening call (5 min) just confirming CGPA and availability. tips: keep a cheat‑sheet of common SQL patterns, practice a few mock aptitude tests the week before, and talk to seniors who have done TCS internships for the exact interview flow.

selection: 3 rounds. Round‑1: Resume screening (automated) – they filtered on CGPA >8 and keywords like "Java", "OOP". Round‑2: Aptitude + OOPs test (online, 40 min) – 10 MCQs on puzzles and 5 short coding snippets on inheritance/polymorphism. tips: keep a one‑page cheat‑sheet of OOP principles and common DBMS terms. practice writing SQL queries on paper. ask seniors for their exact interview questions; they often recall the DBMS scenario.

selection: 5 rounds – a marathon! Round‑1: HR tele‑call (3 min) just to confirm my CGPA (8.64) and interest in consulting. Round‑2: Online aptitude test (30 min) with 25 mixed questions – logical, quantitative and a tiny data‑interpretation set.
