preparation: did striver sheet + leetcode mediums, watched gaurav sen's system design playlist, revised CN from kurose ross. also did 2 mock interviews with a senior who was in flipkart last year.
experience: interviewers were chill but the system design round was tough cos i never did distributed systems before. the managerial round was more about my projects than dsa.
advice: flipkart loves system design even for interns, so dont skip it. also, they ask a lot of cn stuff so revise that properly.
tips: dont just mug up striver sheet, understand the patterns. and for system design, start with tinyurl or tinyurl-like problems.

selection: 2 rounds. Round 1 was an OA with 20 mcqs on ML basics, stats, and 2 coding qs (one was a pandas manipulation, other was a simple ml model eval). Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked about my ML projects, how i preprocessed data, and why i chose certain hyperparameters. They also asked a probability qs (bayes theorem). Results came next day.
preparation: revised ML from andrew ng's notes, did some leetcode for the coding part, and brushed up stats from a book. also made sure my projects were on github with readmes.
experience: the interviewers were super nice and asked me to explain my projects in detail. the coding part was easy but the ml qs were tricky.
advice: if ur branch isnt core, dont worry, they care more about ur projects and ml knowledge than ur branch.
tips: keep ur github clean and documented. they will ask u to explain every line of code u wrote.

selection: 1 round: a written test with 30 aptitude qs (time, work, distance, percentages) and 20 english comprehension qs. Then a group discussion on a random topic (they gave 'is remote work better than office work'). After that, a short HR round where they asked about my hobbies and why i wanted to join accenture. Results were announced in 2 hours.
preparation: did a few aptitude mocks from indiabix, revised english grammar from high school notes. seniors told me to keep the gd points simple and not to overcomplicate.
experience: the gd was fun, but the aptitude test was a bit lengthy. the hr round was just a formality.
advice: for non-tech companies, aptitude and english matter more than ur branch or cgpa.
tips: practice aptitude daily, even 10 qs a day helps. and for gd, speak first and keep ur points clear.

selection: 3 rounds. Round 1 was a resume shortlist + a 30-min online test with 2 coding qs (one oops concept implementation, other a medium dp). Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked oops concepts (polymorphism, inheritance, abstract classes) and then a system design question: design a notification system for sprinklr's dashboard. Round 3 was an HR round where they asked about my projects and why i wanted to join sprinklr. Offer came after a week.
preparation: revised oops from my sem notes, did leetcode mediums, and watched a system design video on notification systems. also went through my resume with a senior to make sure everything was clear.
experience: the oops qs were easy but the system design was tough cos i never designed a real-time system before. the hr round was relaxed.
advice: sprinklr loves oops and system design, so dont skip those topics even if ur branch isnt cse.
tips: for system design, start with tinyurl or a chat app. and for oops, know the difference between deep and shallow copy.

selection: 3 rounds. Round 1 was a resume shortlist + a written test with 20 mcqs on electrical engg basics (networks, machines, power systems) and 2 numericals. Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked about my projects (i had a power distribution simulation) and then a viva on my summer training report. Round 3 was an HR round where they asked about my interest in the plant role and relocation. Results came next day.
preparation: revised electrical networks and machines from my sem notes, made sure my resume highlighted my projects clearly. also practiced numericals from a book.
experience: the technical interview was chill but the viva was nerve-wracking cos they asked random qs from my report. the hr round was straightforward.
advice: for core companies, ur projects and core subjects matter more than ur cgpa. dont ignore them.
tips: keep ur resume one page and make sure u can explain every project in detail. and practice numericals daily.

selection: round 1: resume shortlisting – they filtered on cgpa >7.5 and the projects i listed (smart grid & iot). round 2: an online assessment of 40 mcqs – 15 aptitude, 10 DBMS (joins, normalization) and 15 OOPs (inheritance, polymorphism). round 3: a timed coding test on hackerearth – simple array & string problems, 2 dbms queries to write sql. round 4: technical interview – they dug deep into my DBMS project, asked about indexing, then a quick OOPs design question on a banking system. round 5: HR round – usual "strengths, weakness, why infosys, location" and a couple of behavioural questions. the whole thing stretched over 10 days.
preparation: started leetcode "striver dsa sheet" about 2 months back, did GFG sql practice every weekend, brushed up OOPs from my semester notes and watched a couple of SPOC videos on database fundamentals. also solved aptitude mocks from a pdf shared by seniors.
experience: overall decent, the OA felt a bit repetitive but the technical interview was chill thanks to the senior who was from my batch. wait time for result was annoying – almost a month.
advice: keep your resume crisp, put numbers (e.g. "improved data throughput by 20%"), and be ready to talk DBMS basics – they love asking about normalization levels.
tips: dont wait for the last minute, start leetcode + sql practice early summer. use the striver sheet for DSA, GFG for DBMS, and ask seniors for interview stories. also, relax before HR – they just want to see your attitude.

selection: round 1: referral screening – my senior in eee gave me a referral, they just checked my CGPA and a quick glance at my VLSI project (low‑power adder). round 2: technical interview – 30‑minute deep dive on DSA (linked list & segment tree), then they asked specifics about my VLSI design, layout tools and a couple of basic circuit questions.
preparation: since I already had an internship, i focused on revising my project report, went through the striver sheet for linked list problems, and brushed up basic circuit theory from GATE prep notes. also solved a few coding problems on codeforces for speed.
experience: the process felt like a formality after the referral, but the technical round was intense – they really tested my DSA fundamentals which i hadn't expected for a VLSI role.
advice: if you have a referral, treat it seriously – still be ready for solid DSA questions, not just hardware stuff.
tips: apply for referrals early, keep your project docs updated, and don't ignore DSA prep even for hardware roles. a quick striver sheet run‑through can save you.

selection: round 1: aptitude test – 30 mcqs covering quantitative, logical reasoning and a tiny bit of verbal. round 2: online coding assessment – 2 problems (one array manipulation, one simple DBMS query on hackerearth). round 3: technical interview – they asked about my DBMS coursework, a couple of SQL joins, and a coding question on linked list reversal.
preparation: did daily aptitude from indiabix, practiced OA on hackerearth using the "tcs nqt" set, and refreshed DBMS concepts via GFG articles and a short SPOC on sql basics. also solved leetcode easy problems for coding confidence.
experience: fairly smooth, the aptitude was easy, the OA was the toughest part but manageable. the interview panel was friendly, especially the senior who chatted about campus life.
advice: focus on the basics – they won't ask super hard coding but will test fundamentals of DBMS and problem‑solving speed.
tips: start aptitude prep at the beginning of the semester, mix OA practice with DBMS revision. keep a one‑page resume with clear project outcomes.

selection: single round: resume shortlisting followed by a quick online assessment – 20 MCQs on logical reasoning and a couple of coding snippets to write a function that checks palindrome. they decided within 2 days.
preparation: just cleaned up my resume (added quantifiable results), solved a few GFG puzzles on strings and did a mock OA on hackerearth for the same pattern. also skimmed through a senior's interview experience on the campus forum.
experience: super fast process, felt a bit rushed but the interviewers were polite. got the offer almost instantly.
advice: make sure your resume is error‑free; they scan it quickly before sending the OA link.
tips: even for a 1‑round process, do a mini OA practice – 15‑20 mins of coding daily keeps the brain active.

selection: round 1: aptitude test – 25 questions covering quantitative, logical and a tiny bit of verbal. round 2: DSA coding round – 2 problems (one two‑pointer on arrays, another binary search tree traversal) on hackerearth. round 3: technical interview – they asked about my AI coursework, then gave a DSA problem on recursion and finally a short discussion on system design basics.
preparation: started leetcode "striver dsa sheet" two months ago, did daily aptitude from a pocket book, and watched GFG videos on recursion and tree traversals. also brushed up AI basics from my semester notes because they love to link it with coding ability.
experience: the aptitude was easy, the coding round was moderate – I solved one problem fully, the other I stuck on but managed a partial solution. the interview was friendly, the interviewer even shared his own internship story.
advice: be ready for mixed questions – they love to combine AI theory with DSA coding, so don't ignore any subject.
tips: balance your prep: allocate time for aptitude, DSA, and core subject revision. use the striver sheet for DSA, GFG for quick concept refresh, and discuss your AI projects with seniors for confidence.

selection: OA: 3 DSA questions in 90 mins, 2 easy-medium, 1 medium-hard. Interview R1: 2 DSA questions, 1 easy, 1 medium. R2: system design round, design a recommendation system. R3: HR round, mostly about my resume and projects. Got selected.
preparation: Did Striver's SDE sheet, leetcode daily, and system design prep from GFG. Also revised OOPs concepts from my course textbooks.
experience: Good. The OA was tough, but I managed to solve all questions. The interviews were also good, but the system design round was a bit challenging.
advice: Focus on DSA and system design. Also, know your OOPs concepts well.
tips: Practice coding in a shared editor, as that's what they use for interviews. Also, be prepared for behavioural questions in the HR round.

selection: OA: 2 DSA questions in 60 mins, both medium. Interview R1: 1 DSA question, medium. R2: 1 OS question, medium. R3: 1 CN question, medium. R4: HR round, mostly about my resume and projects. Got selected.
preparation: Did leetcode and Striver's OS and CN sheets. Also revised my OS and CN course textbooks.
experience: Good. The OA was tough, but I managed to solve both questions. The interviews were also good, but the OS and CN questions were a bit challenging.
advice: Focus on DSA, OS, and CN. Also, know your projects well.
tips: Practice coding in a shared editor, as that's what they use for interviews. Also, be prepared for behavioural questions in the HR round.

selection: OA: aptitude test, 30 mins, quant and verbal. Interview R1: mostly about my resume and projects. R2: HR round, mostly about my resume and projects. Got selected.
preparation: Did aptitude practice on indiabix. Also revised my resume and projects.
experience: Good. The OA was tough, but I managed to solve all questions. The interviews were also good, but the aptitude test was a bit challenging.
advice: Focus on aptitude and know your projects well.
tips: Be prepared for behavioural questions in the HR round. Also, keep your CGPA decent, as many companies have a cutoff.

selection: OA: aptitude test, 30 mins, quant and verbal. Interview R1: mostly about my resume and projects. R2: OOPs question, medium. R3: HR round, mostly about my resume and projects. Got selected.
preparation: Did aptitude practice on indiabix. Also revised OOPs concepts from my course textbooks.
experience: Good. The OA was tough, but I managed to solve all questions. The interviews were also good, but the aptitude test and OOPs question were a bit challenging.
advice: Focus on aptitude and know your OOPs concepts well.
tips: Be prepared for behavioural questions in the HR round. Also, keep your CGPA decent, as many companies have a cutoff.

selection: OA: 2 DSA questions in 60 mins, both medium. Interview R1: mostly about my resume and projects. R2: HR round, mostly about my resume and projects. Got selected.
preparation: Did leetcode and Striver's SDE sheet. Also revised my resume and projects.
experience: Good. The OA was tough, but I managed to solve both questions. The interviews were also good, but the DSA questions were a bit challenging.
advice: Focus on DSA and know your projects well.
tips: Practice coding in a shared editor, as that's what they use for interviews. Also, be prepared for behavioural questions in the HR round.

selection: 5 rounds, started with an OA on leetcode mediums, then resume based screening, followed by 2 technical interviews (OOPs + ML concepts) and a final HR round. Google kept asking about my projects and how they relate to ML, so be ready with ur project explanations.
preparation: revised OOPs from GFG, did striver sheet for DSA, brushed up ML basics from andrew ng course notes. seniors helped with resume pointers.
experience: felt like a rollercoaster, was nervous for the ML interviews but they were chill. got grilled on my project's dataset cleaning part which i hadnt thought about much.
advice: dont just do leetcode blindly, understand the why behind solutions. projects matter more than u think.
tips: OA is key, practice on leetcode premium for google style questions. keep ur resume updated with quantifiable points.

selection: 2 rounds only! OA with 2 DSA questions (medium) and a system design round where they asked to design a distributed cache system. HR was just a formality.
preparation: did leetcode mediums and watched a youtube video on system design basics. OA prep was from striver sheet.
experience: felt too easy after the stress of other companies. system design round was fun, they gave hints when i got stuck.
advice: atlassian looks for clean code and scalable thinking, not just brute force solutions.
tips: practice writing clean code with comments. system design is not as scary as it seems.

selection: 1 round only! Just a 1-hour interview where they asked OOPs questions (inheritance, polymorphism) and a DBMS question on joins and indexing. Super quick process.
preparation: revised OOPs from GFG and did a few DBMS questions from leetcode. nothing fancy needed.
experience: felt like a breeze after all the other company interviews. they were very friendly.
advice: dont overthink, uber's process is straightforward if u know basics.
tips: keep ur OOPs concepts crystal clear. DBMS basics like joins and indexing are must.

selection: 5 rounds: OA with aptitude and basic coding, then 3 technical rounds (DSA, CN, OOPs) and HR. Wipro kept asking about my projects and how they relate to software development.
preparation: did aptitude from indiabix, practiced DSA on GFG, revised CN from a youtube playlist. seniors shared their Wipro prep tips.
experience: felt like a marathon, was exhausted by the end. HR round was just about location and bond.
advice: dont ignore aptitude, it's a big part of the process. projects matter a lot here.
tips: start early with aptitude prep. keep ur projects updated with clear descriptions.

selection: 4 rounds: OA with DSA questions, then 2 technical interviews (OOPs + CN) and HR. Salesforce asked a lot about my internship experience and how it relates to SDE role.
preparation: revised OOPs from GFG, did leetcode mediums, brushed up CN from a youtube video. internship experience was key here.
experience: felt like a mix of stress and excitement. technical rounds were tough but HR was chill.
advice: dont just focus on DSA, ur internship experience matters a lot for salesforce.
tips: keep ur internship projects updated. practice writing clean code with comments.

selection: uber AI internship, 5 rounds total. r1: online coding test (cn + dsa) 60 min, 2 medium leetcode style q's. r2: take‑home assignment on data pipelines (python + pandas). r3: technical interview (system design + ml basics). r4: HR chat about why AI, city pref, intern‑to‑full‑time talk. r5: final HR round + salary talk. all rounds were spaced over 2 weeks.
preparation: started with striver's dsa sheet, did ~150 leetcode easy/medium, brushed up cn concepts from gfg and coursera ml notes. practiced system design on exponents, used mock OA from geeksforgeeks. seniors who interned last yr gave me the take‑home template, i also solved a few past uber assignments on hackerearth.
experience: first test was okay, but the take‑home felt heavy (got stuck on data cleaning). interviewers were chill, they asked about my project on traffic prediction and some basic conv nets. HR was friendly, asked about relocation to gurgaon. overall a mix of stress and excitement, got the offer in 3 days.
advice: show genuine interest in AI products, not just coding. be ready to discuss any ML project you listed, even if it was a class demo.
tips: keep a repo of your ml notebooks, practice coding on a plain editor (no IDE), do mock HR calls with seniors, and dont forget to ask about intern‑to‑ppo path.

selection: mercedes‑benz r&d internship, 5 rounds. r1: aptitude (quant + verbal) + core ece quiz (circuits, control). r2: GD on "future of electric vehicles". r3: project deep‑dive (i explained my power‑electronics capstone). r4: technical interview covering motor control and PCB design. r5: HR round – relocation, stipend, full‑time PPO talk.
preparation: revived my 3rd sem notes for control systems, solved past core questions from gfg. did daily aptitude from indiabix, watched youtube videos on motor drives. practiced GD with friends, used striver sheet for dsa just in case. asked seniors for typical mercedes interview questions, they sent a few pdfs.
experience: the aptitude was easy, core quiz a bit tricky but i cleared it. GD was lively, many of us argued about battery tech. technical interview was deep – they asked me to derive a PWM duty cycle formula on the spot, i fumbled a bit. HR was polite, told me about possible PPO after 6 months. got the offer, but stipend was lower than expected.
advice: be solid on your core ece subjects, especially power electronics, and have a clear story for your project. show that u know about mercedes future tech.
tips: don’t ignore the aptitude, many lose there. prepare 2‑3 bullet points for your project, practice quick sketch of circuit diagrams, and ask seniors about the interview flow.

selection: tcs mechanical internship, only 1 round – an online OA that mixed aptitude, basic coding (java), and a short HR chat after you submit the test.
preparation: did a quick run through of aptitude on indiabix, solved a few java basics on hackerearth, and read tcs campus interview experiences on quora. seniors told me the OA is usually 30 mins, so i timed myself.
experience: the OA was straightforward, 10 aptitude q's, 2 coding problems (both easy). got a generic HR call later, they asked about my CGPA and why mechanical, nothing technical. got the intern offer next day, but the stipend was just 10k/month – kinda low.
advice: if you just want an easy win, tcs is good, but weigh the pay vs effort. be ready to talk about any mini‑project you did, even if it’s just a CAD model.
tips: focus on speed for the OA, keep your resume simple, and ask the HR about future conversion chances (ppo).

selection: arista eee internship, 3 rounds. r1: online OA (coding + cn questions) 90 mins. r2: technical interview focusing on projects and networking basics. r3: HR round – culture fit, internship duration, possible full‑time offer.
preparation: cracked the arista OA list from geeksforgeeks, solved 80 leetcode cn problems (graphs, trees). refreshed my senior design project on IoT sensor network, wrote a short ppt. practiced mock interviews with seniors who interned at arista last yr, they gave me the typical system‑design question on packet switching.
experience: the OA was tough – two coding q's on trie and sliding window, plus a cn question on spanning tree. i cleared it after 2 attempts. technical interview dug deep into my sensor project, asked about power budget calculations, and a couple of networking protocols. HR was chill, talked about relocation to bangalore. got the offer after a week, stipend was decent.
advice: be ready to discuss both hardware and software sides of your project, arista likes full‑stack thinking. also, show enthusiasm for networking tech.
tips: keep a one‑pager of your project handy, practice explaining hardware schematics in plain English, and do a timed OA practice every other day.

selection: microsoft ece internship, single round – a technical interview covering OOPs, dsa and a mini system‑design case. no separate HR, they merged it.
preparation: used leetcode blind 75, focused on medium OOP questions, reviewed system design basics from educative. brushed up dsa from striver's sheet, especially trees and dp. asked a senior who interned at ms about the interview flow, got a few sample design prompts.
experience: the interview started with a quick OOP scenario (design a car class hierarchy), then a coding problem on binary tree traversal, and finally a design question about a low‑latency cache. I stumbled on the cache part but managed to propose a simple LRU solution. interviewer was supportive, gave hints. got the offer after 5 days, stipend was great.
advice: focus on clear OOP fundamentals, be ready to whiteboard design even if you’re on a call. microsoft values clarity over raw speed.
tips: practice explaining your thought process out loud, keep a cheat‑sheet of common design patterns, and do a mock interview with a friend to simulate the merged format.

selection: Mu Sigma had a 5 round selection process: resume screening, aptitude test, puzzles, technical interview, and HR interview. The aptitude test was straightforward, but the puzzles were a bit tricky. The technical interview was based on my final year project and ECE core subjects. The HR interview was about my interests and why I wanted to join Mu Sigma.
preparation: I prepared for aptitude by solving puzzles from GFG and Indiabix. For the technical interview, I revised my project and ECE core subjects.
experience: The experience was good. The puzzles were a bit challenging, but the SPOCs were helpful.
advice: Be thorough with your project and ECE core subjects. Also, practice puzzles regularly.
tips: Start preparing early. The puzzles can be tricky, so give them enough time.

selection: Qualcomm had a 2 round selection process: resume screening and technical interview. The technical interview was based on my final year project, OOPs concepts, and a coding question.
preparation: I prepared for the technical interview by revising my project and OOPs concepts. I also practiced coding questions from Leetcode.
experience: The experience was good. The technical interview was straightforward.
advice: Be thorough with your project and OOPs concepts. Also, practice coding questions regularly.
tips: Start preparing early. The technical interview can be straightforward, but it's important to be prepared.

selection: Salesforce had a 3 round selection process: online assessment, technical interview, and HR interview. The online assessment included DSA questions, CN questions, and a resume review. The technical interview was based on DSA and CN.
preparation: I prepared for the online assessment by solving DSA questions from the Striver sheet and CN questions from GFG. I also prepared for the technical interview by revising DSA and CN.
experience: The experience was good. The online assessment was a bit challenging, but the SPOCs were helpful.
advice: Be thorough with DSA and CN. Also, practice coding questions regularly.
tips: Start preparing early. The online assessment can be challenging, so give it enough time.

selection: Optiver had a 4 round selection process: online assessment, puzzles, technical interview, and HR interview. The online assessment included ML questions and a resume review. The puzzles were a bit tricky. The technical interview was based on ML and a coding question.
preparation: I prepared for the online assessment by solving ML questions from Kaggle and a resume review from seniors. I also prepared for the technical interview by revising ML and practicing coding questions from Leetcode.
experience: The experience was good. The puzzles were a bit challenging, but the SPOCs were helpful.
advice: Be thorough with ML and coding questions. Also, practice puzzles regularly.
tips: Start preparing early. The puzzles can be tricky, so give them enough time.

selection: Walmart Global Tech had a 5 round selection process: resume screening, system design, ML interview, technical interview, and HR interview. The system design was a bit tricky. The ML interview was based on ML concepts and a coding question. The technical interview was based on system design and a coding question.
preparation: I prepared for the system design by solving system design questions from GFG and a resume review from seniors. I also prepared for the ML interview by revising ML concepts and practicing coding questions from Leetcode. For the technical interview, I revised system design and practiced coding questions from Leetcode.
experience: The experience was good. The system design was a bit challenging, but the SPOCs were helpful.
advice: Be thorough with system design, ML concepts, and coding questions. Also, practice puzzles regularly.
tips: Start preparing early. The system design can be tricky, so give it enough time.

selection: only 1 round, HR interview. They asked about my metallurgy projects, summer internships, and why i wanted to join l&t. basic hr stuff like strengths, weaknesses, family background. result came in 2 days.
preparation: revised some core subjects like extractive metallurgy and material science. went through my resume and projects once. nothing fancy, just confidence.
experience: super chill round, interviewer was very supportive. cgpa 8.85 helped but they didn't even ask for it. got the offer within a week.
advice: keep ur metallurgy basics strong, they ask random stuff from ur projects too.
tips: if u have a metallurgy project, highlight it. l&t is a good start for core companies.

selection: 1 coding round on hackerrank, 2 questions in 60 mins. one was a dp problem, other was a tree traversal variant. no interview, just the coding test. result mailed after 3 days.
preparation: did striver sheet dp and tree sections. practiced on hackerrank only. didn't touch anything else, was too confident lol.
experience: easy peasy, but i messed up the dp question due to time pressure. still got selected because the other question was clean.
advice: dont be overconfident, time management is key in these short rounds.
tips: practice striver sheet on hackerrank interface, it's different from leetcode.

selection: 4 rounds: 1. online assessment (leetcode medium 2 ques, 75 mins), 2. technical interview (dsa + ml basics), 3. system design round (they gave a problem to design a recommendation system), 4. HR round (culture fit, relocation). result after 2 weeks.
preparation: revised leetcode patterns, did a few ml projects on kaggle. prepared system design basics from grokking the system design interview. got a referral from a senior which helped a lot.
experience: stressful but fun. technical round was tough, interviewer kept asking follow-ups. system design was new for me, struggled a bit.
advice: if u have a referral, use it. walmart's ml round is not easy, be ready with ur projects.
tips: keep ur projects clean and explainable. they ask a lot about ur approach.

selection: 2 rounds: 1. aptitude test (quant, logical reasoning, english), 2. case study + personal interview (they gave a business problem to solve, then discussed resume and general fit). result in 5 days.
preparation: did a few aptitude mocks from indiabix. revised my resume and mechanical projects. didn't prepare much for case study, just common sense.
experience: aptitude was easy, case study was tricky but manageable. interviewer was chill, asked about my mech projects and why zS.
advice: mechanical guys, don't skip aptitude prep. zS loves quant and logical reasoning.
tips: practice case studies from mckinsey or bcg prep sites, they are similar.

selection: 5 rounds: 1. online assessment (leetcode medium 2 ques), 2. technical interview (dsa + oops), 3. system design round (design a url shortener), 4. another technical round (more dsa + low level design), 5. HR round (culture fit, relocation). result after 3 weeks.
preparation: did striver sheet twice, practiced leetcode medium-hard. revised oops and system design from grokking. got a lot of help from seniors who had given google before.
experience: super intense, especially the system design rounds. technical rounds were okay but low level design was tough. hr was just formality.
advice: google's process is long but worth it. dont skip system design prep, it's the make or break round.

selection: Round 1: a single online assessment on HackerRank. 45 min puzzle section (logic & pattern games) + 2 coding questions (one easy array, one medium DP). I solved the puzzle but got stuck on the DP, ended with 1.5/2.0. They also asked a quick project snippet from my resume, but it was just a chat.
preparation: Did a lot of puzzles on brainzilla and leetcode easy set. Followed Striver DSA sheet (~200 qns) and brushed up project basics from my 3rd year IoT module. Senior who interned at a bank gave me OA tips, especially time‑boxing puzzles.
experience: It was kinda fast paced, felt like they wanted to see if u can think under pressure. The interviewers were polite, no crazy brain‑teasers.
advice: Maybe give a bit more time for the DP question, it felt rushed. Also a small intro about your projects could help.
tips: Start practising puzzles early, set a timer. Do at least 3 mock OAs a week. Consistency beats cramming.

selection:

Round 2: technical interview on data science – they asked about regression, a Kaggle mini‑project and a quick Python coding on pandas.

experience: Overall good vibe, interviewers were tech‑savvy and asked real‑world stuff. The project round felt like a mini‑presentation, which was fun.

selection:
Round 1: resume screening + basic aptitude test (verbal & quantitative). Got 62% and moved ahead.

preparation: Solved aptitude packs from GATE prep, focused on quantitative and verbal. Watched a few YouTube videos on basic mechanical design concepts. Asked seniors from last batch who interned at Vedanta for interview pointers.

selection:
Round 1: resume & HR screening – 15 min call, they checked my GPA and asked why Qualcomm. 
Round 2: technical interview – 45 mins covering DBMS (SQL joins, indexing) and a system design question about building a URL shortener. I sketched high level components. 
Round 3: coding round on LeetCode style – 2 problems, one medium arrays and one hard graph, 70 mins total. I solved the array but ran out of time on the graph.
preparation: Did Striver sheet + DBMS cheat sheet from GFG. Followed system design videos on YouTube (Gaurav Sen). Practised coding on LeetCode (300 qns) and mock system design on Pramp. Seniors who interned at Qualcomm gave me interview anecdotes.
experience: Mixed feelings – the HR call was super casual, the technical rounds were intense but fair. The system design part was the toughest for me.
advice: More emphasis on scaling basics would help. Also, give a clear trade‑off analysis in design questions.
tips: Write down the core components of common systems (caching, DB, queue) on a sticky note. Do at least one mock system design per week. Keep practising graphs.

selection:

preparation: did leetcode hard set, striver sheet, and ml basics from andrew ng's course. practiced mental math on a quant site. seniors shared some past OA qs.

experience: technical mcqs were tough, but i managed to clear. HR was straightforward. overall, not too bad for a mechanical internship.

selection: Hindalco was a single round: resume shortlist + HR round. No technical round, just HR questions like why metallurgy, relocation, and basic HR stuff. Super chill, no pressure.

selection: 5 rounds total. Round1 was an OA (30 mins) with 15 aptitude q's and 2 easy coding problems. Round2 was a DSA interview where they asked medium leetcode style questions on trees and DP. Round3 was a ML round – they showed a tiny dataset and asked to explain a simple linear regression and a couple of feature engineering ideas. Round4 was a PPO/fit interview where they discussed my previous internship and whether I could join as a full‑time after the internship. Finally Round5 was HR – they asked about my campus life, why Google and my salary expectations. All rounds spread over a week.
preparation: Did the Striver DSA sheet on leetcode, solved a bunch of GFG problems for trees & DP, practiced OA on HackerRank using past Google OA sets. For ML I brushed up Coursera ML specialization notes and did a quick Kaggle mini‑project. Also asked seniors from 2022 batch to mock interview me for the fit round.

tips: Start OA practice at least a month early, keep a one‑page cheat sheet for ML formulas, and rehearse your project story with a friend. Sleep well before the fit round!

selection: 2 rounds. First was a pure aptitude test (20 MCQs on quantitative, logical and verbal) lasting 30 mins on their portal. Second was an HR round where they asked about my interest in materials, why Kolkata and what I expect from the internship.
preparation: Aptitude from Indiabix and a few practice sets on PrepInsta. For HR I watched some interview videos of senior metallurgists and practiced answering “why this company?” with my own reasons.
experience: Aptitude was easy, I finished in 12 mins. HR was relaxed, the recruiter was friendly and even asked about my final year project on corrosion. Felt good overall.
advice: Be ready with a short, crisp story about why you chose mining/materials – they love genuine passion.
tips: Do a quick mock HR with a senior or friend, and keep a notebook of key project points. Also keep your webcam tidy – background matters!

selection: 1 round only – a technical interview focusing on DSA and my hardware projects. They asked me to solve a medium level array problem on the whiteboard and then deep‑dove into my PCB design project, asking about signal integrity and component choices.
preparation: Cracked the Striver sheet for arrays & bit manipulation on leetcode, reviewed my own project slides, and asked a senior from the robotics club to do a mock project Q&A. Also skimmed a few GFG articles on signal integrity basics.
experience: Nerves were high at the start, but once I started talking about my project the vibe changed – the interviewer seemed genuinely interested. The DSA question was straightforward, I solved it in 7 mins.
advice: Don’t just memorize project specs, be ready to explain why you chose each part. That often decides the interview.
tips: Keep a one‑page summary of your top project (block diagram, challenges, results) handy. Practice coding on paper to avoid IDE reliance.

selection: 1 round – a combined interview on my projects and computer networks (CN). They asked me to walk through my IoT gateway project and then threw a few CN questions like OSI layers, TCP three‑way handshake and a simple routing scenario.
preparation: Re‑watched my own project demo videos, wrote a TL;DR script for it. For CN I read the NPTEL lecture notes and solved a couple of GFG networking quizzes. Also chatted with seniors from the networking lab for quick pointers.
experience: The interview felt like a conversation; the interviewer liked the hands‑on part of my project and only asked basic CN concepts which I knew well. Finished in under 30 mins.
advice: Even if the role is not pure networking, expect at least one CN question – keep the basics fresh.
tips: Prepare a 2‑minute elevator pitch for any project and memorize the OSI model order. A quick mock with a friend helps a lot.

selection: 4 rounds. First was the TCS Ninja online test with aptitude, verbal and 2 coding questions (one easy string, one medium array). Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked DBMS stuff like normalization, ACID properties and a DSA question on linked list reversal. Round 3 was another technical round with OS concepts like paging, deadlocks and a DSA question on finding the longest substring without repeating characters. Final round was HR where they asked about relocation, why TCS and my projects.
preparation: Started leetcode after 5th sem, did around 100 problems. Revised DBMS from gate smashers youtube and OS from neso academy. Aptitude from indiabix and some mock tests.
experience: Interviewers were chill but the online test link had issues in the lab. SPOCs helped but it was a bit messy. Overall smooth but tiring day.
advice: Dont stress too much on hard problems, basic DSA and CS fundamentals are enough. Be clear with DBMS and OS concepts.
tips: TCS comes early so dont wait for other companies. Start prepping from 5th sem itself, dont leave it for last moment.

selection: 3 rounds. First was the online assessment with 2 DSA questions (one medium tree, one hard graph) and some OS questions. Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked about process synchronization, virtual memory and a DSA question on finding the kth smallest element in a BST. Round 3 was a bar raiser round with system design basics like designing a url shortener and some OOPs concepts like polymorphism and inheritance.
preparation: Did striver sheet completely, around 200 problems. Revised OS from gate smashers and system design from grokking the system design interview. Also did some GFG OOPs questions.
experience: Interviewers were very strict but the process was smooth. Got the offer after the bar raiser round which was a relief.
advice: Amazon focuses a lot on DSA and OS, so be strong in those areas. System design is also important even for VLSI roles.
tips: Start prepping early, dont leave it for the last moment. Join some coding groups on whatsapp for daily problems and discussions.

selection: 3 rounds. First was the online assessment with aptitude and some core mechanical questions. Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked about thermodynamics, heat transfer and a case study on process optimization. Round 3 was the HR round where they asked about my projects, why Bosch and my expectations.
preparation: Revised all core subjects from 6th sem onwards. Did some aptitude from indiabix and practiced case studies with seniors. Also revised some process safety basics.
experience: Interviewers were very experienced and asked detailed questions. The process was smooth but a bit tiring. Got the offer after the HR round.
advice: Be clear with your core subjects, they ask a lot of basics. Also be prepared for case studies and HR questions.
tips: Bosch comes late in the season so dont lose hope if u dont get any core offers early. Keep trying and u will get one eventually.

selection: 4 rounds. First was the online assessment with aptitude and 2 coding questions. Round 2 was a group discussion on a case like improving customer experience for a telecom company. Round 3 was a technical interview where they asked about OS concepts like scheduling, memory management and a DSA question on finding the longest palindromic substring. Final round was the HR round where they asked about my projects, why Wipro and my expectations.
preparation: Started DSA after 5th sem, did around 150 problems. Revised OS from neso academy and practiced GD with friends. Also did some aptitude from indiabix.
experience: Process was smooth but a bit long. Got the PPO after the HR round which was a nice feeling. Interviewers were friendly.
advice: Be clear with OS concepts and basic DSA. Also practice GD and HR rounds as they are important for PPOs.
tips: Wipro comes early so start prepping from 5th sem itself. Dont wait for other companies to start prepping.

selection: 3 rounds. First was the online assessment with 2 DSA questions (one medium array, one hard dynamic programming) and some OOPs questions. Round 2 was a technical interview where they asked about system design basics like designing a chat application and some OOPs concepts like inheritance and polymorphism. Round 3 was a bar raiser round with a DSA question on finding the longest common subsequence and some questions about my projects and expectations.
preparation: Did striver sheet completely, around 200 problems. Revised system design from grokking the system design interview and OOPs from GFG. Also did some mock interviews with seniors.
experience: Interviewers were very experienced and asked detailed questions. The process was smooth but a bit tiring. Got the offer after the bar raiser round.
advice: Uber focuses a lot on DSA, system design and OOPs, so be strong in those areas. Also be prepared for detailed questions about your projects.
tips: Start prepping early, dont leave it for the last moment. Join some coding groups on whatsapp for daily problems and discussions.

selection: 3 rounds total. Round 1 was an online assessment – 30 min DSA (mix of arrays & strings) + 10 min resume‑screen questions. Round 2 was a technical interview where they dug into my ML projects, asked a couple of probability‑based questions and gave a live coding problem on pandas. Round 3 was a short HR chat about why Salesforce and my future goals. Got the offer same week.
preparation: Did ~180 leetcode problems (focus on easy+medium), followed the Striver DSA sheet, skimmed GFG for quick tricks, brushed up ML basics from Coursera SPOC and Kaggle notebooks. Got my resume reviewed by seniors from CSE batch‑2022 and added a tiny “impact” metric for each project.
experience: The coding part was smooth – I solved the array question in 8 mins. The ML interview was a bit nerve‑wracking; they asked me to explain feature engineering for time‑series, which I hadn’t practiced enough. HR was chill, just asked about campus life. Overall mixed feelings – happy with the package but wish I’d prepped more on system design.
advice: Don’t just grind DSA, also be ready to talk end‑to‑end ML pipelines. Keep your project stories short but data‑driven. If you have a friend who interned there, ask for a referral – it speeds up the resume filter.
tips: Practice coding on a whiteboard or shared doc (Google Meet) to simulate the live coding. Keep a one‑pager for each project with problem, solution, impact. Sleep well before the OA and stay hydrated during the interview.

selection: 4 rounds. First a 45‑min aptitude + OS MCQ test. Then an OA (2 hrs) with 3 coding questions (one graph, one DP, one concurrency). After that a technical interview on OS concepts and a system‑design chat. Finally an HR round where they asked about why Pune and my campus activities.
preparation: Cracked 200+ GFG aptitude questions, re‑watched NPTEL OS videos, solved the Striver sheet for graphs & DP, and practiced a few OAs from recent campus drives (mostly on HackerRank). I also did a mock system‑design with a senior who got placed at Microsoft.
experience: Aptitude was okay, I made a couple of silly mistakes on bit‑masking. OA was the toughest – the concurrency problem made me freeze for a minute. Technical interview was friendly; they liked my explanation of page replacement algorithms. HR was pretty generic. Got the offer after 2 weeks.
advice: Focus on OS fundamentals – page tables, deadlocks, scheduling – they love those tiny scenario questions. Also, time‑manage during OA; if stuck, move to the next problem and come back later.
tips: Do a quick 5‑minute revision of OS key formulas before the test. Use a timer while solving OAs to build stamina. Bring a small notebook to jot down quick algorithm steps during the interview.

selection: 3 rounds. Round 1: a 30‑min aptitude test (numeric & logical). Round 2: an online assessment (2 coding problems, one on string manipulation, another on basic data‑structures). Round 3: HR round – they asked about my interest in digital transformation and campus clubs.
preparation: Solved 120 aptitude questions from previous Wipro drives, practiced coding on LeetCode (focus on easy/medium strings), and went through a couple of Wipro OA examples shared on GFG. Also brushed up my resume with help from seniors in the IT batch.
experience: Aptitude was straightforward, but I mis‑read a question on series sum. The OA was moderate – I could solve the string problem quickly but got stuck on the linked‑list one for a while. HR was relaxed, just a quick chat. Got the internship offer after a week.
advice: Read the OA instructions carefully, they sometimes hide constraints in the description. For digital roles, be ready to talk about any small automation project you did, even if it was just a script.
tips: Practice at least one string problem daily for a week before the drive. Keep a one‑line bullet for each project in your resume – it helps HR remember you.

selection: Only 1 round – a 90‑min online assessment (coding OA) that was shared via a Google Form. It had 2 problems: one greedy array task and one back‑tracking puzzle. A referral from a senior who works at Google also popped up in the email, so the screen was fast.
preparation: Did the Striver sheet’s greedy section, solved the back‑tracking problems on LeetCode (approx. 30), and practiced a few Google‑style OAs from recent campus batches. Also asked a senior for a quick resume check – they suggested adding the ‘Google Cloud’ badge I earned.
experience: The greedy problem was easy, solved in 12 mins. The back‑tracking one was tricky; I spent 40 mins but eventually got it right after a small hint from the test’s sample input. Felt a rush when the result popped up – got the offer same day!
advice: Even if you have a referral, the OA still decides everything. Focus on writing clean code fast, and always test edge cases before submitting.
tips: Use the “run” feature often to catch bugs early. Keep a cheat‑sheet of common patterns (two‑pointer, sliding window, back‑track) handy on your desk.

selection: 4 rounds. Round 1: a puzzle‑heavy aptitude test (logic & lateral thinking). Round 2: OA with 2 DSA questions (one on segment trees, one on probability). Round 3: technical interview covering ML concepts and a quick coding on numpy. Round 4: HR + PPO discussion – they talked about converting the internship into a full‑time Quant role.
preparation: Did a lot of puzzle books (mind‑teasers from interviewbit), solved probability problems from the Striver sheet, practiced segment tree implementation on GFG, and brushed up ML basics via Coursera’s “ML Foundations”. Also went through past PPO stories from seniors in the AI club.
experience: Aptitude was fun but time‑pressured – I missed a couple of puzzles. OA was decent; segment tree took me 30 mins but I got it right after a small bug fix. Technical interview was intense – they asked about Monte‑Carlo simulations and I could only give a high‑level answer. HR was nice, explained the PPO timeline clearly. Got the PPO after 3 weeks.
advice: For quant roles, be comfortable with both DSA and math puzzles. Practice probability in a coding context (simulate in python). Show genuine interest in finance during HR.
tips: Keep a small notebook of common puzzles and their solution tricks. Do a quick mock interview on probability coding with a friend. Sleep early before the day of the OA – mental stamina matters.

selection: OA was the first round. It had 4 parts: 1) 2 coding questions (one was a hashmap thing, the other was a string manipulation), 2) 5 system design questions, 3) 10 puzzles, 4) 10 DSA questions. Then there was a 2 hour coding test with 2 questions (one was a simple linked list question, the other was a DP problem). The final round was a technical interview with 2 coding questions (one was a medium level DSA question, the other was a string manipulation question).
preparation: Did the leetcode easy and medium questions, and the striver sheet. Also practiced system design from the system design primer. For puzzles, I just searched for common ones online.
experience: The OA was tough, but I managed to clear it. The coding test was also tough, but I managed to solve the first question. The interview was fine, I think I did well.
advice: Start preparing for the OA early. Make sure you understand the basics of DSA and system design. Also, practice puzzles regularly.
tips: For the coding test, make sure you understand the problem statement clearly. Also, dont panic if you cant solve a question, just move on to the next one.

selection: Just 1 round, which was an online test. It had 2 parts: 1) 50 aptitude questions, 2) a short personality test. The results were announced after 2 days.
preparation: Practiced aptitude questions from indiabix and the GFG aptitude sheet. For the personality test, I just searched for common questions online.
experience: The aptitude test was easy, but the personality test was tough. I managed to clear both, though.
advice: Start preparing for the aptitude test early. Make sure you understand the basics of civil engineering. Also, practice the personality test regularly.
tips: For the aptitude test, make sure you understand the problem statement clearly. Also, dont panic if you cant solve a question, just move on to the next one.

selection: 3 rounds. Round 1: resume shortlist + referral check. Round 2: 90 min OA with 3 sections: DSA (2 medium leetcode-style), DBMS (sql queries, normalization), and aptitude (time-speed-distance, percentages). Round 3: 2 back-to-back technical interviews, first on DSA (graph + greedy), second on OS concepts (deadlocks, paging) and a system design question (design a rate limiter). Result came in 3 days.
preparation: did striver sheet twice, 300 leetcode problems, and dbms from gate smash notes. seniors helped with referral. weekly mock oas on hirepro.
experience: oa was easy but the interviews were brutal. interviewers kept pushing for optimal solutions and edge cases. one interviewer asked me to write a deadlock detection algo on whiteboard.
advice: referral helps a lot but dont rely only on it. practice writing clean code and explaining ur thought process.
tips: keep ur resume 1 page, highlight projects with quantifiable impact. for dbms, revise joins and indexing.

selection: only 1 round: 2-hour OA on hackerrank. 15 puzzles (river crossing, weighing problems) + 20 DSA (arrays, strings, recursion). no interviews. result in 24 hrs.
preparation: puzzles from geeksforgeeks and puzzles book by shakuntala devi. leetcode easy-medium for DSA. did 2 mock oas on mettl.
experience: oa was fun but time was tight. puzzles were tricky but solvable if u think outside the box. DSA was standard.
advice: dont get stuck on one puzzle, move on and come back. time management is key.
tips: practice puzzles with timer. for DSA, focus on edge cases like empty strings or large inputs.

selection: 5 rounds. Round 1: written test on core civil (fluid mechanics, structural analysis, geotech). Round 2: ML basics (supervised vs unsupervised, bias-variance). Round 3: technical interview on projects + core subjects. Round 4: psychometric test. Round 5: panel interview (research interests, SOP discussion). Result took 2 weeks.
preparation: revised core from semester notes and made short notes. did andrew ng ml course on coursera. seniors helped with sop and lor drafts.
experience: process was long but smooth. interviewers were very supportive and gave feedback. the psychometric test was weird though.
advice: start early with sop and lor. core subjects are important but they also value research potential.
tips: for core, practice numerical problems. for ML, revise basics and be ready to explain projects in detail.

selection: 3 rounds. Round 1: aptitude test (100 questions, 60 mins, negative marking). Round 2: technical test (core ece: signals, networks, control systems). Round 3: HR + technical combined. HR asked about family background, willingness to relocate, and shift timings. Technical was on resume projects and basic ece concepts. Result in 1 day.
preparation: aptitude from rs agarwal and online tests. core subjects from semester notes and gate material. seniors shared previous year papers.
experience: process was quick and efficient. interviewers were professional but not very interactive. hr round was straightforward.
advice: core ece fundamentals are crucial. be clear about ur willingness to work in shifts or relocate.
tips: for aptitude, practice speed and accuracy. for core, focus on understanding concepts rather than mugging up formulas.

selection: 5 rounds. Round 1: aptitude (30 questions, 30 mins). Round 2: technical test (thermodynamics, strength of materials, manufacturing). Round 3: group discussion (topic: 'automation in industries'). Round 4: technical interview (resume + core subjects). Round 5: HR interview (cultural fit, expectations). Result in 3 days.
preparation: aptitude from rs agarwal. core subjects from semester notes and made formula sheets. seniors helped with gd topics.
experience: gd was fun but some ppl dominated. technical interview was chill, interviewer was very encouraging. hr round was casual.
advice: dont underestimate aptitude and gd. they matter more than u think.
tips: for gd, speak clearly and confidently. for technical, revise formulas and be ready to explain concepts with examples.

selection: 3 rounds total. Round‑1 was an online aptitude test (quant + logical) followed by a short coding snippet on OOPs (write a class for a chemical reaction). Round‑2 was a technical interview where they dug deep into OOP concepts, inheritance and asked me to explain my final year project on process simulation. Round‑3 was HR + PPO discussion – they talked about the PPO offer, salary and relocation to Mumbai. The whole thing felt like a typical TCS drive but with a bit more focus on OOPs because of the chemical branch tag.
preparation: I brushed up OOPs from Java videos on YouTube, solved a bunch of aptitude papers from previous TCS NQT, and did daily leetcode easy problems (mainly strings & arrays). My seniors gave me the TCS striver sheet and a few GFG OOP lists. Also went through some SPOC notes on chemical process modelling to sound confident about my project.
experience: It was kinda smooth after the first aptitude glitch (my laptop froze for 2 mins). The OOP interview was a bit nerve‑racking but the interviewers were chill. PPO talk was a pleasant surprise – got a 9.4 LPA offer which felt good for a placement.
advice: Know your OOP fundamentals inside out and be ready to map them to your branch projects. Don't underestimate the aptitude – time‑manage well. Also ask clear questions during the PPO chat, like growth path and location support.
tips: Keep a cheat‑sheet of OOP concepts, practice at least 5 leetcode easy/day, and do a mock OA on your phone before the real test. Talk to seniors who cleared TCS recently – they know the exact pattern.

selection: Only 2 rounds. First was an OA with 2 DSA questions (one array rotation, one simple graph traversal) plus a short aptitude section. Second round was a combined technical + HR where they asked DSA basics, my mechanical projects, and then discussed the PPO offer and salary. The whole drive was quick – got the result the next day.
preparation: Since I'm a mech student, I focused on GFG DSA basics and solved the Striver sheet up to linked lists. Also watched a few videos on how to explain mechanical projects in a software interview. My seniors who interned at Wipro shared their OA papers and gave me a quick cheat‑sheet for aptitude.
experience: The OA was a bit tough for a non‑CS kid – I spent too much time on the graph problem. The interview was friendly, they even asked about 3D printing work I did. Got a PPO at 7.2 LPA, which is decent for a mech batch.
advice: Don't ignore DSA even if you're from a core branch – they will test basic coding. Be ready to tie your mechanical knowledge to problem‑solving skills. During PPO talk, negotiate the training period if you want more exposure.
tips: Start coding at least 30 mins daily, even if it's just easy problems. Use GFG's 'Must‑Do' list for DSA. Keep a one‑page summary of your projects handy for the interview.

selection: 3 rounds as per the tags. Round‑1: a puzzle‑hunt style online test (pattern recognition, logical puzzles, a few brain‑teasers). Round‑2: a data‑science technical interview – they asked me to explain a simple regression model, do a quick Python snippet for data cleaning and discuss my ECE coursework. Round‑3: HR + PPO talk where they offered a PPO for a Data Scientist role and discussed the compensation (9.3 LPA).
preparation: I solved a bunch of puzzles from the 'MindYourDecisions' channel and practiced logical reasoning on puzzles sites. For the DS part, I went through the Mu Sigma prep guide, did Kaggle micro‑projects, and refreshed Python basics on GFG. Senior alums shared their interview experiences and gave me a list of common DS questions.
experience: The puzzle test was fun but stressful – some puzzles had ambiguous answers. The technical interview felt like a mini‑case study, and I managed to code a small pandas script on the spot. The PPO was a nice surprise, though the role is quite data‑heavy.
advice: Take the puzzles seriously – practice them because Mu Sigma loves quirky logic. Be comfortable with Python data libraries (pandas, numpy) and be ready to explain any ECE project in data terms. During PPO negotiation, ask about training and mentorship.
tips: Do at least one puzzle a day from sites like Brilliant or Puzzling StackExchange. Run a quick Python notebook with common data‑wrangling tasks. Connect with alumni on LinkedIn for insider tips.

selection: 4 rounds total. Round‑1: resume screening (they called me for a 5‑minute phone chat). Round‑2: an online assessment – 60 min OA with MCQ aptitude + a coding problem on DSA (binary search on a sorted array). Round‑3: technical interview focused on ML – they asked about supervised vs unsupervised learning, a simple linear regression derivation and a coding task to implement a basic K‑means in Python. Round‑4: HR + internship‑to‑PPO discussion where they offered a full‑time PPO after the internship and talked about the 88 k stipend in Gurgaon.
preparation: I polished my resume with help from the campus placement cell, did the Striver sheet for DSA up to medium level, and completed the Coursera ML Specialization (the basics). Practiced OA on HackerRank and watched a few Uber interview experiences on YouTube. Seniors who interned at Uber shared their coding templates.
experience: The OA was smooth, but I almost timed out on the coding part – ended up using a pre‑written template. The ML interview was intense; they wanted both theory and code. HR was friendly and the PPO offer felt rewarding after a decent internship stipend.
advice: For Uber, be strong on both DSA and ML fundamentals. Have a ready‑to‑run code snippet for common algorithms. During PPO chat, clarify the conversion timeline and the kind of projects you'll get as a full‑timer.
tips: Keep a small repo of ML snippets (linear regression, K‑means) you can copy‑paste. Do at least one OA per week on platforms like CodeSignal. Network with seniors who have interned at big tech – they often share the exact OA format.

selection: 5 rounds – a marathon! Round‑1: resume shortlisting call. Round‑2: OA with 2 DSA questions (one array manipulation, one recursion) and a basic CN (circuit) MCQ section. Round‑3: technical interview on OOPs – they asked me to design a class hierarchy for an embedded sensor system. Round‑4: deep dive CN interview – questions on microcontrollers, interrupts and low‑power design. Round‑5: HR + PPO discussion where they offered a 61 k monthly stipend and a clear path to a full‑time role after graduation.
preparation: I followed the Striver sheet for DSA, solved CN questions from GATE prep books, and brushed up OOPs with Java tutorials. My seniors who did an Oracle internship gave me their OA sheet and a list of typical embedded system design questions. Also did a few SPOC modules on embedded C.
experience: The OA was tough because of the mixed DSA+CN part – I had to switch mindsets quickly. The OOP interview was decent, but the CN round was a brain‑buster; I stumbled on one interrupt question but recovered. Overall, got a solid PPO which feels great for an EEE student.
advice: Balance your prep – don't just focus on DSA, give equal time to core subjects like CN if the tags mention them. For OOP, practice designing real‑world embedded systems. During PPO talk, ask about the mentorship program for fresh grads.
tips: Allocate separate days for DSA and CN prep. Use GFG's 'CN Basics' list and solve at least 5 problems a week. Keep a one‑page cheat‑sheet of OOP design patterns for quick revision before interviews.

selection: American Express Quant Researcher intern, 1 round. First OA had 3 coding questions on hackerrank, I solved 2 fully and 1 partly, thought I failed but got shortlisted. tips: Low CGPA doesnt mean the end, many companies dont filter by it. Build projects, dont lose hope, rejections happen lot, I faced 6 OA rejections before this.
