advice: dont skip ml basics even if ur core is civil. puzzles are easy if u practice a bit. be ready to explain projects in detail.
tips: keep ur resume projects short and crisp. for HR, just say u love travelling and can relocate anywhere.

selection: first round was an OA with aptitude (percentages, ratios) and 1 DSA (medium leetcode). second round was a group discussion on a random topic (like should ai replace humans in jobs) followed by a quick HR round where they asked about my family background and why Mu Sigma.
preparation: did a few aptitude tests on indiabix and solved 50 leetcode mediums. seniors said GD is just about speaking so i practiced with friends.
experience: OA was easy but GD was stressful coz i got stuck in a group of quiet people. HR was just 5 mins. got the offer in a week.
advice: aptitude is key for Mu Sigma. dont overthink GD, just speak something.
tips: for aptitude, time ur self. for GD, try to be the first to speak.

selection: first round OA: aptitude (time-speed-distance, data interpretation) + 2 DSA (medium leetcode). second round was a technical interview where they asked me to code a linked list problem live and then asked about my branch subjects (power systems, control systems). third round was another technical on system design basics (like design a smart grid). fourth round was HR where they asked about my PPO experience and why i want to join.
preparation: did aptitude from rs aggarwal and solved 100 leetcode mediums. for core subjects i just read gfg notes before the interview. seniors told me to expect power system questions so i brushed up on that.
experience: OA was okay but the second technical round was tough coz i blanked on the linked list. system design round was fun. HR was just standard stuff. got the offer in 3 days.
advice: dont ignore aptitude even if ur branch is EEE. core subjects matter more than u think.
tips: for aptitude, practice daily. for technical rounds, explain ur thought process even if u get stuck.

selection: first round was an online coding test with 2 DSA (medium-hard leetcode) and 1 DBMS mcq (sql queries). second round was a technical interview where they asked me to design a small embedded system (like a traffic light controller) and then asked about my projects and os concepts. result was announced in a few hours.
preparation: did striver sheet and leetcode weekly contests for 3 months. for dbms i just read gfg notes. for system design i watched a few youtube videos on embedded systems.
experience: OA was tough but the technical round was fun coz i actually knew the stuff. got the offer in a day.
advice: be thorough with ur projects and os concepts. dbms is important for embedded roles.
tips: for system design, draw diagrams and explain ur thought process. dont just code.

selection: first round was a resume shortlist. second round was a technical interview where they asked about my projects and data structures. third round was a case study on a data science problem (like predict customer churn). fourth round was a final interview where they asked about my gre score, sop, and why NUS.
preparation: did leetcode mediums and watched youtube videos on data science projects. for gre i used a book and did 2 full-length tests. for sop i took help from seniors who got into NUS.
experience: technical round was okay but the case study was tough coz i was nervous. final interview was just standard stuff. got the admit in 2 weeks.
advice: start gre prep early. for sop, highlight ur unique experiences. dont copy paste from internet.
tips: for case study, think aloud and ask clarifying questions. for gre, focus on vocab and math.

selection: 5 rounds total. 1) Online aptitude test (30 MCQs, 20 mins) – straight forward maths & logical. 2) Technical round on signal‑processing basics (they asked me to explain FFT in 2 mins). 3) Coding round – 2 easy problems on arrays & hash‑maps, I used python. 4) HR interview – they probed about why I want GET and my summer project on IoT sensors. 5) PPO discussion – they offered a pre‑placement offer on the spot after I cleared the HR round.
preparation: Did the Strivers' A2Z sheet for DSA (about 80% of it) plus 40 LeetCode easy/medium problems. For aptitude I used Indiabix and a few GFG mock tests. Went through my 3rd‑year signal‑processing notes and asked seniors for quick revs. Also practiced a couple of OA questions from previous batches.
experience: The whole thing felt long but organized. Aptitude was a breeze, technical was a bit nerve‑racking cause I'm from ECE not CS. Coding was okay, I could finish both. HR was chill, they were more interested in my project. PPO was a pleasant surprise – got the offer same day.
advice: Check ur internet speed before the OA, keep a backup laptop handy. For the technical round, revise core subjects (signals, comms) even if you think it's not needed. Show genuine interest in the role, they love that.
tips: CGPA cutoff is strict here, so keep it above 9.0. Practice at least 1‑2 aptitude questions daily. Have a short 1‑minute pitch ready for your projects, it saves time in HR.

selection: 2 rounds only. 1) Aptitude + core mechanical quiz (25 MCQs, mix of maths, physics and GD&T). 2) HR round – they asked about my internship at a plant, why Tata Steel and a few behavioral questions.
preparation: Spent 3 weeks on GFG aptitude sets and solved 30+ MCQs from previous Tata Steel drives. For core topics I revisited thermodynamics and material strength from my 4th‑sem PPTs. Asked seniors for typical HR questions and practiced with a friend.
experience: First round was quick, but the core questions were a bit tricky – some asked about stress‑strain curves. HR was friendly, they liked my plant internship story. Overall smooth, got the offer within a week.
advice: Don't ignore the core mechanical part, even if the role seems generic. Have your project summary ready, they love specifics. Be punctual for the HR call, it shows professionalism.
tips: Maintain a CGPA above 8.5, they filter early. Do at least 15 aptitude questions daily for a month before the drive. Keep a notebook of your internship tasks – quick reference during HR.

selection: 4 rounds. 1) Online aptitude test – 35 questions covering quantitative, logical and basic finance. 2) DSA coding round – 2 medium level problems (one on binary indexed tree, another on sliding window). 3) Quant technical interview – they asked probability puzzles and a quick brain‑teaser on Monte‑Carlo simulation. 4) HR interview – short chat about my interest in finance and why Morgan Stanley.
preparation: Followed the Striver DSA sheet till the 'Graphs' section, solved ~70 LeetCode problems (mostly medium). For aptitude I used a mix of PrepInsta and some finance‑focused MCQs. Watched a few quant interview videos on YouTube and discussed with seniors from the finance club.
experience: Aptitude was easy, got it done in 15 mins. Coding took longer – I had to recall BIT implementation, but managed. Quant interview was intense; they expected you to think out loud. HR was casual, they liked my campus quant club experience.
advice: During the coding round, write clean code – they check readability. For quant interview, practice explaining your thought process, not just the answer. Keep your finance basics fresh.
tips: Aim for a CGPA of at least 8.3 for MS/finance roles. Do daily 1‑hour DSA practice 2 weeks before. Keep a list of common quant puzzles and rehearse them with a friend.

selection: 4 rounds. 1) OA (Online Assessment) – 3 coding problems (array rotation, string palindrome, and a simple system‑design MCQ). 2) System design interview – they asked me to design a basic e‑commerce checkout flow, focusing on scalability. 3) HR round – chat about my internship at a startup, salary expectations and why Flipkart. 4) PPO discussion – after HR they offered a pre‑placement offer with a good CTC.
preparation: Cracked the OA by solving recent Flipkart OA questions from LeetCode discuss and GFG. Followed the System Design guide on Educative (the 10‑page cheat sheet) and practiced a couple of design questions with seniors. For HR, rehearsed my internship story and did mock HR with a friend.
experience: OA was moderate – the system‑design MCQ felt new but I guessed correctly. System design interview was fun, the panel liked my micro‑service breakdown. HR was relaxed, they asked about campus placements. Getting the PPO right after was a nice bonus.
advice: Test your environment before the OA – some problems need Java 11, others Python 3.8. In system design, focus on clear component separation, not just buzzwords. Show enthusiasm for the product during HR.
tips: Keep CGPA above 9.2 for Flipkart; they have a cutoff. Do at least 2 OA mock tests a week before. Draft a 2‑minute pitch for your startup project – it makes HR impressed.

selection: 5 rounds. 1) Project discussion – they asked me to present my data‑analysis project on market trends, 10‑minute demo. 2) Aptitude test – 30 MCQs on quantitative and logical reasoning. 3) Technical interview – focused on SQL queries and a small Python script to parse CSV files. 4) HR interview – typical behavioral questions and why I want a quant role at MS. 5) Final HR/Offer round – they confirmed the offer and discussed PPO details.
preparation: Polished my project deck with help from seniors, rehearsed the demo 5 times. Did 50+ aptitude questions from GFG and a few Quant interview PDFs. Practiced SQL basics on HackerRank and wrote Python scripts for data cleaning. For HR, went through common behavioral Qs and wrote STAR responses.
experience: Project round was the toughest – they probed deep into my methodology, but I managed. Aptitude was okay, I scored 85%. Technical interview was smooth; I wrote the SQL query on a shared doc. HR was friendly, they liked my enthusiasm. Got the PPO in the final round.
advice: Prepare a concise project story – keep it under 10 minutes, focus on impact. Verify your internet and screen sharing tools before the aptitude test. For the technical round, write code on paper first, it helps organize thoughts.
tips: Maintain CGPA above 8.0 for quant roles. Do daily 30‑minute aptitude practice for 3 weeks. Keep a one‑pager of your major projects ready for quick reference.

selection: Arista VLSI Engineer placement, 5 rounds after OA. OA was 1 coding problem (medium), plus a few DBMS questions. Round 1: DSA problem (medium), asked to explain the approach. Round 2: DBMS questions (indexing, transactions). Round 3: VLSI related problem (design a circuit). Round 4: Group discussion on a tech topic. Round 5: HR round.
preparation: Striver sheet, leetcode medium problems, DBMS from GFG, and VLSI from SPOCs. Practised explaining DSA solutions clearly.
experience: Good, interviewers were friendly. The VLSI round was a bit tough but manageable.
advice: Strong DSA and DBMS knowledge is a must. Prepare for VLSI basics.
tips: CGPA 8+ helped in the first screen. Keep practicing DSA and DBMS consistently.

selection: Infosys Systems Engineer placement, 4 rounds after OA. OA was 1 coding problem (easy), plus a few HR questions. Round 1: DSA problem (easy). Round 2: HR round. Round 3: Group discussion on a tech topic. Round 4: HR round.
preparation: Leetcode easy problems, HR questions from seniors, and group discussion topics.
experience: Good, the HR rounds were a bit formal but manageable. The PPO offer was great.
advice: Prepare for HR questions and group discussions. Infosys values teamwork.
tips: CGPA 8+ helped in the first screen. Keep practicing DSA and HR prep consistently.

selection: Oracle Data Scientist placement, 5 rounds after OA. OA was 1 coding problem (medium), plus a few ML questions. Round 1: DSA problem (medium). Round 2: ML questions (supervised vs unsupervised learning). Round 3: OOPs questions (inheritance, polymorphism). Round 4: SQL problem (join queries). Round 5: HR round.
preparation: Leetcode medium problems, ML from Andrew Ng's course, OOPs from GFG, and SQL from SPOCs.
experience: Good, the ML and OOPs rounds were a bit tough but manageable. The HR round was formal.
advice: Strong DSA, ML, and OOPs knowledge is a must. Prepare for SQL basics.
tips: CGPA 9+ helped in the first screen. Keep practicing DSA, ML, and OOPs consistently.

selection: JSW Steel GET placement, 2 rounds after OA. OA was 1 coding problem (easy), plus a few aptitude questions. Round 1: Group discussion on a core topic. Round 2: HR round.
preparation: Leetcode easy problems, aptitude from seniors, and group discussion topics. Resume was clean and well-structured.
experience: Good, the HR round was a bit formal but manageable. The GET offer was decent.
advice: Prepare for aptitude questions and group discussions. JSW Steel values teamwork.
tips: CGPA 8+ helped in the first screen. Keep practicing aptitude and group discussion prep consistently.

selection: L&T Plant Engineer placement, 4 rounds after OA. OA was 1 coding problem (easy), plus a few aptitude questions. Round 1: Group discussion on a core topic. Round 2: Aptitude test. Round 3: Technical interview on core subjects. Round 4: HR round.
preparation: Leetcode easy problems, aptitude from seniors, group discussion topics, and core subjects from SPOCs.
experience: Good, the aptitude test was a bit tough but manageable. The HR round was formal.
advice: Strong aptitude and core knowledge is a must. Prepare for group discussions.
tips: CGPA 7+ helped in the first screen. Keep practicing aptitude and core prep consistently.

selection: Single round: resume shortlisting + video call with prof. Asked about my final year project on IoT-based sensor networks, my role in the team, and why UIUC. Also discussed my GRE scores and SOP briefly. Results came in 2 weeks.
preparation: revised my project notes, did some gre practice from manhattan books, asked seniors for sop review. kept my github clean with all project code.
experience: prof was chill, asked me to explain my project in simple terms. felt like a casual chat but was nervous af.
advice: for ms apps, keep ur projects and sop strong. dont lie in video calls, they can catch u easily.
tips: start gre prep early, dont cram. reach out to seniors who got admits in ur target unis.

selection: One round: online assessment (quant, logical, verbal) + HR interview. OA was easy but time was tight. HR asked about my projects, why consultancy, and location flexibility.
preparation: did indiabix for aptitude, revised my resume projects. seniors told me to keep HR answers short and confident.
experience: OA was fine, HR was a breeze. they told me results in 3 days.
advice: dont overthink HR, just be honest. aptitude is all about speed.
tips: practice timed mock tests. keep ur resume projects relevant to consultancy.

selection: Round 1: online aptitude (quant, logical, verbal). Round 2: group discussion on sustainability in FMCG. Round 3: case study on supply chain optimization. Round 4: HR round with questions on why HUL, location pref. Round 5: final HR with salary discussion and bond signing.
preparation: did rs aggarwal for aptitude, watched some gd prep videos. revised my resume projects and practiced case study basics from youtube.
experience: gd was fun, but case study was tricky. hr rounds were chill but long.
advice: for gd, speak first and keep it structured. for case study, think aloud and ask clarifying questions.
tips: dont only focus on tech roles, core companies also have non-tech rounds. be open to rotational postings.

selection: Round 1: online test with 3 medium leetcode-style questions (DSA + ML basics). Round 2: technical interview on embedded systems (RTOS, interrupts, memory management). Round 3: system design (design a smart home hub). Round 4: ML round (explain a project, how to optimize inference). Round 5: HR with salary negotiation and bond.
preparation: did striver sheet + leetcode hard problems. revised embedded systems from class notes. built a small iot project with sensors to talk about in interviews.
experience: round 2 was tough, interviewer kept grilling me on RTOS. round 3 was fun, i liked system design. hr was straightforward.
advice: for embedded roles, know ur hardware basics. dont just memorize leetcode, understand the concepts.
tips: keep ur github updated with embedded projects. practice explaining ur thought process clearly.

selection: Round 1: online aptitude (quant, logical, verbal). Round 2: technical interview on mineral processing (crushing, grinding, flotation). Round 3: case study on mine safety. Round 4: HR round with questions on why mining, location pref. Round 5: final HR with salary discussion and bond signing.
preparation: revised mineral processing from textbooks. did aptitude from indiabix. practiced explaining my internship on mine surveying to a friend.
experience: technical round was intense, interviewer asked a lot of core questions. case study was new for me, but i managed.
advice: for core companies, know ur subjects cold. dont fake it in technical rounds.
tips: keep ur resume projects relevant to mining. be open to field postings, they pay well.

selection: round 1: an online assessment (OA) of 45 mins – 2 coding problems (one OOPs design, one simple DBMS query) + 10 MCQs on OOP concepts. round 2: face‑to‑face technical interview where they asked me to write a class hierarchy for a banking system and also threw a few SQL join questions.
preparation: followed the Striver DSA sheet, solved easy‑medium leetcode problems daily, brushed up OOP basics from YouTube (my seniors’ playlists) and did a quick DBMS revision on GFG. also practiced a couple of OA mock tests on PrepInsta.
experience: the OA was kinda tight on time but doable. interviewers were chill, they even joked about my coffee habit. felt decent after clearing both rounds in one go.
advice: focus on writing clean OOP code, not just solving the problem. know your basic SQL syntax, they love to ask simple join/aggregation queries.
tips: do at least 3 mock OAs before the real thing, and ask seniors for their interview notes – they save you a lot of panic.

selection: round 1: resume shortlisting – they called me for a 5‑min telephonic screen. round 2: written aptitude test (20 Qs on quantitative, logical & verbal). round 3: core‑subject quiz (basics of power electronics & circuit theory). round 4: technical interview – deep dive into my final year project and some ECE theory. round 5: HR round – behavioural questions and salary discussion.
preparation: revived my old GATE notes for core subjects, solved aptitude puzzles on IndiaBix, and did a couple of mock technical interviews with seniors from the ECE batch. also brushed up my project details on a one‑pager.
experience: the aptitude test was the toughest for me, but the core quiz was surprisingly easy. interviewers were straightforward, no crazy brain‑teasers.
advice: keep your resume crisp, highlight any industry‑relevant project. for the core round, stick to fundamentals – they love textbook definitions.
tips: don’t underestimate the HR round – they sometimes ask about why you chose steel sector. have a short, honest answer ready.

selection: round 1: online coding OA (90 mins) – 2 problems, one on OS scheduling and another on basic graph traversal (CN). round 2: technical interview – OS concepts (process vs thread, deadlock) and a networking scenario (OSI layers). round 3: ML case study – they gave a small dataset and asked me to suggest a model and explain overfitting. round 4: HR/fit interview – team fit and salary expectations.
preparation: crammed the Striver sheet, especially OS and graph sections, solved recent leetcode contests for speed, watched networking tutorials on NPTEL, and refreshed ML basics with Coursera’s intro to ML and a few Kaggle kernels. also did a mock OA on HackerRank with my batchmates.
experience: the OA felt like a marathon but I managed both questions. interviewers were super technical, they even asked me to draw a deadlock graph on the whiteboard. the ML round was a surprise but I survived with a simple linear model explanation.
advice: be ready to explain OS algorithms clearly, and have a couple of networking examples up your sleeve. for ML, they don’t expect deep research – just clear intuition.
tips: practice drawing diagrams on paper, and keep a one‑pager of common ML terms (bias‑variance, regularisation). senior tips saved me from panicking on the networking Q.

selection: single round: onsite interview where they checked my resume, asked core EEE questions (transformers, power factor) and gave a short problem on circuit analysis to solve on a whiteboard.
preparation: re‑read my 3rd‑year power systems notes, solved a few past year EEE interview questions from GFG, and did a quick mock interview with a senior who works in power sector.
experience: the interview was short but intense – they liked my project on renewable micro‑grid, and the circuit problem was straightforward. left feeling relieved.
advice: make sure you can explain any project line on your resume; core concepts just need crisp definitions.
tips: don’t waste time on fancy jargon – clear, concise answers win. a quick revision of basic formulas a day before helps a lot.

selection: round 1: resume screening + a short telephonic chat about my coding background. round 2: online assessment (OA) – 2 quantitative puzzles and a coding problem on probability modelling (quant focus).
preparation: went through the quant OA sheets shared in the campus WhatsApp group, solved probability problems on LeetCode and HackerRank, and brushed up basic statistics from Khan Academy. also did a couple of mock OAs on PrepInsta with a friend from the maths club.
experience: the OA was tricky – time pressure was real but I managed both questions. the recruiter was polite and gave quick feedback. got the offer within a week.
advice: strengthen your basics in probability and statistics, and practice coding problems that involve maths logic. keep your resume focused on any data‑analysis work.
tips: do at least 5 quant mock tests before the real OA, and keep a cheat‑sheet of common formulas (Bayes, variance). seniors who cleared Amex last year were a great resource.

selection: OA was a 1 hr test on hackerrank with 3 sections: 20 aptitude, 20 DSA, and 60 verbal. Then a 1 hr technical interview on zoom with 2 engineers. They asked about my project, how i would improve it, and then a DSA problem on stacks. HR was short, they asked about my internship and why consulting. Offer letter after 4 days.
preparation: Did aptitude and verbal practice for 2 weeks, and leetcode ~200 questions with focus on stacks and queues. Revised OOPs concepts from GFG.
experience: OA was tough, but the interview was fair. Interviewers were helpful with hints. Felt tired after 2 hours of back-to-back coding!
advice: Show some coding skills even if u are from a non-cs branch. Bring one example of ur project and how u would improve it.
tips: Start early with CS fundamentals, not only DSA. 7.25 CGPA was fine for them, so do not lose hope.

selection: First an online assessment (aptitude, verbal, a technical section on basics of programming and excel). Then a second online round for group discussion style/ case recorded video. Then the technical interview, they asked about my site internship, how i would use digital tools in civil projects, what is BIM, plus basic excel/sql question. HR last, relocation, why consulting from civil, working hours. 4 rounds all in about 10 days.
preparation: Aptitude practice for 1-2 weeks, and learnt some basic excel and power bi from youtube because i know consulting asks for it. Prepared my answer on why consulting.
experience: Nice experience overall, HR was very warm. One slight issue was that the video round had a tech glitch for me and i had to email SPOC.
advice: Show some data skills even if u are from a non-cs branch. Bring one example of ur project where u used data.
tips: Dont give up on consulting companies, they come early in the season and many civil students get in. CGPA near 7 was ok for me but check eligibility each time.

selection: OA was a 2 hr test on hackerrank with 2 sections: 30 aptitude, and 90 DSA. Then a 1 hr technical interview on zoom with 2 engineers. They asked about my ML internship, how i would use ML in hardware projects, and then a DSA problem on trees. HR was short, they asked about my internship and why hardware. Offer letter after 3 days.
preparation: Did aptitude practice for 1 week, and leetcode ~300 questions with focus on trees and graphs. Revised ML concepts from Andrew Ng's course on Coursera.
experience: OA was tough, but the interview was fair. Interviewers were helpful with hints. Felt tired after 3 hours of back-to-back coding!
advice: Show some ML skills even if u are from a non-cs branch. Bring one example of ur project and how u would use ML in it.
tips: Start early with CS fundamentals, not only DSA. 7.4 CGPA was fine for them, so do not lose hope.

selection: OA was a 1 hr test on hackerrank with 3 sections: 20 aptitude, 20 DSA, and 60 verbal. Then a 1 hr technical interview on zoom with 2 engineers. They asked about my ML internship, how i would use ML in software projects, and then a DSA problem on dp. HR was short, they asked about my internship and why ML. Offer letter after 4 days.
preparation: Did aptitude and verbal practice for 2 weeks, and leetcode ~300 questions with focus on dp and greedy. Revised ML concepts from Andrew Ng's course on Coursera.
experience: OA was tough, but the interview was fair. Interviewers were helpful with hints. Felt tired after 2 hours of back-to-back coding!
advice: Show some ML skills even if u are from a non-cs branch. Bring one example of ur project and how u would use ML in it.
tips: Start early with CS fundamentals, not only DSA. 8.18 CGPA was fine for them, so do not lose hope.

selection: One round only, and a long one: a 90 min technical interview on zoom by 2 engineers (no OA, shortlist was by resume). First DBMS: indexing, B+ trees, transactions and isolation levels, a query involving window functions. Then a DSA problem on tries (word search) and a second on dp with memoization. Asked complexities at every step. Offer after a day.
preparation: Revised DBMS from a textbook and a few CMU database lectures on youtube, leetcode ~300 questions with focus on trees/tries/dp.
experience: Heavy but fair, interviewers were helpful with hints. Felt tired after 90 mins!
advice: Go deeper in DBMS than just basics. Practice explaining complexity cleanly.
tips: Start early with CS fundamentals, not only DSA. 7.6 CGPA was fine for them, so do not lose hope.

selection: Arista hardware placement had 3 rounds. OA was 2 medium DSA problems (one on trees, one on graphs) plus a system design mcq section. Tech 1 was resume + ML basics (they asked about my ML project and then asked to explain bias-variance tradeoff and overfitting). Tech 2 was system design for a network switch, they wanted me to design the data plane and control plane. Final round was HR about relocation and bond period.
preparation: did striver sheet and leetcode tagged problems. revised my ml project report and watched a few gaurav sen system design videos. seniors helped with resume pointers.
experience: system design round was tough but the interviewers were chill. OA was okay but the system design mcq part was new for me.
advice: dont ignore system design even if ur branch isnt cs. revise ur projects inside out.
tips: core students, dont skip ml subjects if u have interest. pay is good but work life balance is questionable.

selection: Deutsche Bank had 2 rounds. OA was 3 puzzles (river crossing, hourglass, etc.) and 2 DSA problems (one on arrays, one on strings). Tech round was a mix of DSA and puzzles again, they asked me to optimize a solution and explain time complexity. HR was about bond, relocation, and why banking.
preparation: practiced puzzles from geeksforgeeks and did leetcode medium problems. revised time complexity and oops basics. took a few mock interviews with seniors.
experience: puzzles were fun but the tech round was stressful. interviewers were strict but fair.
advice: puzzles are random, dont waste too much time on one. keep ur cool in tech round.
tips: if u get an oa, prepare for puzzles even if u hate them. cgpa wasnt a big filter here.

selection: Amazon sde placement had 5 rounds. OA was 2 dsa problems (one on dp, one on trees) plus work simulation. Tech 1 was resume based, they picked my web project and asked about api design and db schema, then a medium coding on graphs. Tech 2 was more dsa (linked lists, heaps) and system design basics. Bar raiser was leadership principles and a coding problem on arrays. Results came in 3 days.
preparation: did striver sheet and leetcode amazon tagged questions. prepared a story bank for leadership principles. revised dbms and oops with class notes.
experience: it was a rollercoaster, got rejected from 3 companies before this. interviews were conversational but intense.
advice: be ready to justify every design choice in ur projects. practice writing clean code with comments.
tips: dont give up after first few rejections. join mock interview sessions and talk to seniors. cgpa helped but wasnt the main filter.

selection: Sprinklr had 4 rounds. OA was 2 dsa problems (one on strings, one on graphs) plus a work simulation. Tech 1 was resume based, they asked about my projects and then a medium coding on heaps. Tech 2 was more dsa (dp, trees) and system design basics. HR was about relocation and why Sprinklr.
preparation: did striver sheet and leetcode tagged problems. revised my projects and prepared for system design basics. took a few mock interviews with friends.
experience: interviewers were friendly but the tech rounds were tough. OA was okay but the work simulation was new for me.
advice: revise ur projects thoroughly. be ready to explain ur thought process clearly.
tips: dont ignore system design even if u r not from cs. pay is decent but work culture is average.

selection: Vedanta was a PPO conversion. Only 2 rounds: first was a discussion about my internship project (I did it in the same company). Second was HR about plant postings, shift work, and my future plans. Super chill, they just wanted to confirm if I was still interested.
preparation: revised my internship report and prepared for basic hr questions. seniors helped with what to expect in the hr round.
experience: super chill, no pressure at all. panel was friendly and asked mostly about my internship experience.
advice: if u have a ppo, be very clear on what u did in ur internship. hr round is just a formality.
tips: core students, take internships seriously. a ppo saves ur whole placement season. dont ignore hr round, they care about whether u will survive plant life.

selection: round 1: 60‑min aptitude test (numeric, verbal & reasoning) – 30 q’s, cutoff ~55%. round 2: core ECE interview – they asked about PLL, SAR ADC and power electronics, plus a mini‑design problem on a buck converter. round 3: HR chat – resume walk‑through, why Vedanta, campus life question. total 3 rounds, took about a week.
preparation: cracked the GATE 2023 ECE paper once, so revisited signals & control. did daily aptitude from aptitude‑guru pdfs, solved past Vedanta OA on geeksforgeeks. brushed up OOP basics just in case HR asked. seniors from 4th yr helped with mock core interview and gave me a few PLL notes.
experience: first round was a breeze, just timed maths. second was nerve‑racking – they dug deep into my project on solar inverter, but i managed to explain the control loop. HR was super chill, they even asked about my college fests. overall felt decent, got the offer in 5 days.
advice: don’t ignore the core part even if you think placement is just aptitude. be ready to sketch circuits on a whiteboard and talk about trade‑offs. HR will love a clear, honest story about why you want to work in mining‑energy sector.
tips: practice aptitude daily (use timed mock). keep a one‑page cheat sheet of your major projects & key equations. talk to seniors who cleared Vedanta last year – they know the exact type of core questions. and relax before HR – smile!

selection: OA first (online assessment on their portal): 2 coding qs – one greedy array problem and one DP on strings, plus 10 logic puzzles (like knights‑and‑knaves). 90 mins. cleared ~30%. then round 2: puzzle‑heavy interview – they gave a brain‑teaser about a light switch and asked you to explain your reasoning. round 3: technical interview – data‑structures + a quick C++ coding on trees. round 4: HR/fit interview – why Optiver, market‑making basics, salary expectations.
preparation: finished Striver’s A2Z sheet by 5th sem, did LeetCode medium daily. for puzzles I used the “Puzzling StackExchange” and a few YouTube channels (MindYourDecisions). brushed up C++ STL and read up on market‑making basics from QuantInsti blogs. senior batch mates ran mock puzzle rounds for us.
experience: OA was tough – the DP string was weird but I managed after 10 mins. puzzle interview felt like a game, interviewer laughed a lot when I messed up the switch problem, but they liked my thought process. tech round was standard DSA, I solved the tree question in 12 mins. HR was straightforward, they asked about my interest in finance – I talked about my quant elective.
advice: for Optiver you must love puzzles – they use them to see how you think under pressure. don’t try to over‑engineer, just verbalise each step. also know a bit about trading terminology, they love that.

selection: Round 1: a short 30‑min ML quiz (basics of regression, CNN vs RNN, a couple of probability Qs). They also skimmed my resume and asked why I had a referral from a senior alum. Round 2: a 45‑min interview with a professor from the EE dept + a senior researcher. They dug deep into my final year project on signal processing, asked me to design a simple filter on a whiteboard and threw a few brain‑teaser style questions about gradient descent. No HR round because it was a university admission drive.
preparation: Spent 2 weeks on fast.ai courses, brushed up linear algebra from GFG, solved a handful of LeetCode easy/medium problems on arrays to keep the coding edge. Got the referral by chatting with a 3rd‑year senior who did his MS there, so I updated my resume with all the ML internships and made a one‑pager SOP draft early. Also read a few past MS interview experiences on forums.
experience: Honestly mixed – the ML quiz was okay but the whiteboard filter design made me sweat. The professor was friendly, though, and liked my project screenshots. Got the admit but wish I had practiced more on the math side.
advice: Try to show genuine interest in the specific research group you are applying to. A referral helps get past the resume filter, but you still need solid fundamentals.
tips: Start prepping the core ML concepts 1‑2 months before. Keep a one‑page resume with clear metrics. If you have a senior in the program, ask for a referral early – it cuts down the initial shortlisting.

selection: Round 1: Online aptitude test (30 Qs – mix of quantitative, logical and a tiny coding snippet). Round 2: Technical interview (45 min) – they asked about my semester projects, then gave a DSA problem on arrays (two‑pointer) and a mini‑ML case where I had to explain a simple linear model. Round 3: HR chat – salary expectations, team culture and a couple of scenario questions about handling tight deadlines.
preparation: Did Striver's sheet for 2 months, solving at least 2 medium LeetCode problems daily. For ML part I revisited my Kaggle notebooks and read GFG articles on basic regression. Also polished my resume with bullet points on the banking‑related project and asked a senior who interned at DB to give me mock HR questions.
experience: Overall decent. The aptitude was a bit easy, but the DSA question caught me off‑guard because I hadn't practiced two‑pointer patterns recently. HR was friendly, asked about my campus fest experience – weird but okay.
advice: More focus on problem‑solving speed for the coding part. Also, they liked candidates who could tie their projects to finance use‑cases, so be ready with that angle.
tips: Keep a log of all projects with numbers (e.g., reduced processing time by 20%). Practice quick DSA drills – 15‑20 mins per problem. Don’t ignore the HR round; they check cultural fit.

selection: Round 1: Online aptitude (20 min, 20 Qs – basic quantitative & logical). Round 2: Coding OA – two problems, one on string manipulation and another on greedy scheduling. Round 3: Technical interview – they asked me to walk through my IoT project, then gave a case study on data cleaning and asked how I'd approach a decision‑analytics pipeline. Round 4: HR round – typical "strength‑weakness" and why Fractal. Round 5: Final HR/managerial fit – they discussed team structure, shift timings and gave a small situational puzzle about client communication.
preparation: Followed the GFG "Aptitude for Campus" list for 3 days, solved the OA problems from previous year’s Fractal batch on PrepInsta. For the analytics case, I read a couple of blogs on data preprocessing and brushed up pandas. Also compiled a one‑pager of my projects with clear impact numbers and practiced storytelling with seniors from the analytics club.
experience: It was a long haul – the OA felt moderate, but the technical interview was intense with a lot of follow‑up questions on my own code. HR people were polite. Got the offer but felt the pay could've been better.
advice: Try to keep your project explanations concise, focus on the business value. The aptitude part is easy if you revise basics, but the case study can go deep – be ready to talk about metrics.
tips: Do a mock case study with a friend – explain data pipeline steps out loud. Keep your resume project section crisp (use numbers). Practice at least one coding problem every day till the deadline.

selection: Round 1: Online assessment (2 coding questions – one DP on subsequence, one math‑puzzle). Round 2: Face‑to‑face interview – first half was a technical deep‑dive on probability, Monte‑Carlo simulations and a quick coding on a whiteboard (implement a simple random walk). Second half was a chat about my previous summer internship which later turned into a PPO, so they asked about the quant models I built there.
preparation: Did the OA prep from a friend’s sheet (LeetCode medium DP). Spent a week on probability basics from Striver’s maths notes and watched Quant finance videos on YouTube. Reviewed my internship report and rehearsed explaining the models in 2‑3 minutes. Also read a few quant interview experiences on Reddit.
experience: Pretty good – the OA was challenging but manageable. The interviewers were technical and actually liked my internship work, which made the second half flow nicely. Got the PPO offer on the spot.
advice: More emphasis on quantitative reasoning; they love to see you derive formulas on the spot. Also, having a prior internship in a quant role definitely gives you a leg up.
tips: If you have any quant internship, highlight it early in your resume. Practice DP and probability problems daily. Keep a one‑page cheat sheet of common formulas for quick revision.

selection: Round 1: Single aptitude round – 30 questions covering quantitative, logical reasoning and a short chemistry‑based problem (since it’s a chemical core role). They also skimmed the resume for any core project experience.
preparation: Focused on core subject notes – went through my chemical engineering thermodynamics and process design textbooks. Did a quick 2‑day crash on aptitude from IndiaBix and solved a batch of GFG quantitative puzzles. Updated my resume to highlight the catalyst synthesis project.
experience: The test was straightforward, nothing too tricky. Since there was only one round, I got the offer quickly. The HR later called for onboarding, but the interview process itself was painless.
advice: Make sure your resume clearly shows any lab or process‑design projects; they look for that even in a short aptitude round.
tips: Don’t underestimate the chemistry part – revise key equations. Keep your resume bullet points crisp and quant‑oriented (e.g., improved yield by 12%).

selection: OA (ML questions), then 2 technical rounds (ML concepts, coding), then HR. They asked about my ML project and some DSA questions.
preparation: Did the ML SPOCs, solved some leetcode problems, and revised ML concepts from a YouTube playlist.
experience: The OA was tough, but the interviewers were nice. The package was decent for AI.
advice: Prepare well for ML concepts and coding. Be ready to explain your project in detail.
tips: For AI roles, be sure to have a good ML project to showcase.

selection: OA (aptitude + coding), then 3 technical rounds (OOPs, DBMS, resume), then HR. They asked about my Java project and some aptitude questions.
preparation: Revised OOPs and DBMS from the notes, solved some TCS NQT papers, and did some easy leetcode problems.
experience: The process was long but manageable. The package was low, but it was a good backup.
advice: Prepare well for OOPs, DBMS, and one programming language. Be ready to explain your project.
tips: For core branches, its fine to take a safe offer. But dont stop there, keep trying for better ones.

selection: OA (coding), then 2 technical rounds (OS, projects), then HR. They asked about my OS concepts and my project.
preparation: Revised OS concepts from the notes, solved some leetcode problems, and prepared for my project.
experience: The OA was tough, but the interviewers were nice. The package was decent for CSE.
advice: Prepare well for OS concepts and coding. Be ready to explain your project in detail.
tips: For CSE roles, be sure to have a good project to showcase.

selection: OA (aptitude), then technical round (core subjects), then HR. They asked about my core subjects and some aptitude questions.
preparation: Revised my core subjects from the notes, solved some aptitude questions, and prepared for the HR round.
experience: The process was smooth. The package was decent for Mechanical.
advice: Prepare well for your core subjects and aptitude. Be ready for the HR round.
tips: For core branches, be sure to prepare well for your core subjects.

selection: OA (aptitude), then technical round (OOPs, resume), then HR. They asked about my OOPs concepts and my resume.
preparation: Revised OOPs concepts from the notes, solved some aptitude questions, and prepared my resume.
experience: The process was quick. The package was low, but it was a good backup.
advice: Prepare well for OOPs concepts and aptitude. Be ready to explain your resume.
tips: For CSE roles, be sure to have a good resume to showcase.

selection: Round 1: resume shortlist + referral check. Round 2: GRE score + SOP review. Round 3: LOR verification + final interview about research interests. Round 4: visa/financial docs + admission confirmation.
preparation: revised gre quant from manhattan 5lb, wrote sop with seniors help, brushed up on ml basics from andrew ng course.
experience: smooth but stressful. gre cutoff was 320 so i had to retake it once. visa docs took forever.
advice: start gre prep early, dont rely only on referral. keep ur sop honest.
tips: ask ur seniors for real gre scores they got in. dont trust random quora posts.

selection: OA had 2 sql + 1 ml mcq. Round 1: technical about regression models. Round 2: case study on supply chain data. Round 3: manager round + ppo conversion discussion.
preparation: did mu sigma mock tests from their portal, revised stats from khan academy, practiced sql on leetcode database problems.
experience: okay. case study was tricky but they gave hints. ppo was a relief after struggling in other interviews.
advice: mu sigma loves sql joins. dont skip that part.
tips: if u get ppo, chill but dont skip revision. they can still reject u in final rounds.

selection: Round 1: resume + projects shortlist. Round 2: technical about ml algorithms + data structures. Round 3: research proposal discussion. Round 4: final admission interview.
preparation: revised leetcode medium, did uiuc past papers, brushed up on python for data science projects.
experience: felt like a normal interview. they asked about my demand forecasting project in depth.
advice: projects matter more than gpa here. make sure ur github is clean.
tips: ask ur seniors for uiuc specific questions. they have a pattern.

selection: Single round: technical interview about probability, stats, and a leetcode hard problem. They converted ppo on the spot after the interview.
preparation: did striver sheet hard problems, revised probability from a book, practiced quant on leetcode.
experience: nervous but they were chill. the problem was from leetcode weekly contest.
advice: if u get ppo, u r almost in. just dont mess up the final interview.
tips: keep ur leetcode streak alive till the last day.

selection: Round 1: aptitude + technical aptitude. Round 2: core ece subject questions (power systems, control systems). Round 3: hr + ppo conversion discussion.
preparation: revised gate notes for core subjects, did aptitude from rs aggarwal, practiced from coal india past papers.
experience: core subjects were tough. hr round was just formality.
advice: dont ignore core subjects even if u r in ece. they ask everything.
tips: if u get ppo, u r in. but still revise for a week.

selection: round 1: online assessment (OA) with 30 min aptitude + 2 coding q's on python (one matrix rotation, one greedy scheduling). round 2: technical interview (45 min) where they dug deep into my senior year capstone on thermal analysis of mining rigs, asked about CFD tools and material specs. round 3: HR + PPO chat (30 min) – they talked about intern stint last summer, liked my project report and offered a pre‑placement offer (PPO) on the spot. got the offer the same evening.
preparation: since mechanical, I brushed up DSA from Striver SDE sheet (1 hr daily) and solved a bunch of GFG puzzles on greedy. watched a couple of SPOC videos on thermodynamics to polish project talk. senior seniors gave me mock OA on google form and shared their Bosch interview notes. also kept my CAD portfolio ready.
experience: overall kinda smooth. OA was a bit glitchy on my laptop but I managed. tech interview felt like a project defence, interviewer was chill. PPO talk was nice – they even asked about relocation preferences.
advice: make ur project slides crisp, include numbers (e.g., 20% efficiency gain). for OA practice mixed aptitude + coding, not just one. be ready to talk about why you want a core mechanical role in an auto‑tech firm.
tips: keep a small cheat‑sheet of formulas for heat transfer, it helps during quick Q&A. ask seniors for their Bosch referral early – it cuts the resume short‑list. don't stress over cgpa 7.4, they care more about hands‑on work.

selection: got a referral from a senior who interned at Boeing last year, so my resume flew past the initial filter. round 1: quick 15‑min tele‑screen with HR – they just confirmed eligibility and asked why Boeing. round 2: technical interview (1 hr) – 2 DSA problems (binary tree traversal and sliding window max) on a shared doc, plus a discussion on my compiler design mini‑project. got the offer call next day.
preparation: spent 2 months on LeetCode (focus on medium trees & arrays) after the referral. also did Striver sheet for fundamentals, and skimmed GFG for sliding window tricks. revisited my compiler project docs and practiced explaining design choices with a buddy from the coding club.
experience: the referral helped a lot, but the interview was still tough. DSA questions were standard Boeing style – they liked clean code. the project talk was the part where I almost slipped on jargon, but the interviewer was patient.
advice: if you have a referral, still treat it like a regular interview – know your code inside out. brush up on system design basics even for entry‑level roles.
tips: keep the referral email handy in case they ask how you heard about the role. practice coding on a plain text editor, Boeing uses shared docs. don't forget to mention your GPA 8.3, it gives a plus.

selection: only 1 round: online assessment (OA) that combined a 20‑question aptitude section and a short coding task (print pattern of stars). after finishing, they asked 2 quick project questions (my PCB design for motor driver and a summer internship at a power plant). got the call same evening.
preparation: focused on GFG aptitude packs and solved the last 50 pattern problems on LeetCode. refreshed my resume bullet points with senior help, especially the power plant internship. watched a couple of SPOC videos on power electronics to answer any deep dive.
experience: the OA platform lagged a bit, but I managed. project questions were easy – they just wanted to see if I actually did the work. overall not stressful.
advice: make sure your resume projects are quantifiable (e.g., reduced ripple by 15%). OA can be speed‑run, so practice under timer.
tips: keep a pdf of your project report on your laptop for quick reference. ask a senior to do a mock OA with you, it helps with time management.

selection: round 1: OA – 25 aptitude q's + 2 coding problems (array rotation, string palindrome). round 2: technical interview (45 min) – DSA focus, they gave a linked list reversal and a recursion tree problem. round 3: HR interview (30 min) – resume walk‑through, team‑play stories. round 4: final HR/manager round (20 min) – salary discussion and campus‑fit questions. got the offer after a week.
preparation: did the Striver sheet for 2 months, solved daily LeetCode medium problems. practiced OA on a friend’s shared doc to get used to the interface. revised every line on my resume with seniors, especially the hackathon and mini‑project on IoT sensor network. watched a few GFG videos on recursion and linked lists.
experience: the OA was a bit repetitive but okay. technical interview was the toughest – the interviewer liked optimal O(N) solutions. HR rounds were chill, they asked about my college fest role. overall a decent mix.
advice: be ready to explain why you chose each project – TCS loves the story angle. keep your coding style clean, they read your screen.
tips: save a one‑pager of your achievements; it helps in HR rounds. practice the STAR method for behavioral Qs. CGPA 8.3 is good but don’t rely on it alone.

selection: round 1: referral screening – professor from my ML course emailed the admissions team, they set up a 20‑min Zoom to verify my research interest. round 2: interview (45 min) – 2 ML case studies (time‑series forecasting and image classification) plus a short discussion on my resume and why NUS. got the admission email a few days later.
preparation: tightened my ML fundamentals using the CS229 SPOC videos and did a couple of Kaggle micro‑projects for hands‑on practice. polished my resume with help from seniors who got into overseas masters before. rehearsed answering “why NUS” with a friend, and brushed up GRE vocab (though not mandatory).
experience: the referral call was super friendly, they just wanted to see genuine interest. the interview was technical but not too intense – they liked my Kaggle results and asked about feature engineering tricks. felt good overall.
advice: if you have a professor referral, mention specific labs or professors you want to work with. be ready to discuss any ML project in detail, especially the data pipeline.
tips: keep a one‑page summary of each ML project (dataset size, model used, accuracy boost). ask the interviewer about funding/scholarship options – shows seriousness. don’t forget to thank the referrer later!

selection: 5 rounds. Got shortlisted through a referral from a senior. First was an online test with 50 mcqs on mechanical engineering and aptitude. Then a group discussion with 4 others, we had to present a project on a robot arm. Next a technical interview with 2 questions on thermodynamics and fluid mechanics. Then a HR round. Final round was a case study on a manufacturing process. I was offered 10 LPA.
preparation: Revised all my mechanical engineering subjects, especially thermodynamics and fluid mechanics. Did a few projects on robotics and automation. Also did the striver sheet for DSA.
experience: The process was smooth, the spocs were helpful. The case study was a bit tough but I managed to do it.
advice: Prepare well for the online test and the group discussion. Also, have some projects ready to discuss.
tips: A referral can help a lot. Also, maintain a high CGPA.

selection: 2 rounds. Got shortlisted through a referral from a senior. First was a technical interview with questions on digital signal processing and communication systems. Then a HR round. I was offered admission to NUS.
preparation: Revised all my core subjects, especially digital signal processing and communication systems. Also did a few projects on image processing and machine learning.
experience: The process was smooth, the interviewers were friendly. I was offered admission to NUS.
advice: Prepare well for the technical interview. Also, have some projects ready to discuss.
tips: A referral can help a lot. Also, maintain a high CGPA.

selection: 2 rounds. Got shortlisted through a referral from a senior. First was a technical interview with questions on metallurgy and materials science. Then a HR round. I was offered 10 LPA.
preparation: Revised all my metallurgy and materials science subjects. Also did a few projects on metallurgy and materials science.
experience: The process was smooth, the interviewers were friendly. I was offered 10 LPA.
advice: Prepare well for the technical interview. Also, have some projects ready to discuss.
tips: A referral can help a lot. Also, maintain a high CGPA.

selection: 3 rounds. Got shortlisted through a referral from a senior. First was an online test with 3 coding questions. Then a technical interview with questions on computer networks and operating systems. Then a HR round. I was offered 20 LPA.
preparation: Did the striver sheet for DSA. Also revised computer networks and operating systems.
experience: The process was smooth, the interviewers were friendly. I was offered 20 LPA.
advice: Prepare well for the online test and the technical interview.
tips: A referral can help a lot. Also, maintain a high CGPA.

selection: 3 rounds. Got shortlisted through a referral from a senior. First was an online test with 3 coding questions and a few puzzles. Then a technical interview with questions on quant finance and statistics. Then a HR round. I was offered 10 LPA.
preparation: Did a few coding problems on leetcode. Also revised quant finance and statistics.
experience: The process was smooth, the interviewers were friendly. I was offered 10 LPA.
advice: Prepare well for the online test and the technical interview.
tips: A referral can help a lot. Also, maintain a high CGPA.

selection: TCS placement drive for Systems Engineer. Only 1 round: aptitude + coding test. Questions were basic aptitude, some OOPs MCQs, and a simple DBMS question. Cutoff was low, so even with 6.75 CGPA I cleared it easily.
preparation: didnt prep much, just brushed up on OOPs and DBMS from college notes. Aptitude was from indiabix and some random youtube videos.
experience: super chill round, no pressure. felt like a formality after the long wait.
advice: dont stress too much for tcs, its more about clearing the cutoff than actual skills.
tips: even if ur cgpa is low, u can still make it. just do basic prep and u r good.

selection: Walmart Global Tech placement for SWE. 5 rounds in 2 days, felt like a marathon. Round 1: OA with 3 DSA problems (2 medium, 1 hard). Round 2: DSA interview, a graph problem with union-find and some twists. Round 3: CN and OOPs round, asked about tcp/ip, osi model, and oops concepts. Round 4: resume deep dive, they asked about my projects and internships. Round 5: HR round, basic questions about relocation and why walmart.
preparation: solved striver sheet fully, then leetcode hard problems. CN from forouzan book and college notes. did mock interviews with seniors for 2 months.
experience: super intense, interviewers were professional but some were quiet. felt like i was in a pressure cooker.
advice: CN and OOPs can come even for SWE roles. know ur projects inside out.
tips: dont let rejections get to u. i got rejected 3 times before this. rest well between rounds.

selection: Deutsche Bank placement for SDE. 4 rounds in 2 days. Round 1: OA with 2 DSA problems and some resume-based questions. Round 2: DSA interview, a hard problem on trees and graphs. Round 3: resume round, they asked about my projects and internships. Round 4: HR round, basic questions about why DB and relocation.
preparation: revised DSA from striver sheet and leetcode. did mock interviews with seniors. read about DB's tech stack and projects.
experience: felt like a rollercoaster, some rounds were smooth, others were tough. interviewers were professional but some were not very interactive.
advice: DSA is key, but they also care about ur resume. be ready to explain everything on ur resume.
tips: CGPA was 7.67, but they also look for projects and internships. dont just rely on grades.

selection: ZS Associates placement for Business Analyst. 5 rounds in 2 days. Round 1: aptitude test with logical reasoning and quant. Round 2: ML basics test, some questions on regression and classification. Round 3: resume round, they asked about my projects and internships. Round 4: case study round, a business problem to solve. Round 5: HR round, basic questions about relocation and why ZS.
preparation: didnt prep much for aptitude, just practiced from indiabix. for ML, revised basics from andrew ng's course. did some case studies from youtube.
experience: felt like a mix of tech and business rounds. interviewers were professional but some rounds felt too random.
advice: be ready for anything in the resume round. they can ask about any project or internship.
tips: pay was high, but the work-life balance might not be great. think twice before joining.

selection: JP Morgan placement for Technology Analyst. 3 rounds in 2 days. Round 1: OA with 2 DSA problems and some puzzles. Round 2: DSA interview, a hard problem on dynamic programming and some puzzles. Round 3: HR round, basic questions about relocation and why JP Morgan.
preparation: revised DSA from striver sheet and leetcode. did some puzzles from geeksforgeeks. did mock interviews with seniors.
experience: felt like a pressure cooker, but interviewers were chill. some rounds were tough, but overall it was a good experience.
advice: DSA and puzzles are key. be ready for anything in the OA.
tips: CGPA was 8.76, but they also look for problem-solving skills. dont just rely on grades.

selection: round 1: an online aptitude test (quant, logical & a tiny bit of coding). round 2: a resume screening call where they asked about my Kaggle project and why data science. round 3: a final interview that felt like a PPO discussion – they talked about internship possibilities, gave me a small take‑home task and then offered a PPO on the spot.
preparation: did the Striver DSA sheet + Leetcode easy‑medium daily, solved a bunch of GFG data‑science practice problems, practiced aptitude on Indiabix and watched a few senior videos on resume building for DS roles. also brushed up on pandas & sklearn from my semester labs.
experience: first round was a breeze, second felt a bit formal but i managed to sell my project. the last interview was intense, they grilled me on model evaluation metrics and then surprised me with the PPO. mixed feelings – happy but also nervous about the internship load.
advice: show genuine interest in the data‑science pipeline, not just the hype. they love when u can explain a metric like f1‑score in plain words.
tips: don’t skip the resume call – it’s often a filter. keep 2‑3 bullet points ready about each project. practice quick mental math for aptitude, it saves time.

selection: r1: a timed aptitude test (quant + reasoning). r2: a technical round focused on basic C++/OOP concepts and a short coding snippet. r3: HR round where they asked about campus life, why Wipro and my long‑term goals. r4: a PPO talk – they offered an internship first and said full‑time after 3 months if things go well.
preparation: solved daily Leetcode easy problems, went through the Striver sheet for DSA, did a week of mock OA on HackerRank, and asked seniors for OOP interview experiences at Wipro. also skimmed up on company culture from Glassdoor.
experience: the aptitude was average, coding round was okay but i fumbled on a pointer question. HR was chill, they even asked about my cricket team. the PPO part was a pleasant surprise – got an intern slot before final offer.
advice: be ready to talk about why you chose a systems role at Wipro, they love specific examples from college labs.
tips: practice pointer basics and OOP fundamentals, they ask them a lot. keep your answers short in HR, they just want to see confidence.

selection: round 1: a computer‑networking (CN) quiz – 20 MCQs on OSI model, TCP/IP and basics of sockets. round 2: a project discussion where they dug deep into my college IoT project and asked me to design a data pipeline for image classification (DSA flavour).
preparation: re‑watched my networking lectures, solved GFG CN quizzes, and did a mini‑project on socket programming. brushed up DSA via Leetcode easy‑medium and read senior’s notes on project presentation. also read a few Nvidia research blogs to sound tech‑savvy.
experience: the CN round was surprisingly tough, i missed a question on ARP. the project chat was smoother – they liked the edge‑device data handling I described. overall felt like a good mix of theory and hands‑on.
advice: focus on the fundamentals of networking, especially layers and common protocols. they love when you can relate it to real‑world AI pipelines.
tips: prepare a 2‑minute pitch for any project, include challenges & how you solved them. quick revision of TCP handshakes helps a lot.

selection: r1: OOPs round – they asked me to design a class hierarchy for a banking system and discuss polymorphism. r2: a DSA coding round with a medium‑hard Leetcode style problem on graphs. r3: a system design style chat about scaling an ML inference service (they probed my knowledge of micro‑services). r4: HR round, typical fit‑questions and salary expectations. r5: PPO conversation – they told me about a 6‑month internship and a fast‑track to full‑time if I ace the project.
preparation: crammed OOP concepts from my semester notes, solved many OOP puzzles on CodeChef, practiced DSA with the Striver sheet and Leetcode (focus on graphs). did system design prep using Grokking the System Design Interview and watched senior’s mock sessions. also read up on Microsoft’s ML products.
experience: OOP round was okay, they liked my UML sketch. DSA was the toughest – I spent 30 mins on the graph problem but eventually solved it. system design felt like a chat, i managed to talk about load balancers. PPO was a nice bonus, but i’m still weighing the internship load.
advice: draw quick diagrams on the whiteboard for OOP and system design, it shows clarity. also be ready to discuss any ML project you claim to have done.
tips: keep a small cheat‑sheet of OOP principles (inheritance, composition) handy. practice graph traversals – they appear a lot in Microsoft rounds.

selection: round 1: an online OA (coding + a few system design MCQs) lasting 70 mins. round 2: a technical interview focused on system design – they asked me to design a scalable payment gateway. round 3: a coding deep‑dive where I solved a medium Leetcode problem on strings. round 4: a final HR round that turned into a brief PPO discussion – they offered a 3‑month internship before full‑time.
preparation: practised OA on HackerRank, solved similar coding+design mixes on Leetcode and System Design Primer. watched senior’s Intuit interview videos, read the Striver sheet for DSA, and brushed up on distributed systems basics from GFG. also did mock HR chats with friends.
experience: OA was decent, I cleared the coding part but missed a design MCQ. the system design interview was intense, I stumbled on caching strategies but recovered. coding round went smooth. HR was friendly, they hinted at the PPO which was unexpected.
advice: be clear about trade‑offs in system design, they love when u mention consistency vs availability. also show enthusiasm for fintech domain.
tips: time‑box each OA section, don’t get stuck on a single question. for design, have a ready template: requirements → high‑level architecture → components → bottlenecks.

selection: 1 round, online assessment (OA) with 50 questions in 60 minutes. The questions were a mix of aptitude and logical reasoning. The OA was non-eliminatory, and the results were announced after 3 days.
preparation: I used the Indiabix aptitude test series and solved 50-60 questions daily. I also practiced mock tests from the Indiabix website.
experience: The OA was straightforward, but I had to manage my time well. The SPOCs were helpful and guided me through the process.
advice: Start your preparation early and practice mock tests regularly. Be thorough with aptitude and logical reasoning questions.
tips: CGPA cutoffs are strict, so maintain a high CGPA. Be calm during the OA and manage your time well.

selection: Five rounds, mostly online. 1) Online assessment (OA) with 50 questions in 60 minutes. The questions were a mix of aptitude and logical reasoning. 2) Technical interview, 30 minutes. They asked about my intern project and some basic coding questions. 3) HR interview, 15 minutes. 4) Group discussion, 15 minutes. 5) Final interview, 20 minutes. The whole process was from morning to evening. Results were released after 5 days.
preparation: I used the Indiabix aptitude test series and solved 50-60 questions daily. I also practiced mock tests from the Indiabix website. For the technical interview, I revised my intern project and practiced basic coding questions.
experience: The process was long and tiring, but the SPOCs were helpful and guided me through the process. I had to manage my time well during the OA.
advice: Start your preparation early and practice mock tests regularly. Be thorough with aptitude and logical reasoning questions. Revise your intern project and practice basic coding questions.
tips: CGPA cutoffs are strict, so maintain a high CGPA. Be calm during the long process and eat something in between lol.

selection: 4 rounds total. first was an online OA on HackerRank (2 coding q's + a small OS theory part). second round was a system design chat where they asked me to design a simple pipelined VLSI block and talk about trade‑offs. third was a pure OS round – questions on process scheduling, memory paging and a quick whiteboard on deadlock detection. final was HR/fit where they probed my internship project on low‑power design and asked why I want a software‑heavy role in a VLSI team.
preparation: did leetcode medium‑hard for the coding q's, skimmed GFG OS notes and watched a couple of YouTube system‑design vids (especially "design a cache"). also revisited my VLSI class notes for the design round and asked a senior who interned at a fab for some pointers. used Striver's A2Z sheet for the basics.
experience: the OA felt ok, but the system‑design round was nerve‑racking – they expected a block diagram on a whiteboard. OS part was straight forward if you know the basics. HR was chill, they liked my project story. overall mixed vibes, but got the offer.
advice: don’t ignore the OS bits even if the role is VLSI – they love to test fundamentals. be ready with a quick sketch for design round, and have a clear story why you are shifting from pure hardware to a hybrid role.
tips: keep a one‑page cheat sheet of common OS algorithms & scheduling policies. practice drawing simple pipelines on paper. talk to seniors who interned at hardware firms – they can give you the exact kind of design questions they ask.

selection: 4 rounds. first was resume shortlisting (they screened on CGPA and a brief project line). second was a 30‑min aptitude test (verbal, numeric & basic coding MCQs). third was a technical interview – 2 DSA problems (linked‑list reversal & array rotation) plus a quick discussion on one of my EEE power‑converter project. final round was HR where they asked about why TCS, campus life and availability.
preparation: cracked a couple of aptitude books (quant and logical). brushed up leetcode easy‑medium and revisited my 3rd‑year EEE lab reports. asked a senior who did a TCS summer stint to share his interview flow. also read a few GFG articles on linked‑list basics.
experience: the aptitude test was kinda generic but time‑pressured. technical interview was decent – they didn’t go deep into circuits, just wanted to see problem‑solving. HR was friendly, a bit of small talk about movies. got the internship after 2 weeks.
advice: focus on clear communication for the project part – they love to hear the practical impact. keep your aptitude speed up; use mock tests.
tips: keep a 2‑minute pitch ready for every project you list. practice mental math tricks for numeric aptitude. a quick GFG refresh on common data‑structures helps a lot.

selection: 5 rounds. round‑1: online OA on HackerRank – 2 DSA coding q's (one array sliding window, one graph DFS) + a short aptitude section. round‑2: a pure DSA interview where they dug into recursion and DP (asked to count ways to climb stairs). round‑3: another aptitude round (verbal + puzzles). round‑4: technical interview focused on software basics – OOP concepts and a tiny Java coding on string manipulation. round‑5: HR/fit where they asked about my civil background, why software, and my 3‑month project on construction‑site monitoring app.
preparation: followed Striver's A2Z sheet for 2 weeks, solved medium leetcode problems daily, and did a GFG “DSA cheat sheet”. for aptitude, used a quant prep book and practiced puzzles from previous campus placements. brushed up OOP basics from a SPOC video. also rehearsed my civil‑to‑software story with seniors.
experience: OA was the hardest part – the graph problem had a hidden edge‑case. DSA interview felt fair, they liked my DP explanation. aptitude rounds were a bit repetitive. HR was the most interesting – they actually cared about my civil project and how I used sensors. overall tiring but rewarding.
advice: don’t skip the aptitude part even if you think you’re a coder – many companies still use it to filter. have a solid narrative on why you switched streams; it will come up in HR.
tips: keep a list of common DP patterns (stairs, knapsack, house‑robber) handy. practice speed‑solving graph problems on a timer. rehearse your project story in 1‑minute bursts.

selection: 4 rounds. round‑1: OA on Codility – 2 coding q's (one binary search, one array manipulation) and a short MCQ on OOP basics. round‑2: OOP interview – they asked me to design a simple class hierarchy for an image‑processing pipeline and discuss inheritance vs composition. round‑3: DSA interview – a medium‑hard problem on longest increasing subsequence and a quick whiteboard on hash‑maps. round‑4: HR where they talked about my ML coursework, why Adobe, and my expectations about remote work.
preparation: solved leetcode medium‑hard for the coding part, revisited my ML project notes, and watched a couple of OOP design videos on YouTube. used GFG to refresh hash‑map and binary‑search patterns. also read some Adobe blog posts to get a feel of their product culture. asked a senior who interned at Adobe for the exact OOP design they like.
experience: OA was smooth, time‑limit was generous. OOP round was the curveball – they wanted a clean class diagram on a whiteboard, which I hadn’t practiced much. DSA interview was fair, they liked my explanation of LIS DP. HR was relaxed, they even asked about my favorite Adobe app. got the offer after a week.
advice: practice drawing class diagrams quickly; even a rough sketch earns points. be ready to talk about any ML model you built – they love specifics.
tips: keep a one‑page cheat sheet of OOP principles (SOLID) and common design patterns. do at least one whiteboard design practice per week before the interview.

advice: Don’t ignore the networking part even if you’re a CS kid – they love to mix DSA with CN. stay calm, talk your thought process.
tips: check the eligibility cgpa cutoff early, but focus on solving at least one easy + one medium problem in the OA. keep a cheat‑sheet of common CN protocols.

selection: 5 rounds. round1: online test – 30 MCQs (aptitude + OS basics) and a short coding task on circular buffer. round2: technical phone – they dug into my past projects, especially the FPGA one, asked OS scheduling questions. round3: onsite coding – 2 DSA problems (one on segment tree, another on deadlock detection). round4: system design – design an embedded sensor network, they wanted OS level details. round5: HR – usual "why Nvidia?" and relocation talk. finally got the intern spot.
preparation: SPOC videos on OS concepts, GFG OS cheat‑sheet, Striver sheet for DSA (focus on segment trees, graphs). practiced project talks with seniors, mock design sessions on Discord. did a couple of OA on HackerRank for embedded topics.

advice: Show genuine excitement for hardware projects, and be ready to discuss OS scheduling and memory management. don’t just recite theory – give real examples from your labs.
tips: Keep a one‑pager of your projects ready, rehearse explaining them in <2 mins. practice deadlock detection problem a few times before the onsite.

selection: 2 rounds. round1: OA with 3 sections – 20 aptitude Qs, a mini‑case on a marketing ML model, and a coding problem on pandas data‑frame manipulation. selection: 4 rounds. round1: OA – 2 coding problems (one on recursion, another on OOP design) plus a short resume‑based questionnaire. round2: technical interview – they asked me to design a class hierarchy for an e‑commerce platform (OOPs) and then a quick live coding on binary search. round3: resume deep‑dive – senior asked about my data‑science project, metrics used, and a couple of stats questions. round4: HR – relocation, stipend, and culture fit. got the intern offer.
