selection: 4 rounds: (1) online aptitude test (quant + logical puzzles, 30 min), (2) a 45‑min ML case‑study where we had to suggest a data‑pipeline for churn prediction, (3) a coding OA on Hackerearth (2 DSA questions – one greedy, one array‑manipulation) and (4) HR/fit interview where they asked about my Kaggle projects and why I want to work in analytics. cleared all, got the internship.
preparation: Did the Striver A‑to‑Z sheet for DSA, solved ~150 LeetCode easy/medium, brushed up ML basics from Andrew Ng SPOC, practiced GFG ML‑case questions and solved a bunch of aptitude mock tests from PrepInsta. My seniors gave me a quick resume review and shared their Mu Sigma interview notes.
experience: The aptitude was a bit tricky but manageable. The ML case felt like a mini‑project – had to talk about feature engineering, I was a bit nervous but the panel was friendly. OA was smooth; I finished both questions in time. HR was chill, just asked about campus life.
advice: Don’t ignore the non‑coding part – they really care about how you frame a data problem. Be ready to explain any ML project you list, even the tiny ones.
tips: Keep a one‑pager of your ML projects ready, practice explaining them in <2 mins. Do timed aptitude drills, and rehearse the STAR format for HR.

selection: 4 rounds: (1) online coding test on Codility – 2 DSA problems (one graph traversal, one DP) + a short DBMS query question, (2) technical interview focused on my past ML projects and a design question on data pipelines, (3) a system design round where we built a simple recommendation engine, (4) HR round discussing culture fit and internship logistics. All cleared, landed the ML Engineer internship.
preparation: Cranked up LeetCode (300+ problems, especially graphs & DP) and did Striver’s sheet for the last 2 weeks. For DBMS revisited GFG SQL basics and solved a few HackerRank queries. Spent evenings on Coursera’s ML specialization and re‑watched my senior’s Intuit project demo. Also did mock interviews on Pramp with seniors.
experience: Coding test was tight – I spent 10 mins on the DP question and still got it right. The project interview was intense; they dug deep into my Kaggle model, so I had to recall hyper‑parameter tuning steps. System design felt more like a brainstorming session, which was fun. HR was super casual.
advice: Show genuine curiosity about the product they are building. Even if you’re not an expert in a specific ML algorithm, explain your thought process clearly.
tips: Keep a short bullet list of all ML tools you used (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit‑learn) ready to drop. Practice writing quick SQL queries on paper. Do at least one mock design interview before the real thing.

selection: 5 rounds: (1) online OA on HackerRank – 3 coding problems (arrays, strings, and a medium‑hard greedy), plus 20 aptitude questions, (2) technical interview covering core CSE subjects – OOP concepts, OS basics and a DBMS query, (3) a second technical round with a mini‑case on cloud migration, (4) HR round asking about strengths, weakness and campus placements, (5) final managerial round focusing on team‑fit and communication. Got the offer for Technology Consultant.
preparation: Followed Striver’s sheet for DSA, solved 200+ LeetCode easy/medium, and brushed up OS and DBMS from NPTEL videos. Did daily aptitude drills on IndiaBix. Asked three seniors who cleared Accenture for their OA screenshots and used GFG for quick revivals. Also read a few blog posts on consulting case basics.
experience: OA was the toughest part – time pressure made me skip the last problem. Technical interview was decent; they asked me to explain page replacement algorithms, which I remembered from my OS class. HR was generic, but the manager asked about why consulting and I fumbled a bit.
advice: Don’t rely only on coding – Accenture loves core subject knowledge. Be ready to discuss a simple real‑world case, even if you’ve never done consulting before.
tips: Make a one‑page cheat sheet of OS, DBMS, OOP basics. Practice coding under 30‑minute timers. For HR, prepare 3–4 short stories using STAR.

selection: 5 rounds: (1) resume screening – got called after senior referral, (2) technical interview on Mechanical design – asked to sketch a simple gearbox and discuss material selection, (3) project discussion – I presented my final year CAD project and answered heat‑transfer questions, (4) HR round covering campus policies and bond, (5) final fit interview with a senior manager where they probed teamwork experiences. Received the Design Engineer offer.
preparation: Spent a week revising core Mechanical subjects (strength of materials, thermodynamics) from my semester notes, and practiced GD&T on SolidWorks tutorials. Went through GFG’s Mechanical interview questions and asked my batch‑mate who interned at L&T for mock interview. Updated resume with bullet points highlighting CAD work and used a senior to proofread it.
experience: The resume call was quick thanks to the referral. Technical interview was intense – they drew a diagram on the whiteboard and expected me to explain torque calculations on the spot. Project talk went well because I had a short video ready. HR was just about bond duration, nothing special.
advice: Show confidence when sketching on the board – even if you’re not 100% sure, explain your assumptions. Also, be clear about your availability for the bond period.
tips: Carry a small notebook to quickly jot down formulas during the interview. Have a 2‑minute video of your CAD project ready to share. Practice explaining design choices in layman terms.

selection: 1 round: a single OA on CodeSignal – 2 DSA questions (one linked‑list manipulation, one combinatorial math) and a short networking concept quiz. I cleared it and got the SDE internship at Cisco.

Watched a few GFG videos on OS networking basics because the quiz had a question on TCP three‑way handshake. Did a mock OA on CodeSignal with a friend to get used to the interface.
experience: The OA was straightforward; I finished both coding questions in 18 minutes and got full marks. The networking quiz was easy – just a recall of OSI layers. Got the mail the same day, which felt awesome.
advice: Even if it’s a single round, treat it like a full interview – time yourself and double‑check edge cases.
tips: Keep a cheat‑sheet of common DSA patterns (two‑pointer, sliding window). Practice on the exact platform (CodeSignal/CodeChef) to avoid surprise UI issues.

selection: Round 1 was a timed aptitude test on the portal (basic maths, logical reasoning and a couple of puzzles). Round 3 was a short technical interview – they asked me about my data‑analysis project and threw a couple of SQL queries. Finally Round 4 was an HR chat where they checked my CGPA, asked why I wanted a Mumbai internship and if I could join full‑time later.
preparation: I brushed up on aptitude from GFG, solved the Striver DSA sheet for arrays and strings, and did a couple of mock OAs on HackerRank. My seniors gave me their old OA pdfs and I also watched a SPOC on basic C++ I/O tricks.
experience: Overall smooth, except the OA server lagged a bit. The interview panel was friendly, but the HR guy sounded like a robot. Pay 56 LPA is decent for a 1‑yr stint, and the Mumbai vibe was a plus.
advice: The OA could use clearer constraints and a test‑case for edge values. Also, a brief intro about the analyst role in the HR round would help candidates align expectations.
tips: Start practising aptitude early, keep a cheat‑sheet of common pattern problems, and rehearse a 2‑min pitch about your project. Don’t forget to test your internet before the OA!

selection: Round 1 – referral call: my senior who works there gave me a quick phone chat, checked my CGPA (8.4+) and asked why I was shifting from ECE to software. Round 2 – a 45‑minute HR interview where they discussed my internships, salary expectations and the campus culture in Hyderabad. Round 3 – a final technical interview with a senior SDE, who gave me a medium‑level LeetCode problem on trees and a short design question about a notification system.
preparation: Since it was a referral, I focused on polishing my DSA on LeetCode (medium tags) and revisited OOP concepts from my 3rd‑year SPOCs. I also read up on Salesforce products from their Trailhead community and asked a senior for mock HR questions.
experience: The referral call was super chill, but the HR round felt a bit generic. The technical interview was tough – they expected an optimal O(log n) solution for the tree problem, which I barely managed. The offer of 101 LPA was amazing though.
advice: HR could dig deeper into why ECE students want to code – a quick note on your coding journey would make the chat smoother. Also, share a couple of real‑world project outcomes in the technical round.
tips: If you have a referral, treat the first call as a warm‑up, not a free pass. Keep a one‑pager of your projects ready, and practice explaining them in <2 mins. LeetCode medium + a quick design prep is enough.

selection: Round 1 – online coding test (DSA + DBMS). They gave a SQL join problem and a graph traversal question. Round 2 – a technical interview focusing on VLSI concepts: layout design, timing analysis and a mini‑design on a flip‑flop. Round 3 – HR discussion where they asked about my ML coursework, why I applied to Salesforce and my future plans.
preparation: I solved DBMS queries from GFG, brushed up on graph algorithms via the Striver sheet, and revisited VLSI notes from my 4th‑year labs. A senior who interned there shared his interview questions, and I watched a couple of ML SPOCs to be ready for the HR talk.
experience: The OA was a bit flaky – the SQL editor crashed once. The VLSI interview was intense, they expected me to draw timing diagrams on a virtual whiteboard. HR was pleasant and even asked about my recent ML project. The stipend of 117 LPA is huge for a VLSI intern.
advice: Fix the OA platform stability and give a clear time‑limit for the SQL part. In the VLSI round, allow candidates to use a sketch pad or share a PDF of their diagram instead of drawing on a whiteboard.
tips: Practice a mix of DSA and DBMS – LeetCode for graphs, GFG for SQL. Keep a concise VLSI cheat‑sheet (timing, layout rules). And be ready to talk ML – even a 2‑line summary can impress HR.

selection: Round 1 – a 30‑minute online coding test (DSA). I solved a two‑pointer array problem and a basic DP question. Round 2 – a technical interview with a senior engineer: they asked about my final‑year project (machine‑learning based image classifier) and threw a medium‑level ML question on overfitting. Round 3 – HR round where they discussed the Bangalore office vibe, CTC, and my long‑term goals.
preparation: I went through the Striver DSA sheet, especially arrays and DP, and practiced ML basics on Coursera SPOCs. I also solved a few Kaggle micro‑projects to speak about during the interview. Seniors helped me with mock HR questions and gave feedback on my project demo.
experience: The coding test was straightforward, but the interview panel was a bit aggressive on the ML part – they wanted me to explain bias‑variance trade‑off in under a minute. HR was friendly and gave a clear picture of the role. Offer of 57.7 LPA for a full‑time position felt fair.
advice: Technical interview could be balanced – give candidates a bit more time for the ML question. Also, share some sample projects beforehand so candidates know what depth to expect.
tips: Do the Striver sheet, but also revise core ML concepts (cross‑validation, regularisation). Have a 2‑minute elevator pitch of your project ready. Practice coding on a plain editor to avoid surprises in the OA.

selection: Round 1 – an online assessment (OA) with 2 sections: a coding problem on OOP (inheritance hierarchy) and a short OS question on deadlock detection. Round 2 – a project‑based interview where they asked me to walk through my data‑science internship and the models I built. Round 3 – a technical interview on algorithms, they gave a medium LeetCode problem on heaps. Round 4 – a system design chat about building a recommendation pipeline. Round 5 – HR round covering salary, relocation to Pune and my future plans.
preparation: I solved OOP and OS questions from GFG, did the Striver DSA sheet for heaps and priority queues, and refreshed my DS project details. I also went through a few Uber‑specific data‑science case studies shared by seniors and practiced mock interviews on Pramp.
experience: The OA was a bit glitchy on the coding editor, but manageable. The project interview was the best part – they loved the details of my Kaggle competition. The system design round was surprisingly deep for an internship. HR was crisp and gave a clear offer of 95 LPA.
advice: Stabilise the OA platform and maybe give a sample OOP problem beforehand. In the system design round, guide candidates on the expected depth for an intern level – a high‑level flow is enough.
tips: Mix DSA practice (heaps, trees) with OS fundamentals. Keep a one‑page summary of your projects (datasets, models, metrics). Do a quick mock system design with a friend – focus on data flow, not micro‑optimisation.

selection: 4 rounds only, no OA. Shortlisting was by resume and CGPA. Round 1 was technical, 1 hr. First 20 mins was pure probability and puzzles: 100 doors, two eggs from a tall building, expected tosses to get two heads in a row. Then 2 DSA questions, an LRU cache and a medium tree one (lowest common ancestor type). He wanted optimal solution plus complexity for each. Round 2 was a case study, 45 mins, asked about my time series forecasting project and how i would approach a real world problem. Round 3 was HR, 30 mins, asked why quant, about my time series forecasting project, and if i was fine relocating to Chennai. Round 4 was a fit round with a senior person, asked about my background, why quant, how i handle pressure, a time i failed. They also tested mental math a bit, like multiply two 2 digit numbers fast. Result came after 2 days.
preparation: Mostly leetcode (150 or so questions), and a probability book that a senior lent me for puzzles. Revised conditional probability and expectation from the stats course. Also practiced explaining solutions out loud. Did a case study on a real world problem and practiced explaining it out loud.
experience: Interviewer was friendly and gave hints when I got stuck on the eggs puzzle. Overall nice.
advice: Puzzles are not a joke here, practice atleast 30-40 of them. Also say ur thinking aloud, they care more about approach than the final number. Do a case study on a real world problem and practice explaining it out loud.
tips: AI branch folks, dont only do ML projects, DSA and probability matter a lot for quant type roles. Dont panic if u get rejected in the first few companies, our season is long.

selection: Round 1: online test with 2 sections - aptitude (easy) and technical (chemistry basics + 1 coding question on arrays). Round 2: group discussion on a case study (design a water treatment plant). Round 3: HR round, discussed my PPO from last summer, why Bosch, and relocation.

selection: round 1 was an online OA (2 coding problems on arrays & strings, plus 5 MCQs on basic SQL/DBMS concepts). round 2 was a technical interview where they dug into my DBMS project, asked about normalization and some DSA like binary search. round 3 was a short HR chat, they asked about why Infosys and my future plans. round 4 was a manager round, more behavioural, they wanted to know how i handle deadlines and team conflicts.
preparation: i did ~250 leetcode easy/medium, followed the striver dsa sheet, brushed up GFG DBMS notes, solved a few Infosys OA mocks from geeksforgeeks, watched NPTEL DBMS SPOC videos and asked seniors for last year question banks.

tips: keep your CGPA decent (7.5+ helps), but a solid resume with projects can offset it. practice speaking your thought process out loud while coding.

selection: round 1 was a puzzlers test – 10 logical puzzles on an online portal, time‑bound. round 2 was a pure aptitude paper (quant + verbal, 40 q in 45 min). round 3 was the OA where they gave 2 coding problems (one array, one greedy) and a short case‑study question. round 4 was the final HR/fit interview, they asked about why ZS, my teamwork stories and a few brain‑teasers.
preparation: i solved daily puzzles on brainzilla, did aptitude practice from previous ZS batches, did 300 leetcode problems (focus on arrays & greedy), used the striver sheet for fast DSA, and watched a couple of ZS OA walkthrough videos on YouTube. seniors helped me with the case‑study prep.
experience: the puzzle round was weird but fun, aptitude was standard. OA was tough because of the case‑study, but the interviewers were supportive. HR felt a bit generic but okay. got the offer, felt relieved.
advice: don't ignore the puzzlers – they test logical thinking. time‑manage the aptitude section, and for OA practice both coding and quick business case analysis.

selection: just one round – a face‑to‑face interview where the recruiter went through my resume, asked me to explain my final year ECE project and threw a couple of core questions on analog circuits and signal processing.
preparation: re‑read my project report, revisited core ECE notes from NPTEL SPOCs, brushed up basic circuit theory from GFG, and asked a senior who cleared HUL last year for interview tips.

advice: be ready to talk in depth about any project you put on your resume. core subject basics can pop up even for a marketing/GET role.

selection: round 1: OA with 2 coding problems (linked list & DP) and 6 MCQs on basic aptitude. round 2: a separate aptitude test (quant + logical reasoning, 30 q). round 3: technical interview focusing on DSA – they gave a tree traversal problem and asked about time‑complexity. round 4: HR round – standard behavioural questions and why TCS. round 5: final manager round – they discussed team fit, project expectations and salary negotiation.

selection: Amazon placement for Software Engineer, 5 rounds. R1: resume screening. R2: online assessment with 3 DSA qs. R3: technical interview with 2 DSA qs and 1 ML qs. R4: manager interview with 2 DSA qs and 1 ML qs. R5: HR.

selection: EY Mechanical Analyst placement. PPO route, no extra rounds. They came for internship and converted to PPO based on internship performance. Internship was 2 months in Gurgaon office.

selection: L&T Design Engineer placement for EEE. One round: written test on aptitude + core subjects (networks, control systems, power systems). 90 mins, 80 questions. Result came in 5 days.
